A quantitative descriptive survey design was used, involving 418 mothers selected through multistage sampling. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire and analysed with descriptive statistics and chi-square tests. Mothers reported measles and pertussis as prevalent diseases, with a pooled response rate of 9.1%. They also held moderately positive beliefs about immunisation and perceived sociodemographic factors as linked to disease occurrence. The study suggests that these factors are influential in shaping perceptions of vaccine-preventable disease burden. The findings can inform public health strategies to address vaccine hesitancy and improve immunisation rates. However, the reliance on self-reported data introduces potential bias, limiting the strength of the evidence.

papers.abstract_zh: 背景:本研究调查了尼日利亚夸拉州伊洛林西部地方政府区五岁以下儿童中母亲对 疫苗 可预防疾病 (VPD) 的感知和自我报告的 患病率,以及她们感知到的 VPD 发生的社会文化和社会人口决定因素。方法:对伊洛林西部地方政府地区居住的五岁以下儿童的母亲采用了定量描述性调查设计。采用分层、简单随机抽样和系统随机抽样的多阶段抽样程序选择了 418 名受访者。使用研究人员结构化调查问卷来收集数据。使用描述性统计和 0.05 alpha 水平的卡方检验对数据进行分析。结果:母亲们报告,疫苗 可预防疾病,主要是 麻疹 (21.3%) 和百日咳 (16.3%),被认为在她们的孩子中流行,七种疾病项目的汇总肯定反应率为 9.1%。母亲们还持有适度积极的有利于免疫接种的社会文化信仰、态度和做法(总体平均值 = 2.68/4.00),并认为社会人口因素,特别是母亲教育、家庭收入和产前护理就诊率(总体平均值 = 2.76/4.00),与 VPD 的发生有关。结论:社会文化和社会人口因素仍然具有影响力,是夸拉州伊洛林西地方政府地区 疫苗 可预防疾病负担的决定因素。

analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果可以为有针对性的公共卫生干预措施提供信息,以解决 疫苗 犹豫不决的问题,并提高伊洛林西部地方政府地区的免疫覆盖率,特别是通过解决社会人口和文化障碍。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究基于自我报告的数据和看法,这可能会引入偏见。由于依赖于调查数据而不是直接的生物学或临床测量,证据的强度中等。

analysis.brief_en: On November 17, 2026, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) issued a call to action for countries in the Americas to intensify their efforts in stopping measles outbreaks and moving towards elimination. The report highlights the ongoing challenges posed by measles in the region, emphasizing the need for improved prevention and control measures. While the document does not provide specific confirmed cases, deaths, or exposure numbers, it underscores the risk of continued spread and the importance of addressing public health priorities. PAHO's initiative focuses on strengthening health systems and promoting comprehensive immunization strategies to combat the disease. The report serves as a reminder of the critical role of international cooperation in managing infectious diseases like measles. No detailed data on the scale of the outbreak or specific interventions are included, leaving the situation as a general call for action rather than a confirmed event.

Give to MUSC arrow_forward MUSC Children's Health Hollings Cancer Center Careers Giving MUSC Education Health Research With U.S. loss of measles elimination status, here’s what virus expert wants you to know By Helen Adams Nov. 20, 2026 Share The child’s cheek shows the characteristic rash associated with measles. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention This is not a moment that Scott Curry, M.D., at MUSC Health, would have predicted earlier in his career as an infectious diseases specialist. “The idea that we would have an almost thousand-patient outbreak in South Carolina or anywhere else in the U.S. was once unthinkable to me.” Curry’s comment comes as the United States loses its measles elimination status – a decision by the Pan American Health Organization. The U.S. failed, for the first time in more than a quarter century, to go 12 months or longer without locally transmitted measles infections or outbreaks. I think people should have an appropriate level of concern. South Carolina was part of the problem, with an outbreak mostly affecting Spartanburg County. That outbreak ended in April. But concerns linger about the virus’s reemergence here and across the country. “I think people should have an appropriate level of concern,” Curry said. “It’s super contagious. Pretty much, apart from norovirus in a school or on a cruise ship, measles is the winner for how many other people can get sick if you’re mixing it up in an unvaccinated crowd.” Measles’ effects Symptoms of measles include a fever as high as 105 degrees, fatigue, nasal congestion, pink eye and a rash. The rash usually shows up about two weeks after a person is exposed to measles. Kids under 5, adults over 20, pregnant women and people with weakened immune systems are at higher risk for complications. “One in 1,000 kids with measles is going to die, and about 1 in 10 will get pneumonia, encephalitis or something else that lands them in a hospital,” Curry said. Dr. Scott Curry “We know there are other bad downstream side effects. The scariest is subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, or SSPE, which is this thing where you get a mild case of measles, get better and then you die from an incurable neurological condition up to 30 years later. There’s no treatment for SSPE. You just recognize that it’s an aftereffect of a measles case.” Measles can also lead to deafness and immune amnesia, Curry said. “That’s where you get over measles, but you’re susceptible to other known infectious diseases for a period of months to years afterward. You’re at risk of bacterial infections, including ones that can be fatal, like meningitis and pneumonia, for a long period after measles recovery.” Prevention So taking steps to keep from getting measles is important, Curry said. “As an infectious diseases specialist, I recommend having two good modern vaccine doses. If you had one shot back in the early '60s, you didn’t get a very good version of the measles vaccine, and you really should get a second dose. Back when we had eliminated measles in the U.S., it was kind of a low priority to worry about that. But if you really want to be fully protected, you should have two doses of MMR.” MMR stands for measles, mumps and rubella, a vaccine protecting you from all three conditions. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says getting the MMR shot “is much safer than getting measles.” If you’re not sure if you’ve had two doses of it, Curry suggested asking your doctor to help you find out. “If you did get two doses, your risk of getting measles is crazy low. But I’m worried about the unvaccinated group.” That includes people who can’t get the measles vaccine for health reasons. “I can’t give it to people who have uncontrolled HIV or if they’re on certain biologic medicines that are commonly used nowadays for managing rheumatoid arthritis, sarcoidosis and other autoimmune diseases. Those folks just cannot have a live virus vaccine. And there is no alternative vaccine or prophylaxis,” Curry said. Immune-suppressed patients have to rely on others getting vaccinated, also known as herd immunity, while trying to minimize their exposure to measles and keeping an eye out for symptoms. What healthcare providers are doing in the current environment The reemergence of measles means a few things for healthcare providers, too, Curry said. “The biggest impact is to family medicine and pediatrics physicians who have never seen a case of this because vaccines were so successful. Now we have to remember to get the vaccine history whenever you see fever and a rash.” They also need to be ready to test for measles when appropriate, Curry said. “It’s become a lot easier to order the test. But I never thought I’d have to maintain system readiness to test for measles.” Measles’ contagiousness can also make things challenging for doctors’ offices. “If you're managing things like a pediatrics urgent care or pediatrics office, how do you safely see somebody who may have measles? They need to learn the logistics of seeing and testing sick kids in their cars, which, as we’ve learned, is doable – but not easy.” MUSC News + Infectious Diseases Share Meet the Author Helen Adams Recent MUSC News stories MUSC News + Wellness Gratitude during holidays and beyond can have real health benefits MUSC News + Primary Care When healthcare meets you where you are Breast Cancer + Cancer Patient Journeys Through breast cancer treatment, she kept moving forward See All MUSC News Stories

analysis.location_and_population: United States, South Carolina, Spartanburg County.
analysis.event: The United States has lost its measles elimination status, with a significant outbreak in South Carolina, raising concerns about the virus's reemergence.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: An outbreak in South Carolina affected over 1,000 patients, with measles being highly contagious and leading to complications such as pneumonia, encephalitis, and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis. The risk is particularly high for children under 5, adults over 20, pregnant women, and those with weakened immune systems.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Healthcare providers are adapting to the reemergence of measles by maintaining system readiness to test for the virus and ensuring vaccination history is recorded. The status is under investigation, with ongoing efforts to prevent further spread through vaccination and herd immunity.

analysis.brief_en: The United States has lost its measles elimination status due to a significant outbreak in South Carolina, affecting over 1,000 patients. Measles is highly contagious and can lead to severe complications like pneumonia and encephalitis. Healthcare providers are adapting by maintaining readiness to test for the virus and ensuring vaccination history is recorded. The risk is particularly high for children under 5, adults over 20, pregnant women, and those with weakened immune systems.
analysis.summary_en: The United States has lost its measles elimination status due to a significant outbreak in South Carolina, affecting over 1,000 patients. Measles is highly contagious and can lead to severe complications like pneumonia and encephalitis. Healthcare providers are adapting by maintaining readiness to test for the virus and ensuring vaccination history is recorded. The risk is particularly high for children under 5, adults over 20, pregnant women, and those with weakened immune systems.

news.content_title: How dangerous is a measles outbreak?
news.content: Skip to main content Patients & Visitors Research & Clinical Trials For Clinicians Health & Science News Careers Give MyChart Comer Children's Hospital MyChart Find a Doctor Find a Location Conditions & Services Patients & Visitors Research & Clinical Trials For Clinicians Health & Science News Careers Give MyChart Comer Children's Hospital Search Virtual urgent care, 24/7 — wherever you are Home Forefront Pediatrics How dangerous is a measles outbreak? Measles is a highly contagious and potentially dangerous disease, but it is preventable with vaccination. A coordinated effort to vaccinate children with the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine led to the elimination of measles in the U.S. in 2000. But measles cases have increased in recent years, fueled in part by vaccine misinformation and declining vaccination rates in some communities. On November 17, the United States lost its measles elimination status, the Pan American Health Organization announced. The designation was withdrawn because measles has continued to spread in the country for more than a year. As of mid-November 2026, the U.S. had reported: More than 5,400 measles cases in 2026 Ten measles-related deaths in 2026 2,289 cases in all of 2025 285 cases in 2024 The 2026 total is more than double the number of cases reported in all of 2025, according to public health statistics, highlighting the sharp acceleration of measles infections. As an infectious diseases specialist at UChicago Medicine, I want to share important facts about measles prevention that can help keep you and your loved ones safe. What is measles — and what are the symptoms and complications? Measles is an infection caused by a virus that primarily affects unvaccinated children and nonimmunized adults. Symptoms of measles include fever, cough, runny nose, rash and red eyes ("pink eye," or conjunctivitis), and they typically show up eight to 12 days after initial exposure to the virus. The characteristic measles rash appears three to five days after the first symptoms appear. Additional complications, such as ear infections, pneumonia and diarrhea, can occur. A serious complication of measles is acute encephalitis, or inflammation of the brain, which can result in permanent brain damage in one of every 1,000 cases. In the U.S., death from neurologic or respiratory complications of measles occurs in one to three of every 1,000 cases. In addition, there is a late-onset complication called subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE). This rare, degenerative and fatal central nervous system disease can occur seven to 11 years after a primary measles infection, with the highest rates seen in children infected before 2 years of age. How contagious is measles and how long is a person contagious? Measles is one of the most highly communicable infections. It’s spread through direct contact with infectious droplets or through the air. Patients with a measles infection are contagious from four days before the rash through four days after the rash appears. If you are not vaccinated or immune, there is a 9 in 10 chance you’ll get sick if you’re exposed — even from sharing the same air, briefly or hours later, with someone who has measles. How effective is the measles vaccine? Can I get the measles if I’ve been vaccinated? More than 97% of people who receive two doses of the MMR vaccine develop immunity to measles. The second dose of the vaccine protects those who fail to respond to their primary dose. While it is possible to contract measles after two doses of the vaccine, it is very uncommon. Importantly, immunization is not harmful to those with established measles immunity and immunized persons do not transmit measles vaccine virus. When should children get vaccinated for measles? Children should be vaccinated after their first birthday and receive an additional dose of MMR vaccine before entering kindergarten (when they’re 4 to 6 years old). The second dose provides additional protection to the approximately 5% of people who do not respond to their first dose. Given the risk of measles associated with international travel, a first dose can be given as early as 6 months of age for infants who will be traveling abroad. This does not, however, replace the need for additional MMR doses administered at the traditional timepoints of over 1 year of age and 4 to 6 years of age. Find a Pediatrician Should adults get vaccinated for measles? Adults are considered immune to measles if they have documentation of at least one dose of MMR vaccine on or after their first birthday, documentation of two doses of MMR vaccine for individuals at high risk, laboratory evidence of measles immunity, laboratory confirmation of measles infection, or birth before 1957. Adults who do not meet these criteria should be vaccinated with at least two doses of the MMR vaccine — unless their physician recommends against it due to special circumstances, such as severely compromised immunity. During measles outbreaks, health departments may provide additional recommendations to protect their communities, including a second dose of MMR for adults who have received only one dose previously. Currently, a third dose of MMR vaccine during measles outbreaks is not recommended. Find a Primary Care Provider How dangerous is measles? Fortunately, for most people, measles is not life-threatening — but the problem is that you can't predict who will become seriously ill. Three in 1,000 people who contract measles will die. For those who are vulnerable due to preexisting conditions that impact their immune system, measles can be even more dangerous. However, if everyone is vaccinated, no one will die. Before the vaccine, there were up to 500 U.S. deaths each year from measles, and now it's completely preventable. With vaccine-preventable illnesses, most people don't get sick, but that doesn’t mean it’s smart to forego the vaccine. Why take the risk when the protection is safe and effective? Should vitamin A and cod liver oil be used to prevent measles infection? The only way to prevent measles is with the MMR vaccine. Vitamin A does not prevent measles, and in high doses, it can lead to toxic side effects such as nausea, vomiting, headache, blurred vision, liver damage and coma. Treatment with once-daily vitamin A for two days is recommended for those with an established diagnosis of a measles infection to help the illness from becoming more severe. Cod liver oil contains high amounts of vitamin A, vitamin D and fatty acids, which can be harmful if intake exceeds the recommended daily amount; it should not be administered to prevent measles infection. Should I be worried if measles is found in my community? Community outbreaks of measles should always be taken seriously. Even when overall vaccination rates are robust, outbreaks can still spread among certain populations, such as people who are immunocompromised or live in under-vaccinated areas. Some environments also pose more risks. If a patient with measles arrives in the emergency department of a hospital, for example, the illness would have to be quickly identified and the patient placed in isolation to keep the virus from spreading rapidly to other sick individuals. Everyone has a responsibility to take precautions to avoid the virus and to ensure their vaccinations are up-to-date to protect themselves and their neighbors. What should I do if I’m exposed to measles or think I may have measles? Measles is highly contagious, and you can be infectious prior to developing symptoms. Be extremely cautious in the event of a possible exposure. Wear a mask and isolate from others Contact your doctor immediately if you believe you have been exposed Contact your care team via MyChart Your care team can help determine if you are at risk of contracting the virus. For the unvaccinated, getting the MMR vaccine or an injection of immune globulin may reduce the risk of illness. If you or your child are fully vaccinated (two doses of MMR vaccine), monitor for symptoms for at least 21 days and call your provider immediately if you or your child begin to experience any symptoms. Do not go into a healthcare facility without calling ahead to ensure that you do not put other patients at risk. Where can I find additional information about measles? Among these, 5,394 measles cases were reported by 47 jurisdictions: Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, District of Columbia, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York City, New York State, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, West Virginia, Wisconsin, and Wyoming. A total of 18 measles cases were reported among international visitors to the United States. There have been 43 new outbreaks reported in 2026, and 96% of confirmed cases (5,216 of 5,412) are outbreak-associated (3,831 from outbreaks starting in 2026 and 1,385 from outbreaks that started in 2025). news.content_original: Skip to main content Patients & Visitors Research & Clinical Trials For Clinicians Health & Science News Careers Give MyChart Comer Children's Hospital MyChart Find a Doctor Find a Location Conditions & Services Patients & Visitors Research & Clinical Trials For Clinicians Health & Science News Careers Give MyChart Comer Children's Hospital Search Virtual urgent care, 24/7 — wherever you are Home Forefront Pediatrics How dangerous is a measles outbreak? Measles is a highly contagious and potentially dangerous disease, but it is preventable with vaccination. A coordinated effort to vaccinate children with the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine led to the elimination of measles in the U.S. in 2000. But measles cases have increased in recent years, fueled in part by vaccine misinformation and declining vaccination rates in some communities. On November 17, the United States lost its measles elimination status, the Pan American Health Organization announced. The designation was withdrawn because measles has continued to spread in the country for more than a year. As of mid-November 2026, the U.S. had reported: More than 5,400 measles cases in 2026 Ten measles-related deaths in 2026 2,289 cases in all of 2025 285 cases in 2024 The 2026 total is more than double the number of cases reported in all of 2025, according to public health statistics, highlighting the sharp acceleration of measles infections. As an infectious diseases specialist at UChicago Medicine, I want to share important facts about measles prevention that can help keep you and your loved ones safe. What is measles — and what are the symptoms and complications? Measles is an infection caused by a virus that primarily affects unvaccinated children and nonimmunized adults. Symptoms of measles include fever, cough, runny nose, rash and red eyes ("pink eye," or conjunctivitis), and they typically show up eight to 12 days after initial exposure to the virus. The characteristic measles rash appears three to five days after the first symptoms appear. Additional complications, such as ear infections, pneumonia and diarrhea, can occur. A serious complication of measles is acute encephalitis, or inflammation of the brain, which can result in permanent brain damage in one of every 1,000 cases. In the U.S., death from neurologic or respiratory complications of measles occurs in one to three of every 1,000 cases. In addition, there is a late-onset complication called subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE). This rare, degenerative and fatal central nervous system disease can occur seven to 11 years after a primary measles infection, with the highest rates seen in children infected before 2 years of age. How contagious is measles and how long is a person contagious? Measles is one of the most highly communicable infections. It’s spread through direct contact with infectious droplets or through the air. Patients with a measles infection are contagious from four days before the rash through four days after the rash appears. If you are not vaccinated or immune, there is a 9 in 10 chance you’ll get sick if you’re exposed — even from sharing the same air, briefly or hours later, with someone who has measles. How effective is the measles vaccine? Can I get the measles if I’ve been vaccinated? More than 97% of people who receive two doses of the MMR vaccine develop immunity to measles. The second dose of the vaccine protects those who fail to respond to their primary dose. While it is possible to contract measles after two doses of the vaccine, it is very uncommon. Importantly, immunization is not harmful to those with established measles immunity and immunized persons do not transmit measles vaccine virus. When should children get vaccinated for measles? Children should be vaccinated after their first birthday and receive an additional dose of MMR vaccine before entering kindergarten (when they’re 4 to 6 years old). The second dose provides additional protection to the approximately 5% of people who do not respond to their first dose. Given the risk of measles associated with international travel, a first dose can be given as early as 6 months of age for infants who will be traveling abroad. This does not, however, replace the need for additional MMR doses administered at the traditional timepoints of over 1 year of age and 4 to 6 years of age. Find a Pediatrician Should adults get vaccinated for measles? Adults are considered immune to measles if they have documentation of at least one dose of MMR vaccine on or after their first birthday, documentation of two doses of MMR vaccine for individuals at high risk, laboratory evidence of measles immunity, laboratory confirmation of measles infection, or birth before 1957. Adults who do not meet these criteria should be vaccinated with at least two doses of the MMR vaccine — unless their physician recommends against it due to special circumstances, such as severely compromised immunity. During measles outbreaks, health departments may provide additional recommendations to protect their communities, including a second dose of MMR for adults who have received only one dose previously. Currently, a third dose of MMR vaccine during measles outbreaks is not recommended. Find a Primary Care Provider How dangerous is measles? Fortunately, for most people, measles is not life-threatening — but the problem is that you can't predict who will become seriously ill. Three in 1,000 people who contract measles will die. For those who are vulnerable due to preexisting conditions that impact their immune system, measles can be even more dangerous. However, if everyone is vaccinated, no one will die. Before the vaccine, there were up to 500 U.S. deaths each year from measles, and now it's completely preventable. With vaccine-preventable illnesses, most people don't get sick, but that doesn’t mean it’s smart to forego the vaccine. Why take the risk when the protection is safe and effective? Should vitamin A and cod liver oil be used to prevent measles infection? The only way to prevent measles is with the MMR vaccine. Vitamin A does not prevent measles, and in high doses, it can lead to toxic side effects such as nausea, vomiting, headache, blurred vision, liver damage and coma. Treatment with once-daily vitamin A for two days is recommended for those with an established diagnosis of a measles infection to help the illness from becoming more severe. Cod liver oil contains high amounts of vitamin A, vitamin D and fatty acids, which can be harmful if intake exceeds the recommended daily amount; it should not be administered to prevent measles infection. Should I be worried if measles is found in my community? Community outbreaks of measles should always be taken seriously. Even when overall vaccination rates are robust, outbreaks can still spread among certain populations, such as people who are immunocompromised or live in under-vaccinated areas. Some environments also pose more risks. If a patient with measles arrives in the emergency department of a hospital, for example, the illness would have to be quickly identified and the patient placed in isolation to keep the virus from spreading rapidly to other sick individuals. Everyone has a responsibility to take precautions to avoid the virus and to ensure their vaccinations are up-to-date to protect themselves and their neighbors. What should I do if I’m exposed to measles or think I may have measles? Measles is highly contagious, and you can be infectious prior to developing symptoms. Be extremely cautious in the event of a possible exposure. Wear a mask and isolate from others Contact your doctor immediately if you believe you have been exposed Contact your care team via MyChart Your care team can help determine if you are at risk of contracting the virus. For the unvaccinated, getting the MMR vaccine or an injection of immune globulin may reduce the risk of illness. If you or your child are fully vaccinated (two doses of MMR vaccine), monitor for symptoms for at least 21 days and call your provider immediately if you or your child begin to experience any symptoms. Do not go into a healthcare facility without calling ahead to ensure that you do not put other patients at risk. Where can I find additional information about measles? A total of 18 measles cases were reported among international visitors to the United States. news.content_zh: 芝加哥大学医学 (UChicago Medicine) 于 2026 年 11 月 18 日发表的文章讨论了 麻疹 在美国的死灰复燃,该疾病于 2026 年 11 月 17 日失去了消除状态。截至 2026 年 11 月中旬,美国在 2026 年报告了超过 5,400 例 麻疹 病例,是 2025 年全年病例数的两倍多,以及 10 起与 麻疹 相关的死亡。文章强调了 麻疹 的风险,包括急性脑炎和 亚急性硬化性全脑炎 (SSPE),每 1000 例病例中死亡率为 3 例。它强调了 疫苗接种 的重要性,并指出 MMR 疫苗 在两次给药后有效率超过 97%。文章还提到,麻疹 具有高度传染性,通过飞沫或空气传播,未接种疫苗的个体面临很大风险。卫生部门可能会建议在 暴发 期间额外注射剂量,但不建议注射第三剂。该文章作为公共卫生指南,强调需要使用 麻疹 来预防 麻疹 及其并发症。

news.title: Highly contagious: US loses 26-year measles elimination status as cases more than double
news.excerpt: The U.S. lost its measles elimination status after 26 years as cases surged nationwide. Here's what's behind the uptick and why the status was lost.
news.rss_summary_html: The U.S. lost its measles elimination status after 26 years as cases surged nationwide. Here's what's behind the uptick and why the status was lost.

news.content_title: Highly contagious: US loses 26-year measles elimination status as cases more than double
news.content: Skip to Article Set weather Back To Main Menu Close Weather in - Change Location Current -Mostly Sunny TonightLow -Mostly Sunny TomorrowHigh -Mostly Sunny Full Weather Report News Highly contagious: US loses 26-year measles elimination status as cases more than double Published: Nov. 18, 2026, 11:59 a.m. The highly contagious respiratory disease spreads through coughing and sneezing, and the virus can remain in the air for up to two hours after an infected person leaves.Canva Illustration for NJ.com Set as Google Preferred Source By Dallas Gagnon | MassLive.com After 26 years, the United States has officially lost its measles elimination status, meaning the virus has circulated continuously for more than a year. Measles cases have more than doubled in 2026, with 5,412 confirmed cases reported as of Nov. 12 compared with 2,289 during all of 2025. That surge has come with serious consequences. Measles is highly contagious and can cause pneumonia, brain swelling and death, with young children, pregnant women and people with weakened immune systems among those at greater risk of serious complications. At least five measles deaths have been confirmed by the CDC in 2026. Earlier this month, the Wisconsin Department of Health Servicesreported that an infant died amid an ongoing outbreak in the state, with a coroner listing measles as the immediate cause of death. Just days earlier, New York reported its first known measles-associated death in more than 30 years after a child in Lewis County died amid an ongoing outbreak. Against that backdrop, the Pan American Health Organization issued a formal letter to U.S. health officials last week declaring the country lost its status after “it was determined that a single measles chain of transmission, which commenced on 20 January 2025, has persisted for more than twelve months in the United States.” The U.S. is one of three countries that has lost its elimination status in 2026, joining Bolivia and Mexico. Find a Doctor FindCare Cardiology Dentistry Dermatology Neurology OB-GYN Orthopedic Surgery Pediatrics Primary Care Psychiatry Urology Search Healthline Subscribe Health NewsFact Checked U.S. Loses Measles-Free Status After 26 Years, a Major Public Health Setback Written by Kristen B. Reed — Fact checked by Jill Seladi-Schulman, Ph.D. — Updated on November 17, 2026 Add Healthline on Google Share on Pinterest A certified medical assistant administering the MMR vaccine to patients at the Parkside Pediatrics practice in Spartanburg, SC, on January 30, 2026. The United States has lost its measles elimination status after 26 years, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) announced on November 17. U.S. measles cases reached 5,412 in 2026, the highest total in 35 years, according to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) data. About 96% of this year’s measles cases were in people who were unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination status. Two doses of the MMR vaccine are about 97% effective and offer the best protection against measles, according to the CDC. The United States has officially lost its measles elimination status, a major public health achievement that was secured 26 years ago. The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the World Health Organization’s (WHO) regional office for the Americas, determined that measles has spread continuously in the U.S. for more than 12 months. On November 17, PAHO announced the end of the country’s measles elimination status, which it has held since 2000. “Losing a measles elimination status has broader implications than losing a public health designation,” PAHO’s director, Jarbas Barbosa, MD, MPH, PhD, said in a media briefing. “It means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period of time, putting families and communities at risk of a preventable illness, hospitalization, and death.” PAHO’s review examined measles spread starting January 20, 2025, when the first person became ill in a large West Texas outbreak, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)Trusted Source. CDC dataTrusted Source show 5,412 confirmed measles cases this year as of November 12. That’s the highest annual total since 1991 and more than double the 2025 count of 2,289 cases. Andi Shane, MD, chief of pediatric infectious diseases at Children’s Healthcare of Atlanta, called the U.S. losing measles elimination status “a public health alarm that we are not being effective and we’re not controlling measles as well.” The measles virus is highly contagious. It spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. People can catch it in a room up to two hours after an infected person has left, according to the CDCTrusted Source. What losing measles-free status means for the U.S. “There’s really been very little measles in the United States over the past 25 years until January 2025,” William Moss, MD, a professor of epidemiology at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, told Healthline. Losing the status itself doesn’t change much about daily life for most Americans, Moss said. The concern is the measles outbreaks, hospitalizations and deaths behind the loss, he said. He called the loss “a big red flag” after “enormous efforts over the past 26 years” to keep the status. A country loses its elimination status when there is “uninterrupted circulation of the same virus genotype and lineage for 12 months or more,” according to PAHO. Shane explained it this way: “For the past 12 months in the United States, we’ve had ongoing circulation of the measles virus and person-to-person transmission is occurring.” Canada lost its elimination status in November 2025, and the U.K. and five European countries lost theirs earlier in 2026. The U.S. can regain the status. “Other countries have done that,” Moss said. Brazil, which lost its status in 2019, regained it in November 2024. Venezuela, which lost its status in 2018, regained it in 2023, according to PAHO. Among reported cases, about 400 to 500 people died each year, 48,000 needed hospital care, and 1,000 developed encephalitis, or brain swelling. Here’s a timeline of measles elimination in the U.S.: 1954: Scientists isolate the measles virus during an outbreak in Boston (CDCTrusted Source). 1963: The U.S. licenses its first measles vaccine (CDCTrusted Source). 1968: An improved, more weakened live-virus vaccine goes into use. (CDCTrusted Source). 1971: The U.S. licenses the combined measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine (CDCTrusted Source). 1978: The CDC sets a goal to eliminate measles by 1982. The announcement comes as the US endures the worst measles outbreak since 1991, with more than 5,400 cases and eight deaths in 2026. “Measles is resurging globally amid the persistent gaps in vaccination coverage, and this global trend is also affecting the Americas,” said Dr Jarbas Barbosa da Silva Jr, the director of the Pan American Health Organization, a regional branch of the World Health Organization. “The endemic measles transmission has now been re-established in Bolivia, Mexico and United States.” Silva made the final decision on US elimination status. In a statement to the Guardian on Tuesday, Barbosa da Silva commended “the significant efforts undertaken by the United States to manage the measles outbreak through strengthened surveillance, timely case detection and response, targeted vaccination activities and coordination across the public health system”. Measles is one of the most contagious viruses known to medicine and requires 95% of the community to be vaccinated to prevent outbreaks. The measles vaccine is safe and highly effective. However, pockets of low vaccination have grown in the US following pandemic-era disruptions and widespread misinformation. Measles, mumps and misinformation: how Crunchy Moms became ‘the most dangerous’ group on Facebook Read more The nation’s largest doctors group, the American Medical Association, described loss of measles elimination status as a “deeply troubling and entirely preventable setback for our nation”. The loss of measles-free status comes after Donald Trump and his health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, spent nearly two years sowing confusion about the safety of vaccines. In just one recent example, Trump called for the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) combination vaccine to be split into separate shots, arguing without evidence that “together, there could be a possibility they’re quite lethal”. “As a pediatrician, I saw firsthand how decisions made in Washington hurt our children and families,” said Dr Annie Andrews, a Democratic senator-elect. “Nothing makes that clearer than the loss of our measles elimination status.” The loss of elimination status has already heightened criticism of Kennedy. High-profile epidemiologists called Kennedy’s work at the health department “malpractice” and equivalent to a “crime scene”. In a statement posted on X late on Tuesday afternoon, Kennedy said the US “will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status”. He added that he would “continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles” and that officials with the Department of Health & Human Services “are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust. We will answer families’ questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment.” Barbosa da Silva called the role of misinformation in measles transmission “dynamic” and urged health departments to develop bespoke campaigns tailored to undervaccinated communities. Experts caution against piling blame for measles outbreaks solely on the Trump administration. The MMR vaccine has been the target of misinformation for more than two decades, including work by Kennedy before his White House role. “There is a profound problem with measles in all three North American countries,” said Noel Brewer, a behavioral scientist at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill who studies vaccination behaviors, and specifically measles. He chairs a committee that considers evidence on US measles elimination status, and contributed to the scientific work that underpinned Pan American Health Organization’s decision. “The US has had large outbreaks and exported those to Canada and Mexico, and those cases have come back again to the US,” said Brewer. Canada lost its measles-free status in 2025, but Barbosa da Silva said the country now represented the “good news” in the region. The nation stopped measles transmission for 60 days. This is the first step on the way to regaining measles elimination status. The UK and several European nations have also recently lost elimination status. “What we’re experiencing is not a United States-specific thing,” said David Margolius of the Big Cities Health Coalition. Instead, there is a, “global surge in cases, global decline in vaccination rate”. Public health leaders with the Big Cities Health Coalition (BHC), which leads health departments that serve 47 million Americans, described the announcement as a “profoundly sad moment for our country”. “Recent declines in measles vaccination rates have opened the door to outbreaks across the country, resulting in preventable illness, hospitalizations, and tragic loss of life,” BHC members said in a statement. “These outcomes are especially heartbreaking because measles is a disease that we know how to prevent. Yet too many voices spreading fear and false information are exacerbating the problem.” Expert epidemiologists recommended US measles status change during a closed-door meeting in Washington DC. A range of evidence would have been presented, including interviews with positive patients collected by local US health authorities and whole genome sequencing that can provide a fingerprint of the virus’s origin. Although measles elimination status is an official designation, it carries real consequences for Americans. Where measles cases were once typically imported by international travelers, endemic measles transmission means Americans face new risks of infection, and are being asked to dig up decades-old vaccination certificates and possibly quarantine for 21 days. “Now is the time to go and find that evidence, because now this is a real day-to-day life thing that could happen to you,” Margolius said earlier in November. Re-establishing elimination status will require “a national plan to eliminate measles again”, said Brewer, “an integrated plan that’s publicly communicated with specific tasks assigned to named parties”. He added that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the president should speak out “forcefully” in favor of vaccination, and Congress should allocate more funding. analysis.time: The US lost its measles elimination status in 2026, with the announcement made on November 17, 2026. The outbreak has been ongoing since the beginning of the year, with more than 5,400 cases and eight deaths reported by the end of 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreak occurred in the United States, affecting communities and populations across the country, particularly those with low vaccination rates. The Pan American Health Organization confirmed the re-establishment of endemic measles transmission in the US, Mexico, and Bolivia.
analysis.event: The US has lost its measles elimination status, marking a significant setback in public health. This was confirmed by global health authorities, including the Pan American Health Organization, which stated that measles is now continually spreading in the US after being eliminated for 26 years.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The outbreak resulted in more than 5,400 cases and eight deaths in 2026. The risk of continued transmission is high due to pockets of low vaccination rates, which have grown following pandemic-era disruptions and misinformation. The loss of elimination status has raised concerns about the effectiveness of public health measures and the potential for further outbreaks.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The US public health system has been working to manage the outbreak through strengthened surveillance, timely case detection, targeted vaccination activities, and coordination across health departments. Efforts are ongoing to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust. The Pan American Health Organization’s decision was based on evidence including interviews with positive patients and whole genome sequencing of the virus.

analysis.brief_en: The US has lost its measles elimination status, marking a major setback for public health after 26 years of being measles-free. This decision, made by the Pan American Health Organization, was based on the re-establishment of endemic measles transmission in the US, Mexico, and Bolivia. The outbreak in 2026 resulted in over 5,400 cases and eight deaths, highlighting the impact of low vaccination rates fueled by pandemic-era disruptions and misinformation. Public health officials have emphasized the need for strengthened surveillance, timely case detection, and targeted vaccination efforts to address the issue. The loss of elimination status has drawn criticism, particularly against former health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, who faced accusations of spreading vaccine misinformation. Efforts are ongoing to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust, with officials working to prevent further outbreaks and support timely treatment. The situation reflects a broader global trend of declining vaccination rates and rising measles cases, underscoring the importance of addressing vaccine hesitancy and misinformation to protect public health.

measles-free nation, more than 25 years after it eliminated the highly contagious virus. The director of the Pan American Health Organization made the final call that measles is endemic — or always present — in the U.S. following 12 months of continuous transmission. It’s a devastating step backward for American public health, as declining childhood vaccination rates help to fuel outbreaks that have sickened thousands and led to a string of preventable deaths. A vial of MMR vaccine is prepared at Dr. Gary M. Kramer’s pediatric office in Coral Gables, Florida, Sept. 12, 2025. Joe Raedle | Getty Images The U.S. on Tuesday lost its official designation as a measles-free nation, more than 25 years after it eliminated the highly contagious virus. The Pan American Health Organization announced the decision, which came after an independent panel of eight scientific experts convened last week to consider the country’s epidemiological evidence. The director of PAHO, the regional branch of the World Health Organization, made the final call that measles is endemic — or always present — in the U.S. following 12 months of continuous transmission. In other words, measles is spreading regularly in the country again, with ongoing outbreaks sparking new ones. “The commission concluded that endemic measles transmission has now been reestablished in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States, and recommended that their measles elimination status be withdrawn — a recommendation which I have accepted,” Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO director, said during a news briefing on Tuesday. It’s a devastating step backward for American public health, as declining childhood vaccination rates and vaccine hesitancy fuel outbreaks across the country that have sickened thousands of people and led to a tragic string of preventable deaths. Among the deaths where vaccination status was reported, all were unvaccinated. More than 5,400 measles cases had been reported nationwide in 2026 as of mid-November, marking the country’s worst outbreak in more than three decades. States have confirmed 10 deaths associated with the disease so far in 2026: seven in Pennsylvania, one in New York and two in Wisconsin. The commission found that out of 52 U.S. states and territories it tracked, 48 experienced measles outbreaks during the reporting period between January 2025 and January 2026, PAHO Assistant Director Dr. Rhonda Sealey-Thomas said during the briefing. But Barbosa said the countries are already taking action to control outbreaks, such as strengthening vaccination, surveillance for timely case detection and outbreak response efforts. The U.S. in particular has ramped up vaccination efforts to close immunity gaps, particularly in areas with low immunization coverage experiencing outbreaks, said Dr. Daniel Salas, executive manager of PAHO’s Special Program for Comprehensive Immunization. He said PAHO expects the U.S. to present its corrective action plan in the coming weeks, outlining strategies to regain its designation. In a Tuesday release, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said it will continue to ensure all communities have the resources to prevent and respond to outbreaks and is committed to working with states and other local partners to restore the U.S.’s measles elimination status. CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz said in the release that the measles elimination designation “is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does.” She said the agency has invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach communities where transmission is occurring. Last week, Schwartz told Reuters that the agency is going to be “doing the same exact thing that we’ve been doing today” if the U.S. loses its measles-free status. The decision also poses a new test for the Trump administration and its Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has taken steps to change recommendations for the childhood measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine and has a long history of questioning its safety without evidence. But Kennedy, in a Tuesday X post, said he continues to recommend MMR vaccination as “the most effective way to prevent measles.” “We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust,” Kennedy said. “We will answer families’ questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment.” CNBC previously reported on how the return of measles in the U.S. exposes weaknesses in the nation’s public health system that raise concerns about the return of other eliminated diseases. The resurgence of measles exposes eroding trust in health institutions and growing challenges in persuading people to protect themselves, their children and their communities. Public health experts previously told CNBC that the return of measles ultimately boils down to fewer children getting vaccinated. The MMR vaccine is about 97% effective against measles after two doses, while a single dose is 93% effective, according to the CDC. Yet data aggregated by the CDC shows that vaccination coverage for that shot among U.S. kindergarteners fell to 92.4% in the 2025-2026 school year, which is below the 95% threshold public health officials generally recommend to prevent sustained transmission. The American Medical Association urged the public to get vaccinated after PAHO’s announcement. “We must treat the current measles outbreaks as an urgent call to rebuild trust in science-based recommendations and restore strong, fully-funded public health infrastructure to protect families and communities and prevent the return of diseases once eliminated,” AMA President Dr. Willie Underwood said in a statement. In a separate statement, the pharmaceutical industry’s largest lobbying group called on policymakers to provide “clear, accurate information about the seriousness of measles infection and the effectiveness of vaccines against it, restore and sustain high vaccination coverage in every community, strengthen vaccination efforts, and invest in disease surveillance and rapid outbreak response.” “We have the tools to eliminate measles again and what we need now is the commitment to use them,” said Dr. Michael Ybarra, chief medical officer of the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America. Measles isn’t just a public health threat — it’s also a huge financial burden on the healthcare system, CNBC reported. Based on this year’s case count, a new tool developed by researchers at Johns Hopkins University estimates an economic cost of nearly $83 million for the outbreaks. That total includes $56 million in public health response costs, almost $25 million in lost productivity and more than $1.8 million in direct medical expenses. The U.S. now joins Canada, Spain and the U.K., which all recently lost their measles-free status after a review by experts at the World Health Organization. While the U.S. dropped out of the WHO, it remains a member of PAHO, its Americas branch. designation as a measles-free nation, more than 25 years after it eliminated the highly contagious virus. The director of the Pan American Health Organization made the final call that measles is endemic — or always present — in the U.S. following 12 months of continuous transmission. It’s a devastating step backward for American public health, as declining childhood vaccination rates help to fuel outbreaks that have sickened thousands and led to a string of preventable deaths. A vial of MMR vaccine is prepared at Dr. Gary M. Kramer’s pediatric office in Coral Gables, Florida, Sept. 12, 2025. Joe Raedle | Getty Images The U.S. on Tuesday lost its official designation as a measles-free nation, more than 25 years after it eliminated the highly contagious virus. The Pan American Health Organization announced the decision, which came after an independent panel of eight scientific experts convened last week to consider the country’s epidemiological evidence. The director of PAHO, the regional branch of the World Health Organization, made the final call that measles is endemic — or always present — in the U.S. following 12 months of continuous transmission. In other words, measles is spreading regularly in the country again, with ongoing outbreaks sparking new ones. “The commission concluded that endemic measles transmission has now been reestablished in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States, and recommended that their measles elimination status be withdrawn — a recommendation which I have accepted,” Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO director, said during a news briefing on Tuesday. It’s a devastating step backward for American public health, as declining childhood vaccination rates and vaccine hesitancy fuel outbreaks across the country that have sickened thousands of people and led to a tragic string of preventable deaths. Among the deaths where vaccination status was reported, all were unvaccinated. More than 5,400 measles cases had been reported nationwide in 2026 as of mid-November, marking the country’s worst outbreak in more than three decades. States have confirmed 10 deaths associated with the disease so far in 2026: seven in Pennsylvania, one in New York and two in Wisconsin. The commission found that out of 52 U.S. states and territories it tracked, 48 experienced measles outbreaks during the reporting period between January 2025 and January 2026, PAHO Assistant Director Dr. Rhonda Sealey-Thomas said during the briefing. But Barbosa said the countries are already taking action to control outbreaks, such as strengthening vaccination, surveillance for timely case detection and outbreak response efforts. The U.S. in particular has ramped up vaccination efforts to close immunity gaps, particularly in areas with low immunization coverage experiencing outbreaks, said Dr. Daniel Salas, executive manager of PAHO’s Special Program for Comprehensive Immunization. He said PAHO expects the U.S. to present its corrective action plan in the coming weeks, outlining strategies to regain its designation. In a Tuesday release, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said it will continue to ensure all communities have the resources to prevent and respond to outbreaks and is committed to working with states and other local partners to restore the U.S.’s measles elimination status. CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz said in the release that the measles elimination designation “is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does.” She said the agency has invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach communities where transmission is occurring. Last week, Schwartz told Reuters that the agency is going to be “doing the same exact thing that we’ve been doing today” if the U.S. loses its measles-free status. The decision also poses a new test for the Trump administration and its Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has taken steps to change recommendations for the childhood measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine and has a long history of questioning its safety without evidence. But Kennedy, in a Tuesday X post, said he continues to recommend MMR vaccination as “the most effective way to prevent measles.” “We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust,” Kennedy said. “We will answer families’ questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment.” CNBC previously reported on how the return of measles in the U.S. exposes weaknesses in the nation’s public health system that raise concerns about the return of other eliminated diseases. The resurgence of measles exposes eroding trust in health institutions and growing challenges in persuading people to protect themselves, their children and their communities. Public health experts previously told CNBC that the return of measles ultimately boils down to fewer children getting vaccinated. The MMR vaccine is about 97% effective against measles after two doses, while a single dose is 93% effective, according to the CDC. Yet data aggregated by the CDC shows that vaccination coverage for that shot among U.S. kindergarteners fell to 92.4% in the 2025-2026 school year, which is below the 95% threshold public health officials generally recommend to prevent sustained transmission. The American Medical Association urged the public to get vaccinated after PAHO’s announcement. “We must treat the current measles outbreaks as an urgent call to rebuild trust in science-based recommendations and restore strong, fully-funded public health infrastructure to protect families and communities and prevent the return of diseases once eliminated,” AMA President Dr. Willie Underwood said in a statement. In a separate statement, the pharmaceutical industry’s largest lobbying group called on policymakers to provide “clear, accurate information about the seriousness of measles infection and the effectiveness of vaccines against it, restore and sustain high vaccination coverage in every community, strengthen vaccination efforts, and invest in disease surveillance and rapid outbreak response.” “We have the tools to eliminate measles again and what we need now is the commitment to use them,” said Dr. Michael Ybarra, chief medical officer of the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America. Measles isn’t just a public health threat — it’s also a huge financial burden on the healthcare system, CNBC reported. Based on this year’s case count, a new tool developed by researchers at Johns Hopkins University estimates an economic cost of nearly $83 million for the outbreaks. That total includes $56 million in public health response costs, almost $25 million in lost productivity and more than $1.8 million in direct medical expenses. The U.S. now joins Canada, Spain and the U.K., which all recently lost their measles-free status after a review by experts at the World Health Organization. While the U.S. dropped out of the WHO, it remains a member of PAHO, its Americas branch. news.content: 0 seconds of 2 minutes, 3 seconds Volume 0% Press shift question mark to access a list of keyboard shortcuts Keyboard Shortcuts Play/Pause SPACE Increase Volume ↑ Decrease Volume ↓ Seek Forward → Seek Backward ← Captions On/Off c Fullscreen/Exit Fullscreen f Mute/Unmute m Decrease Caption Size - Increase Caption Size + or = Seek % 0-9 Live 00:00 02:03 02:03 Measles resurgence costs U.S. long-held elimination status 02:03 Get more news on Nov. 17, 2026, 12:41 AM UTC / Updated Nov. 17, 2026, 10:12 PM UTC By Aria Bendix Measles is no longer eliminated in the United States, reversing one of the country’s greatest public health achievements this century. An independent commission of the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a group within the World Health Organization, revoked the U.S.’ measles-elimination status after determining that the virus has circulated nonstop for more than a year. PAHO announced the decision Tuesday. “Losing a measles elimination status has broader implications than losing a public health designation,” PAHO’s director, Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, said in a media briefing. “It means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period of time, putting families and communities at risk of a preventable illness, hospitalization and death.” The U.S. earned the elimination status in 2000. Now, measles is once again endemic. “As a pediatrician and a parent, I am heartbroken that we have reached this point,” said Dr. Richard Besser, president of the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, a health-focused philanthropic organization. “Too many families in America are once again having to worry that their children could get this preventable infection and suffer its most severe consequences.” Upward of 5,400 cases have been recorded this year — more than double last year’s count and the highest since 1991. Ten people have died , according to state health departments. PAHO determines whether countries in the Americas meet the requirements for measles elimination. The group deliberated for four days last week in Washington, D.C., to assess whether transmission in the U.S. and other countries in the region had been sustained from January 2025 to January 2026. In addition to the U.S., the group determined that measles is no longer eliminated in Mexico or Bolivia. A commission made up of eight public health experts evaluated genetic data from “homegrown” cases (those not related to international travel) to figure out whether outbreaks across U.S. states were linked. The commission also weighed levels of vaccination coverage, the quality of measles surveillance and whether there are sufficient strategies and resources to respond to outbreaks. As in many countries, vaccination rates in the U.S. have declined in recent years: 92% of kindergartners had been vaccinated for measles as of the 2025-26 school year, down from 95% — the threshold needed to prevent outbreaks — in the 2019-20 school year. Nationwide among kindergartners, 75% of counties and jurisdictions with measles vaccine data fall below the 95% rate, according to an NBC News investigation . “The United States has an extraordinary measles problem. We’ve had more measles cases in the last 18 months than we’ve had in the previous 25 years combined,” said Noel Brewer, a public health professor at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Endemic measles poses a serious risk to people who are unvaccinated, said Dr. Walter Orenstein, former director of the U.S. immunization program at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The risk is especially pronounced for infants, who are not typically eligible for the first dose of the vaccine until they turn 1, as well as those who cannot get the shot because they are immunocompromised. “People can go into a supermarket and get infected,” he said. At least four of the measles deaths this year were in babies too young to be vaccinated. Some health departments in outbreak zones are recommending an early dose for infants as young as 6 months. Measles is among the most contagious viruses known to humans: One infected person can spread the virus to 9 out of 10 others in close proximity. It can linger in the air for up to two hours. Infections in unvaccinated people can lead to deadly complications such as pneumonia or brain swelling. Brewer said the U.S. desperately needs a strategy for tackling measles. “The lack of action to address the growing outbreak is clear negligence,” he said. Under past presidential administrations, the CDC has responded to measles outbreaks with media briefings and vaccination campaigns, but the agency has not done so this year. Pan American Health Organization headquarters in Washington, D.C. Tony Quinn / Sipa USA via AP Dr. Daniel Salas, executive manager of PAHO’s Special Program for Comprehensive Immunization, said Tuesday that the U.S. is expected to submit a corrective plan of action in the coming weeks. He added that the country is already taking steps to close immunity gaps in undervaccinated communities. The CDC and its healthcare partners said Tuesday in a joint statement that they will encourage MMR vaccination, expand access to shots, strengthen data sharing and “hold ourselves accountable for measurable progress.” A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services said that the CDC has “mounted an aggressive response to measles outbreaks,” including allocating $100 million in additional funding in October and deploying experts to support state responses. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz “continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles,” the spokesperson said. “We know where transmission is occurring and we’re working with state and local health departments to reach those communities,” Schwartz said in a separate statement. “Losing a designation doesn’t mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks.” Kennedy said on X that HHS will work to regain the country’s measles elimination status. “We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust. We will answer families’ questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment,” he said. Since taking office, Kennedy has questioned the safety and effectiveness of measles vaccines and touted unproven remedies like inhaled steroids . President Donald Trump, meanwhile, falsely suggested in August that the combined measles shot could be “quite lethal,” despite decades of evidence demonstrating its safety. “We have seen frequent and damaging public comments that have been shaking the confidence of parents about vaccination,” Brewer said. A measles, mumps and rubella vaccine is displayed at a Pennsylvania Department of Health measles vaccination clinic in Lancaster County on Oct. 20. Matt Rourke / AP The pandemic accelerated the downward vaccination trend. Some parents avoided taking their children to the pediatrician , which meant delaying routine shots. An onslaught of misinformation about the Covid vaccines also reignited debunked theories, including the false notion that measles shots are linked to autism. Since 2019, 82% of counties and jurisdictions across the U.S. have reported declines in measles vaccination rates. Three small, rural counties — Catron County, New Mexico, and Adams and Custer counties in Idaho — have rates for kindergartners below 50%. Even before the pandemic, the World Health Organization warned that vaccine hesitancy was contributing to a global resurgence of measles. “It’s not just a U.S. problem, and it’s not just this administration,” Brewer said. Last year, Canada’s measles elimination status was revoked following an outbreak that led to more than 5,000 cases. “It wasn’t for a lack of effort in Canada. There was a political commitment at the highest level to sustain measles elimination and to stop that outbreak,” said Dr. Jon Andrus, a global health professor at George Washington University and the chair of the PAHO commission that determines measles elimination status. “That was for me the sad part of the story, because they really did try.” Barbosa, PAHO’s director, said Tuesday that Canada has interrupted measles transmission in its outbreak but that the country needs to keep up with vaccinations and surveillance to reclaim its elimination status. It could take years, experts said, for the U.S. to do the same. Follow relevant topics Health See your feed ›

A commission made up of eight public health experts evaluated genetic data from “homegrown” cases (those not related to international travel) to figure out whether outbreaks across U.S. states were linked. The commission also weighed levels of vaccination coverage, the quality of measles surveillance and whether there are sufficient strategies and resources to respond to outbreaks. As in many countries, vaccination rates in the U.S. have declined in recent years: 92% of kindergartners had been vaccinated for measles as of the 2025-26 school year, down from 95% — the threshold needed to prevent outbreaks — in the 2019-20 school year. Nationwide among kindergartners, 75% of counties and jurisdictions with measles vaccine data fall below the 95% rate, according to an NBC News investigation . “The United States has an extraordinary measles problem. We’ve had more measles cases in the last 18 months than we’ve had in the previous 25 years combined,” said Noel Brewer, a public health professor at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Endemic measles poses a serious risk to people who are unvaccinated, said Dr. Walter Orenstein, former director of the U.S. immunization program at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The risk is especially pronounced for infants, who are not typically eligible for the first dose of the vaccine until they turn 1, as well as those who cannot get the shot because they are immunocompromised. “People can go into a supermarket and get infected,” he said. At least four of the measles deaths this year were in babies too young to be vaccinated. Some health departments in outbreak zones are recommending an early dose for infants as young as 6 months. Measles is among the most contagious viruses known to humans: One infected person can spread the virus to 9 out of 10 others in close proximity. It can linger in the air for up to two hours. Infections in unvaccinated people can lead to deadly complications such as pneumonia or brain swelling. Brewer said the U.S. desperately needs a strategy for tackling measles. “The lack of action to address the growing outbreak is clear negligence,” he said. Under past presidential administrations, the CDC has responded to measles outbreaks with media briefings and vaccination campaigns, but the agency has not done so this year. Pan American Health Organization headquarters in Washington, D.C. Tony Quinn / Sipa USA via AP Dr. Daniel Salas, executive manager of PAHO’s Special Program for Comprehensive Immunization, said Tuesday that the U.S. is expected to submit a corrective plan of action in the coming weeks. He added that the country is already taking steps to close immunity gaps in undervaccinated communities. The CDC and its healthcare partners said Tuesday in a joint statement that they will encourage MMR vaccination, expand access to shots, strengthen data sharing and “hold ourselves accountable for measurable progress.” A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services said that the CDC has “mounted an aggressive response to measles outbreaks,” including allocating $100 million in additional funding in October and deploying experts to support state responses. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz “continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles,” the spokesperson said. “We know where transmission is occurring and we’re working with state and local health departments to reach those communities,” Schwartz said in a separate statement. “Losing a designation doesn’t mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks.” Kennedy said on X that HHS will work to regain the country’s measles elimination status. “We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust. We will answer families’ questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment,” he said. Since taking office, Kennedy has questioned the safety and effectiveness of measles vaccines and touted unproven remedies like inhaled steroids . President Donald Trump, meanwhile, falsely suggested in August that the combined measles shot could be “quite lethal,” despite decades of evidence demonstrating its safety. “We have seen frequent and damaging public comments that have been shaking the confidence of parents about vaccination,” Brewer said. A measles, mumps and rubella vaccine is displayed at a Pennsylvania Department of Health measles vaccination clinic in Lancaster County on Oct. 20. Matt Rourke / AP The pandemic accelerated the downward vaccination trend. Some parents avoided taking their children to the pediatrician , which meant delaying routine shots. An onslaught of misinformation about the Covid vaccines also reignited debunked theories, including the false notion that measles shots are linked to autism. Since 2019, 82% of counties and jurisdictions across the U.S. have reported declines in measles vaccination rates. Three small, rural counties — Catron County, New Mexico, and Adams and Custer counties in Idaho — have rates for kindergartners below 50%. Even before the pandemic, the World Health Organization warned that vaccine hesitancy was contributing to a global resurgence of measles. “It’s not just a U.S. problem, and it’s not just this administration,” Brewer said. Last year, Canada’s measles elimination status was revoked following an outbreak that led to more than 5,000 cases. “It wasn’t for a lack of effort in Canada. There was a political commitment at the highest level to sustain measles elimination and to stop that outbreak,” said Dr. Jon Andrus, a global health professor at George Washington University and the chair of the PAHO commission that determines measles elimination status. “That was for me the sad part of the story, because they really did try.” Barbosa, PAHO’s director, said Tuesday that Canada has interrupted measles transmission in its outbreak but that the country needs to keep up with vaccinations and surveillance to reclaim its elimination status. It could take years, experts said, for the U.S. to do the same. Follow relevant topics Health See your feed ›
