news.content_title: The United States’ measles elimination status is officially gone. Who should get a booster?
news.content: Although measles boosters aren’t typically recommended, certain people could use another shot, especially with so many outbreaks ongoing in the US. Matt Rourke/AP See all topics The United States has officially lost its measles elimination status, the Pan American Health Organization announced Tuesday. Measles is once again considered endemic in the country, due to more than a year of continuous local transmission. Measles is also re-established in Bolivia and Mexico, Dr. Jarbas Barbosa da Silva Jr., director of PAHO, said Tuesday, adding that the current situation requires “urgent action.” “Losing a measles elimination status has broader implications than losing a public health designation. It means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period of time, putting families and communities at risk of preventable illness, hospitalization, and death,” Barbosa said. Dr. Peter Hotez, co-director of the Center for Vaccine Development at Texas Children’s Hospital in Houston, put it simply: “Basically, measles is back.” Countries that lose elimination status are required to submit a corrective action plan to PAHO that outlines how they’ll regain elimination status. The US is expected to submit its plan in the coming weeks, Barbosa said. “We will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status. I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles,” US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said in a social media post Tuesday. “We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust. We will answer families’ questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment. We will support Americans who become ill, regardless of vaccination status, and for the first time equip health care providers with guidance to diagnose and treat measles and its complications.” Dr. Erica Schwartz, director of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, said Tuesday that the agency knows where transmission is occurring and that it has invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities. “The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does,” Schwartz said in a statement. “Losing a designation doesn’t mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks.” The United States held its measles elimination status for 26 years, and the vast majority of people in the US are protected from the highly contagious virus. But doctors say that if you haven’t been vaccinated, now is the time. Although measles boosters aren’t typically recommended, certain people could use another shot, especially with so many outbreaks ongoing in the US. The country has tallied more than 5,000 cases this year, and the chance of being exposed to the virus is much higher than it has been in decades. What the numbers say At least 5,412 confirmed measles cases have been reported in the United States this year, mostly among unvaccinated people, according to the CDC . Experts say that figure is most likely an undercount. This is the highest number of infections in the US in more than three decades, and unless many more people get vaccinated, it will probably continue to grow. Compared with the millions of people who get the flu each year, 5,000-plus cases may not sound like a lot. But measles is one of the most contagious viruses in the world. If a person with measles walks into a room with 10 unvaccinated people, about nine would catch the virus, research suggests. By comparison, the flu would probably spread to only one person. And measles sticks around: Even after an infected person leaves the room, the virus can linger in the air for at least two hours. A few years ago, when the US had only a handful of cases, most of them happened when someone traveled to countries where the disease was endemic and returned with the virus. Now, most cases in the US result from exposure to someone in the neighborhood, research shows , so it may be at your door sooner than you think. Most people in the US have been vaccinated against the measles, but cases are rising because the vaccination rate has fallen. Experts say that about 95% of a population must be vaccinated to reach what’s called herd or community immunity: when there are enough people vaccinated that the virus can’t get a foothold and will fade away. Before the vaccine was introduced in the US in 1963, the country had 3 million to 4 million measles cases every year, and 400 to 500 people died from the disease annually. Once communities reached the 95% threshold, case numbers fell to almost nothing. What to know about the vaccine The measles vaccine was combined with mumps and rubella vaccines in 1971 to help streamline childhood immunization schedules, improve vaccination rates and reduce the number of shots children would need . The vaccine can be given to older children and adults, as well. And if an unvaccinated person is exposed to the virus, getting a shot within 72 hours could offer some protection or at least result in less serious illness, the CDC says. The MMR vaccine is considered extremely safe. There may be mild side effects, such as soreness, redness and a mild rash at the injection site. Some children may briefly develop a fever or joint pain. Rare risks include febrile seizures, which happen in about 1 in 3,000 to 4,000 children, resolve on their own and cause no long-term harm. Serious allergic reactions are extremely rare. Although a later-retracted study in the 1990s suggested a link between the MMR vaccine and autism, large-scale research involving millions of children has established that there is no link. Who gets the MMR shot Typically, the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that children get the first dose of the combined MMR vaccine between 12 and 15 months old and a second dose between ages 4 and 6. But anyone older than that can also get vaccinated. With a flu or Covid-19 vaccine, doses are recommended every year because those viruses mutate more quickly. But the measles virus stays pretty much the same from year to year, and two doses of the MMR vaccine should provide good protection for life. For people who live in a region where there’s an outbreak, some doctors suggest giving a dose of the MMR vaccine between 6 and 11 months of age in what’s called a zero dose. It’s then recommended that the child receive the first and second doses on the usual schedule. Immunologist Dr. Elisabeth Adkins Marnik says you can also ask your pediatrician to give your child the second dose of the vaccine before age 4. “I personally made the decision to get my daughter a second dose early when measles started circulating so much in the community and I knew we were also going to be doing a lot of traveling,” said Marnik, a science communicator who works to translate evidence into clear and empathetic public communication. “I just didn’t want to take any risks, and getting it a little bit early is fine. It just gave us extra peace of mind.” Who might need more protection There are others groups whose protection might be lacking and who can be vulnerable to infection, or who might be uncertain about whether they’re protected. Here’s what you need to know: If you were born before 1957 The CDC considers adults born before 1957 to be immune to measles, essentially because, before the vaccine, nearly every child caught the virus at some point. If you’ve gotten one dose A single dose of the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine is considered 93% effective at preventing measles. In fact, only one dose was recommended until 1989, when the US government changed the recommendation to two doses after a measles outbreak among vaccinated school-age children. Two doses of MMR boost measles protection to 97%. If you were vaccinated before 1989 and did not receive a second shot, you may want to consider getting one now. If you’ve gotten two doses Doctors don’t typically suggest boosters for people who received two doses of MMR. If you aren’t sure If you don’t know whether you were vaccinated as a child or whether you have been fully vaccinated, talk to your healthcare provider, who may want to give you another shot. Other people who might want an additional shot are those who received the first version of the measles vaccine between 1963 and 1968, which used a killed virus and may not offer as much protection. Testing for measles immunity You can get tested at a doctor’s office or pharmacy. When you have an infection or get vaccinated, your immune cells produce antibodies against the virus that can stay in your body for years and help you fight infection. A simple blood test looks for these antibodies to determine whether you have immunity. Doctors also sometimes order these tests for people with weakened immune systems to see how much immunity they have. The CDC does not recommend this kind of testing, and doctors say it is not necessary if you have had two doses of the vaccine. But this titer test may give you some peace of mind. “Titer tests are not perfect, but certainly if they’re positive, a person likely has a good bit of protection,” said Dr. Jesse Goodman, a professor of medicine and infectious disease at Georgetown University and director of its Center on Medical Product Access, Safety and Stewardship. “But if you’re pretty sure you didn’t get vaccinated or you didn’t get a second dose, you might as well just go ahead. There’s no harm in being vaccinated again.” Measles can cause serious problems The disease can cause serious symptoms. About 11% of Americans who have had measles this year were so sick that they had to go to the hospital, according to the CDC . There have also been at least 10 deaths in people who had measles, according to state data — the most the country has seen in decades. Measles can cause a rash, fever, red eyes, sensitivity to light and cough. It may also lead to severe complications such as pneumonia or encephalitis, a swelling of the brain that can cause convulsions, deafness or brain damage. For pregnant people, measles may cause premature birth or miscarriage , and they can pass the virus to their baby. Measles can also trigger immune amnesia , a condition in which the immune system forgets how to fight other diseases. Some groups are more vulnerable to measles complications, including older adults, infants and young children, as well as people who have suppressed immune systems because they take certain medications or are undergoing cancer treatment. But anyone can develop severe complications. “Most children who get measles as young children are fine and recover, but it can make them pretty sick. Anywhere from 1 in 5 to 1 in 10 even healthy children will end up in the hospital,” Goodman said. Spreading the word Even if you have been vaccinated — and chances are, you have — herd immunity grows as more people get the shot. Although trust in the vaccine has slipped recently, most people still say they believe in it. Studies show that peers and trusted community members can be persuasive, particularly because it can take time to convince people who are reluctant to get the shot. Marnik advises not to get discouraged if people you know don’t change their minds right away. Misinformation about vaccines is increasingly sophisticated, and it can be spread through close friends, anonymous voices online or even leaders . “So it’s no wonder parents are confused and have questions.” Talk to people who are hesitant about vaccines with empathy, she says. Most people just want what is best for their children. “Oftentimes, it takes time and multiple conversations with somebody who is hesitant for them to entertain potentially making the decision to get vaccinated,” Marnik said. “Losing elimination status is a sad thing, but it really makes it so much more urgent to get vaccinated, because now we know that the likelihood people are going to be exposed to measles is so much higher. “I think we can course-correct. We can rebuild trust. It’s just going to take time,” she said. “This didn’t happen overnight, and we’re not going to be able to change it overnight.” CNN’s Deidre McPhillips and Brenda Goodman contributed to this report. news.title: The U.S. has lost measles elimination status. Here's what that means and who is most at risk. - CBS News

news.content: Latest U.S. Iran War Trump Remarks World Politics Entertainment HealthWatch MoneyWatch Crime Space Sports Brand Studio The Free Press Local News Atlanta Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas Live CBS News 24/7 Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas 48 Hours 60 Minutes Shows 48 Hours 60 Minutes CBS Evening News CBS Mornings CBS Morning News CBS Reports CBS Saturday Morning The Daily Report The Dish Face the Nation Sunday Morning The Takeout Things That Matter The Uplift CBS News Investigates CBS News Confirmed Podcasts Newsletters Download Our App CBS News Team Executive Team Brand Studio Paramount+ Join Our Talent Community RSS Feeds Watch CBS News HealthWatch The U.S. has lost measles elimination status. Here's what that means and who is most at risk. By Kerry Breen Kerry Breen News Editor Kerry Breen is a news editor at CBSNews.com. A graduate of New York University's Arthur L. Carter School of Journalism, she previously worked at NBC News' TODAY Digital. She covers current events, breaking news and issues including substance use. Read Full Bio Kerry Breen Updated on: November 17, 2026 / 4:24 PM EST / CBS News Add CBS News on Google The United States has officially lost its measles elimination status, global health officials announced Tuesday. The decision from the Pan American Health Organization came after the U.S. recorded over 5,400 measles cases so far this year — more than double last year's total. The Pan American Health Organization is a regional office for the World Health Organization, covering North and South America. Researchers with knowledge of the decision had previously confirmed it to CBS News partner KFF Health News on Saturday. A country is considered as having eliminated the measles if there are "no locally transmitted measles infections or outbreaks lasting 12 months or longer," according to the World Health Organization. The United States did not meet that standard for the first time since 2000. According to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, about a third of this year's measles cases are linked to outbreaks that began in 2025 and continued to spread. After a 30-year record of 2,242 cases last year, the CDC has tallied 5,412 cases to date in 2026, resulting in more than 590 hospitalizations and at least six measles-related deaths, with some states reporting additional fatalities. "It's profoundly sad and disappointing," Dr. William Schaffner, a professor of preventive medicine and infectious diseases at the Vanderbilt University Medical Center, told CBS News. "What a tragedy. We have had children die of measles this past year. That should never have happened. Those deaths and all those cases, 5,000-plus, were completely preventable." The biggest outbreak has been in Pennsylvania, where state health officials have reported more than 1,500 cases and seven deaths associated with the disease this year. Wisconsin reports two children have died and New York had its first measles death in more than 30 years. Measles cases have been confirmed so far this year in 45 states and Washington, D.C. "The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does," CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz said in a statement. "We know where transmission is occurring and we've invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities." She said the CDC remains focused on stopping outbreaks. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said Tuesday on social media, "We will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status. I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles." Kennedy pointed to "COVID-era disruptions" in childhood vaccinations and cited other countries, including Canada, Mexico, Spain and the United Kingdom, that have also lost measles elimination status. Sen. Bill Cassidy, a Republican from Louisiana who is also a doctor, said health officials, including Kennedy, should be doing more to promote the importance of vaccination to protect against measles. "Speaking as a physician, you may decide not to be vaccinated because it's your free will, but the child who's too young to be vaccinated is vulnerable if you come into that child's presence, and we're seeing children die from measles who are too young to be vaccinated," Cassidy said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan." "So if you've not been vaccinated, you could be the person that brings death to another. That's something to remember." What does it mean to lose measles elimination status? A country or region loses its measles elimination status once its population immunity lowers enough that there is sustained spread of the disease, CBS News medical correspondent Dr. Céline Gounder explained. When a country has measles elimination status and a high rate of vaccination, a case of measles or small outbreak will soon fizzle out. But when there are this many gaps in the population's immunity, there can be "ongoing chains of transmission," Gounder said. "It means that we're at risk of being exposed to measles and getting measles if we're not vaccinated," Gounder said. "It means ERs and pediatricians need to consider measles in anyone with a fever and rash, whether they've traveled overseas or not. And we may now become an exporter of measles to other countries." Dr. Omer Awan, a trained epidemiologist and senior public health contributor for Forbes, said that the loss of measles elimination status is a setback to the nation's public health infrastructure. "It's frustrating and heartbreaking ... because we have the tools to fight this. The tool is the MMR vaccine, which we know is 97% effective at preventing the onset of measles," Awan said. "It'd be one thing if we didn't have the tools to fight this, but the tools are at our disposal, we just aren't using the tools that can help us mitigate the spread and beat measles." How can the U.S. regain measles elimination status? A country earns measles elimination status by ensuring there is no local spread of the disease or outbreaks that last for more than a year. PAHO says that the best way to maintain the elimination of measles is maintaining a vaccination rate of 95% or higher. Countries should also have sensitive surveillance systems to detect cases quickly, laboratory capacity and a guaranteed rapid response to outbreaks. Data about these trends must be submitted to and verified by the organization. For the U.S. to curb outbreaks and regain measles elimination status, it needs to return to higher rates of vaccination, Awan said. He said battling misinformation and ramping up vaccination campaigns would be key to that effort. Data shows childhood vaccination rates have declined in many communities around the U.S. in recent years, often below the threshold needed to help ward off measles outbreaks. Gounder also noted that lawmakers can create policies that lead to increased vaccination rates. "States set the school vaccine rules. Nine states made opting out of vaccination easier in 2025. States ending nonmedical exemptions saw kindergarten vaccination rise 2 to 4 points," Gounder said. "Most legislatures reconvene in January. Your state lawmakers will write next year's exemption rules." Measles in the U.S. The United States started collecting national data on measles in 1912, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. About 6,000 measles-related deaths were reported each year in the first decade of that data collection. In the decade between 1953 and 1963, nearly all children in the U.S. caught measles before they turned 15, with an estimated 3 to 4 million people infected each year and tens of thousands hospitalized, according to the CDC. In those years, 400 to 500 people, mostly children, died of measles annually. Then in 1963, the measles vaccine first became widely available. The numbers began a sharp decline and several generations of Americans grew up without ever encountering measles. By 1981, reported measles cases had dropped by 80% compared to the previous year, the CDC said. The country was officially declared as having eliminated measles in 2000. The U.S. maintained its elimination status for over 25 years. That didn't mean there were no cases at all — in 2015, an outbreak that spread among unvaccinated people was traced back to overseas visitors at Disneyland in Southern California, and a 2018-19 outbreak in New York was eventually contained by public health measures including curtailing vaccine exemptions. But those spikes were just a fraction of the spread now being seen in the U.S. The nation recorded 2,242 measles cases in 2025, according to CDC data, linked to 48 separate outbreaks. The CDC reported 245 hospitalizations, mostly in children, and three measles deaths last year. Infections were confirmed in at least 44 states. It was the most cases the country had seen in over three decades. That record was shattered in 2026, when the U.S. recorded more than double that number of cases by October — a total that topped 5,000 earlier this month. Almost all of the cases have been in people who were not vaccinated. Measles-related deaths have been reported in Pennsylvania, New York and Wisconsin. The CDC said 43 new outbreaks — defined as three or more related cases — have been reported so far in 2026, while about a third of the cases reported this year are tied to outbreaks that have been ongoing since 2025. Who is at risk from measles? Measles is one of the most contagious infectious diseases. Those who are unvaccinated for the disease are most at risk of getting it. CDC data shows that 96% of people infected with measles in 2026 had not been vaccinated for measles or were unsure of their vaccination status; only 2% of cases were in people who'd been fully vaccinated. Medical research has shown that two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is extremely safe and effective at protecting against measles. But some people — including babies, pregnant women or people with weakened immune systems — cannot get vaccinated and must rely on population immunity to keep the disease from spreading. "They will be the ones that are most vulnerable to getting infected and experiencing the complications," such as pneumonia or encephalitis, Awan said. Many of the recent cases have been occurring in tight-knit and largely unvaccinated Amish or Mennonite communities. "It really shows you who's vulnerable because these are totally unvaccinated communities," said Dr. Deborah Birx, a longtime public health official who was a leader of the White House Coronavirus Task Force during the pandemic. "You can see it in who's hospitalized. The largest percentage are children under 4 and adults over 50." "I hope this is a wake-up call to every parent," Birx told CBS News. "If you had decided to not vaccinate your children, you've been relatively protected by all of us and all of our grandchildren and other children who got vaccinated. But that protection and that shield is going away" as vaccination rates slip. "And so your child is now vulnerable at a level they never were vulnerable before." Measles is known for causing a rash, but Schaffner said that's the least of it. "What's bothersome is children, even with uncomplicated measles, are miserable for a week or a week and a half with red eyes, runny nose, cough, and just debilitating fever and diarrhea. And then you have the complications of dehydration, pneumonia, and on occasion, encephalitis." There can be other lingering health consequences, Birx warned. Measles patients "can end up with what we call immune suppression, so that they're more susceptible to all other diseases after they've had measles." While many people recover, measles can cause severe infections in the lungs and brain that can lead to cognitive issues, deafness or death. "Measles is a nasty, nasty virus," Schaffner said. "In contrast, the vaccine is wonderfully effective." "It really shows you who's vulnerable because these are totally unvaccinated communities," said Dr. Deborah Birx, a longtime public health official who was a leader of the White House Coronavirus Task Force during the pandemic. "You can see it in who's hospitalized. The largest percentage are children under 4 and adults over 50." "I hope this is a wake-up call to every parent," Birx told CBS News. "If you had decided to not vaccinate your children, you've been relatively protected by all of us and all of our grandchildren and other children who got vaccinated. But that protection and that shield is going away" as vaccination rates slip. "And so your child is now vulnerable at a level they never were vulnerable before." Measles is known for causing a rash, but Schaffner said that's the least of it. "What's bothersome is children, even with uncomplicated measles, are miserable for a week or a week and a half with red eyes, runny nose, cough, and just debilitating fever and diarrhea. And then you have the complications of dehydration, pneumonia, and on occasion, encephalitis." There can be other lingering health consequences, Birx warned. Measles patients "can end up with what we call immune suppression, so that they're more susceptible to all other diseases after they've had measles." While many people recover, measles can cause severe infections in the lungs and brain that can lead to cognitive issues, deafness or death. "Measles is a nasty, nasty virus," Schaffner said. "In contrast, the vaccine is wonderfully effective." news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, November 21, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Animal Morbilliviruses Mirror Genetic Mutations Driving Fatal Human Measles Brain Complications by November 17, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 7 mins read 0 Animal Morbilliviruses Mirror Genetic Mutations Driving Fatal Human Measles Brain Complications Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Persistent central nervous system infections caused by animal morbilliviruses share fundamental genetic and phenotypic characteristics with human measles virus variants that cause subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, according to a comparative analysis published in One Health Outlook by Rik L. de Swart and Rory D. de Vries examining recent findings from Daniel Roji and colleagues. Morbilliviruses persisting in wild animal hosts evolve analogous molecular mechanisms that favor long-term viral maintenance in brain tissue, characterized primarily by the inactivation of the matrix protein and the acquisition of hyperfusogenic fusion proteins. Measles virus is an enveloped pathogen possessing a negative-strand RNA genome and represents one of the most infectious viral agents affecting humans. Transmitted via the respiratory route, measles virus initiates infection by targeting myeloid and lymphoid cells through the high-affinity cellular receptor CD150, also known as SLAMF1. This initial phase generates a cell-associated viremia that disseminates the virus throughout host lymphoid tissues, accompanied by infected immune cell infiltration into peripheral organs. In later stages of pathogenesis, the virus utilizes a second receptor, nectin-4, located at epithelial adherens junctions to infect epithelial cells and keratinocytes. The widespread depletion of memory immune cells induces lymphopenia and prolonged immune amnesia, leaving patients susceptible to opportunistic secondary infections such as pneumonia, diarrhoea, and otitis media. While the adaptive immune response typically clears acute measles and provides lifelong immunity, measles virus can in rare instances establish a persistent central nervous system infection. This persistent state can resurface after a clinically silent incubation period lasting several years as subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, a neurological disease that is invariably fatal. Therapeutic interventions currently available provide at best transient clinical improvement, and the infection relentlessly progresses despite high concentrations of measles-specific antibodies in both serum and cerebrospinal fluid. Genomic characterization of measles virus recovered from the brains of deceased subacute sclerosing panencephalitis patients reveals extensive biased hypermutation, often displaying profiles characteristic of adenosine deaminase acting on RNA (ADAR1) activity. Although specific mutational patterns diverge across individual clinical cases, they exhibit marked functional convergence. Specifically, genomes isolated from persistent central nervous system cases consistently encode nonfunctional matrix (M) proteins alongside hyperfusogenic fusion (F) glycoproteins. Inactivation of the matrix gene occurs through premature stop codons, corruption of the translation initiation codon, or hypermutation yielding inactive proteins. Because virion budding requires structural interaction between the matrix protein and the cytoplasmic tail of the fusion glycoprotein, loss of matrix function abolishes the assembly and release of infectious viral particles. Concurrently, mutations in the fusion gene destabilize the fusion trimer, driving a hyperfusogenic phenotype that permits cell-to-cell spread even in host cells lacking CD150 or nectin-4 receptors. In neural tissues where standard morbillivirus receptors are absent, the synaptic cell adhesion molecules CADM1 and CADM2 can trigger viral membrane fusion in cis. This receptor-independent fusion mechanism facilitates the gradual, progressive transfer of viral ribonucleoprotein complexes across synaptic junctions, resulting in widespread brain infection in the absence of budding virions. Related animal morbilliviruses demonstrate comparable pathogenic trajectories across their natural host species. Canine distemper virus in carnivores, phocine distemper virus in seals, and cetacean morbillivirus in whales and dolphins frequently trigger severe disease outbreaks. While canine distemper virus often produces acute neurological complications reminiscent of measles inclusion body encephalitis due to severe immune suppression, it can also produce delayed encephalitis. For instance, old dog encephalitis develops years after initial canine distemper infection, marked by chronic demyelination and persistent viral antigen despite the inability to isolate infectious virus. Similar delayed, chronic central nervous system infections have been observed in stranded harbor seals and dolphins. In the primary study evaluated by de Swart and de Vries, Daniel Roji and colleagues characterized the genomes of morbilliviruses that persisted for multiple years in wild animal brains: canine distemper virus in a lynx, cetacean morbillivirus in a striped dolphin, and phocine distemper virus in two harbor seals. Notably, the harbor seals stranded in 2001 and 2014, approximately 13 and 12 years after major phocine distemper epizootics in 1988 and 2001, mirroring the prolonged latency period observed in human subacute sclerosing panencephalitis. Genomic analysis showed that the viral sequences from the lynx, the dolphin, and one of the seals harbored premature stop codons or hypermutation disrupting the matrix protein, together with mutations conferring thermal instability and hyperfusogenicity in the fusion protein. To evaluate the biological effects of these mutations, the researchers conducted in vitro fusion assays in Vero cells with and without expression of species-specific CD150 receptors from seals, dolphins, dogs, and humans. In three of the four evaluated viruses, cell-to-cell fusion in receptor-negative cells was markedly increased. Furthermore, entry assays using vesicular stomatitis virus particles pseudotyped with morbillivirus glycoproteins bearing truncated cytoplasmic tails confirmed reduced entry capacity in CD150-expressing cells, corroborating the functional shift away from canonical receptor-dependent entry. Detailed experimental investigation of the lynx canine distemper virus isolate revealed that a single amino acid substitution in the fusion protein, designated P479A, was sufficient to explain the hyperfusogenic phenotype. Recombinant canine distemper virus harboring this P479A substitution displayed severe attenuation in CD150-expressing Vero cells and required passaging exclusively through infected canine B cells. However, despite impaired propagation in lymphoid cells, the mutant virus exhibited enhanced infectivity and dissemination in organotypic brain slice cultures derived from ferrets. This shift closely parallels previous experimental findings by Schmitz and colleagues, where chimeric measles virus bearing a fusion gene from a human subacute sclerosing panencephalitis case lost lymphotropism while efficiently propagating through human neural networks. The study highlights how naturally occurring animal morbillivirus infections provide critical insights into human neuropathology, particularly given the absence of tractable animal models that reproduce the multi-year latency of subacute sclerosing panencephalitis. Emerging organoid cultures allow researchers to evaluate the functional consequences of specific viral mutations, yet they cannot determine whether such mutations act as initial seeding requirements for neuroinvasion or emerge during subsequent intra-host persistence. A comparative One Health framework tracking natural morbillivirus infections in diverse hosts could identify predictive molecular biomarkers, potentially enabling the early detection of persistent central nervous system infection before fatal neurological damage occurs. Expanding the current understanding of viral persistence, Roji et al. argue that naturally occurring animal infections offer a distinct advantage for studying subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE). Because clinical reports of SSPE typically focus on the terminal stage of disease, baseline knowledge of the progression during years of silent incubation is limited. By studying animal cases across various species, the researchers suggest that these instances function as natural experiments. This initial phase generates a cell-associated viremia that disseminates the virus throughout host lymphoid tissues, accompanied by infected immune cell infiltration into peripheral organs. In later stages of pathogenesis, the virus utilizes a second receptor, nectin-4, located at epithelial adherens junctions to infect epithelial cells and keratinocytes. The widespread depletion of memory immune cells induces lymphopenia and prolonged immune amnesia, leaving patients susceptible to opportunistic secondary infections such as pneumonia, diarrhoea, and otitis media. While the adaptive immune response typically clears acute measles and provides lifelong immunity, measles virus can in rare instances establish a persistent central nervous system infection. This persistent state can resurface after a clinically silent incubation period lasting several years as subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, a neurological disease that is invariably fatal. Therapeutic interventions currently available provide at best transient clinical improvement, and the infection relentlessly progresses despite high concentrations of measles-specific antibodies in both serum and cerebrospinal fluid. Genomic characterization of measles virus recovered from the brains of deceased subacute sclerosing panencephalitis patients reveals extensive biased hypermutation, often displaying profiles characteristic of adenosine deaminase acting on RNA (ADAR1) activity. Although specific mutational patterns diverge across individual clinical cases, they exhibit marked functional convergence. Specifically, genomes isolated from persistent central nervous system cases consistently encode nonfunctional matrix (M) proteins alongside hyperfusogenic fusion (F) glycoproteins. Inactivation of the matrix gene occurs through premature stop codons, corruption of the translation initiation codon, or hypermutation yielding inactive proteins. news.title: United States officially loses measles elimination status after years of vaccination decline

news.content: Skip to Content Open Navigation Menu The Observer About Staff Contact Us Letters to the editor Farewells Application The Observer Open Search Bar Search this site Submit Search Open Navigation Menu The Observer About The Observer Contact News Life Opinion Sports Fun Videos The Observer Open Search Bar Search this site Submit Search Open Navigation Menu The Observer About The Observer Contact News Life Opinion Sports Fun Videos The Observer Open Search Bar Search this site Submit Search Categories: News United States officially loses measles elimination status after years of vaccination decline Hana Ruran, Contributing Writer November 20, 2026 The United States has officially lost its measles elimination status as of Nov. 13, due to the fact that the virus has circulated for over a year. This decision was made by the Pan American Health Organization after the status was granted 26 years ago. The recent spread could be attributed to the decline in immunization rates of the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine. Nara and Dvids On Nov. 13, the United States lost its measles elimination status. The decision was made by the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) during an annual review meeting held from Nov. 10 through Nov. 13, in which they concluded that the measles virus had circulated continuously within the country for longer than 12 months. This ended the U.S.’s 26-year-long measles elimination status record, which was initially declared in 2000. For measles to be declared “eliminated” in a country, it must have an “absence of endemic measles transmission in a defined geographical area for [at least] 12 months in the presence of a well-performing surveillance system,” according to the World Health Organization (WHO). In the case of the U.S., the virus has been reported to be spreading locally from person to person. Earlier this year, the U.S. National Sustainability Committee for the Elimination of Measles, Rubella, and Congenital Rubella Syndrome and committee chair, Noel T. Brewer, responsible for reviewing the CDC’s evidence and informing the PAHO’s decision regarding the U.S. ‘s measles elimination status, warned that the U.S. could lose its status. “Regardless of the outcome of our meeting and PAHO’s decision in November, the U.S. clearly has a measles problem,” Brewer said. Reasons for the prior speculation of the U.S. losing its measles elimination status include the fact that in 2025, the country faced 2,289 confirmed cases of measles across 45 states, causing three deaths. As of Nov. 12 of this year, there have been 5,412 confirmed measles cases in the U.S. among 47 states, including six confirmed deaths. In 2000, there were only 86 measles cases in the U.S. The increase in measles cases in recent years has been largely attributed to the decrease in two-dose immunization rates of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine among U.S. kindergarteners. The target to achieve herd immunity for a population is for 95% to have a two-dose vaccination status, according to the WHO. Throughout the 2010s, two-dose MMR coverage among U.S. kindergarteners was right below this 95% target, and it reached a national high of 95.2% in the 2019-2020 school year. However, beginning in the 2020-2021 school year, two-dose MMR coverage rates fell to 93.9%, and they have continued to decrease since then. For the 2025-2026 school year, the rate was reported to be 92.4%, according to the Centers for Disease Control (CDC). Brewer said this loss of measles elimination status is evidence that the system we had to prevent measles no longer works and that public health education measures need to be taken to fix this. “The nation needs strong, positive communications to the public about the importance of measles, mumps, and rubella vaccination and promotion of health care providers as trusted advisors on immunizations,” Brewer said. He also stated the importance of the government in cultivating public trust in vaccines. “A dedicated communication campaign led by the federal government would be usual in past years at this stage,” he said. “These communications need clear, vocal, and regular support from the highest levels of the U.S. government.” However, the current executive branch administration does not support the CDC’s child vaccination recommendations. U.S. Health and Human Services secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has been leading the anti-vaccination movement in recent years. On Jan. 5, he led the CDC in reducing the number of diseases covered by recommended vaccines on the childhood immunization schedule from 17 to 11. On Mar. 16, this was preliminarily enjoined by the U.S. District Court in Massachusetts in American Academy of Pediatrics v. Kennedy, but the case remains ongoing. Further, on Aug. 10, President Donald Trump published an executive order calling for a change to the current child vaccination recommendations, including splitting the MMR vaccine into three separate vaccines administered at three separate visits. “Together, there could be a possibility they’re quite lethal,” said Trump, according to The Associated Press. “And separately, it looks like they are not at all lethal but just very effective.” In a statement released on Nov. 17, the CDC insisted that its immediate plan as a result of the status change would be to “equip state, local, tribal, and territorial health departments with tools and technical support to identify communities at increased risk, engage trusted partners, detect cases quickly, and respond effectively to outbreaks.” “The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does,” said CDC director Dr. Erica Schwartz. news.content_original: Skip to Content Open Navigation Menu The Observer About Staff Contact Us Letters to the editor Farewells Application The Observer Open Search Bar Search this site Submit Search Open Navigation Menu The Observer About The Observer Contact News Life Opinion Sports Fun Videos The Observer Open Search Bar Search this site Submit Search Open Navigation Menu The Observer About The Observer Contact News Life Opinion Sports Fun Videos The Observer Open Search Bar Search this site Submit Search Categories: News United States officially loses measles elimination status after years of vaccination decline Hana Ruran, Contributing Writer November 20, 2026 The United States has officially lost its measles elimination status as of Nov. 13, due to the fact that the virus has circulated for over a year. This decision was made by the Pan American Health Organization after the status was granted 26 years ago. The recent spread could be attributed to the decline in immunization rates of the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine. Nara and Dvids On Nov. 13, the United States lost its measles elimination status. The decision was made by the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) during an annual review meeting held from Nov. 10 through Nov. 13, in which they concluded that the measles virus had circulated continuously within the country for longer than 12 months. This ended the U.S.’s 26-year-long measles elimination status record, which was initially declared in 2000. For measles to be declared “eliminated” in a country, it must have an “absence of endemic measles transmission in a defined geographical area for [at least] 12 months in the presence of a well-performing surveillance system,” according to the World Health Organization (WHO). In the case of the U.S., the virus has been reported to be spreading locally from person to person. Earlier this year, the U.S. National Sustainability Committee for the Elimination of Measles, Rubella, and Congenital Rubella Syndrome and committee chair, Noel T. Brewer, responsible for reviewing the CDC’s evidence and informing the PAHO’s decision regarding the U.S. ‘s measles elimination status, warned that the U.S. could lose its status. “Regardless of the outcome of our meeting and PAHO’s decision in November, the U.S. clearly has a measles problem,” Brewer said. Reasons for the prior speculation of the U.S. losing its measles elimination status include the fact that in 2025, the country faced 2,289 confirmed cases of measles across 45 states, causing three deaths. As of Nov. 12 of this year, there have been 5,412 confirmed measles cases in the U.S. among 47 states, including six confirmed deaths. In 2000, there were only 86 measles cases in the U.S. The increase in measles cases in recent years has been largely attributed to the decrease in two-dose immunization rates of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine among U.S. kindergarteners. The target to achieve herd immunity for a population is for 95% to have a two-dose vaccination status, according to the WHO. Throughout the 2010s, two-dose MMR coverage among U.S. kindergarteners was right below this 95% target, and it reached a national high of 95.2% in the 2019-2020 school year. However, beginning in the 2020-2021 school year, two-dose MMR coverage rates fell to 93.9%, and they have continued to decrease since then. For the 2025-2026 school year, the rate was reported to be 92.4%, according to the Centers for Disease Control (CDC). Brewer said this loss of measles elimination status is evidence that the system we had to prevent measles no longer works and that public health education measures need to be taken to fix this. “The nation needs strong, positive communications to the public about the importance of measles, mumps, and rubella vaccination and promotion of health care providers as trusted advisors on immunizations,” Brewer said. He also stated the importance of the government in cultivating public trust in vaccines. “A dedicated communication campaign led by the federal government would be usual in past years at this stage,” he said. “These communications need clear, vocal, and regular support from the highest levels of the U.S. government.” However, the current executive branch administration does not support the CDC’s child vaccination recommendations. U.S. Health and Human Services secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has been leading the anti-vaccination movement in recent years. On Jan. 5, he led the CDC in reducing the number of diseases covered by recommended vaccines on the childhood immunization schedule from 17 to 11. On Mar. 16, this was preliminarily enjoined by the U.S. District Court in Massachusetts in American Academy of Pediatrics v. Kennedy, but the case remains ongoing. Further, on Aug. 10, President Donald Trump published an executive order calling for a change to the current child vaccination recommendations, including splitting the MMR vaccine into three separate vaccines administered at three separate visits. “Together, there could be a possibility they’re quite lethal,” said Trump, according to The Associated Press. “And separately, it looks like they are not at all lethal but just very effective.” In a statement released on Nov. 17, the CDC insisted that its immediate plan as a result of the status change would be to “equip state, local, tribal, and territorial health departments with tools and technical support to identify communities at increased risk, engage trusted partners, detect cases quickly, and respond effectively to outbreaks.” “The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does,” said CDC director Dr. Erica Schwartz. US loses its measles elimination status, a historic setback for American health The San Juan Daily Star 2 days ago 4 min read A vial of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine at a hospital in Seminole, Texas on Feb. 24, 2025. As vaccination rates have dropped, cases of the once-extinguished measles virus have soared. (Desiree Ríos/The New York Times) By TEDDY ROSENBLUTH Measles has come roaring back in the United States, as vaccination rates have fallen and cases of the once-extinguished virus have soared. That backslide has now cost the nation its measles elimination status, after the virus spread uninterrupted for more than a year. “It’s a giant stain on our reputation,” said Jennifer Nuzzo, director of the Pandemic Center at the Brown University School of Public Health. “Everyone ought to be just utterly disgusted by the willing return back to an age of death and high cost.” The announcement, made Tuesday by the Pan American Health Organization, ushers in a new era in which major outbreaks could routinely disrupt communities around the nation, sickening thousands of children. It also marks a highly embarrassing reversal for a country that showed the rest of the world it was possible to rein in the wildly contagious virus when it won elimination status in 2000. State health officials have reported more than 7,700 cases of measles, including 10 deaths, since the resurgence first kicked off in a Mennonite community in Texas in January 2025. Hundreds have been hospitalized, many of them unvaccinated children. Infections have also risen among pregnant women and newborns, who are at increased risk of death and other dire health consequences. “Losing measles elimination status has broader implications than losing a public health designation,” said Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, director of the Pan American Health Organization, in a news conference announcing the decision. “It means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period of time, putting families and communities at the risk of preventable illness, hospitalization and death.” The organization also announced Tuesday that Bolivia and Mexico had also lost measles elimination status, posing another setback for North America’s handle on the highly contagious virus. Canada officially lost its measles elimination status last year. “None of this had to happen,” said Dr. Peter Hotez, a vaccine scientist and pediatrician at the Baylor College of Medicine. “That’s what’s so tragic.” America was once regarded as a global leader for reining in the highly contagious virus. Now, large outbreaks that sicken thousands could become routine. Chart shows outbreaks since Jan. 2025 by week. The circumstances that have allowed measles to take root again in the United States have been brewing for years, public health experts said. Vaccination rates, which began falling during the COVID-19 pandemic, have continued to drop, and now sit well below the 95% needed to establish herd immunity. In some communities, including many of the insular religious groups hit hardest by measles outbreaks, an even smaller share of children are vaccinated. But experts said under the leadership of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., federal health officials did too little to control outbreaks early on. And they criticized Kennedy himself for at times directly undermining efforts to improve vaccination rates, by promoting unproven treatments for measles and undermining confidence in childhood vaccines. “I don’t think it’s an accident that this is happening under the current administration,” said Dr. William Moss, an epidemiologist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health who has studied measles for more than 25 years. Grace Davis Jamison, a spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, said in a statement that the department would continue working to “stop transmission, close vaccination gaps, strengthen outbreak response and protect Americans from measles.” Jamison said that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention convened a meeting this year to develop a national strategy to regain elimination status. (Losing measles elimination status does not carry any formal penalty.) “We know where transmission is occurring and we’ve invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities,” Dr. Erica Schwartz, the director of the CDC, said in a statement. In a post on the social platform X published Tuesday afternoon, Kennedy added that his department would continue to “support Americans who become ill, regardless of vaccination status, and for the first time equip healthcare providers with guidance to diagnose and treat measles and its complications.” Regaining elimination status is likely to be a monumental task, one that experts said may require a vast public education campaign, investment in on-the-ground immunization efforts and a push to strengthen school vaccination requirements, which several states have loosened in recent years. Even if the CDC and cash-strapped state public health departments make that kind of investment, it will probably be “many years before we get the situation back under control,” said Dr. David Kimberlin, a pediatric infectious disease expert at the University of Alabama at Birmingham. While there were measles cases in the United States between 2000 and 2025, there were fewer than 200 cases most years, and many of them tied to international travel. When the virus did strike an unvaccinated community, the outbreaks did not continue for longer than a year, allowing the country to maintain its status. That meant that many doctors around the country had never seen a case of measles before last year, when more children started arriving at hospitals gasping for breath or experiencing life-threatening brain swelling. Many of those infected since 2025 have been young children, and several of the deaths have been in infants too young to be vaccinated. “We are going to see a growing number of children, as well as young adults, dying from measles,” said Dr. Daniel Salas, who helps lead immunization efforts at the Pan American Health Organization. That is not to mention the long-term health repercussions that are now “baked into our future,” said Dr. Cameron Wolfe, professor of infectious diseases at the Duke University School of Medicine. Even patients who appear to have recovered from measles may fall ill with an entirely different infection months or years later, because the virus weakens the immune system and leaves it more vulnerable to other threats. Since 2025, measles has cost the country roughly $125 million in medical care, lost productivity and public health resources, according to one estimate. Public health experts are hopeful that the country will eventually reverse course, but some fear it will happen only after Americans see death and disability caused by measles in their own communities. “Short of that, I’m not sure how to change the direction of this ship,” Kimberlin said. “That would take a lot of small coffins in the ground.” Recent Posts See All The numbers behind a stunning upset in Mississippi New Yorkers are bracing. In a post on the social platform X published Tuesday afternoon, Kennedy added that his department would continue to “support Americans who become ill, regardless of vaccination status, and for the first time equip healthcare providers with guidance to diagnose and treat measles and its complications.” Regaining elimination status is likely to be a monumental task, one that experts said may require a vast public education campaign, investment in on-the-ground immunization efforts and a push to strengthen school vaccination requirements, which several states have loosened in recent years. Even if the CDC and cash-strapped state public health departments make that kind of investment, it will probably be “many years before we get the situation back under control,” said Dr. David Kimberlin, a pediatric infectious disease expert at the University of Alabama at Birmingham. While there were measles cases in the United States between 2000 and 2025, there were fewer than 200 cases most years, and many of them tied to international travel. When the virus did strike an unvaccinated community, the outbreaks did not continue for longer than a year, allowing the country to maintain its status. That meant that many doctors around the country had never seen a case of measles before last year, when more children started arriving at hospitals gasping for breath or experiencing life-threatening brain swelling. Many of those infected since 2025 have been young children, and several of the deaths have been in infants too young to be vaccinated. “We are going to see a growing number of children, as well as young adults, dying from measles,” said Dr. Daniel Salas, who helps lead immunization efforts at the Pan American Health Organization. That is not to mention the long-term health repercussions that are now “baked into our future,” said Dr. Cameron Wolfe, professor of infectious diseases at the Duke University School of Medicine. Even patients who appear to have recovered from measles may fall ill with an entirely different infection months or years later, because the virus weakens the immune system and leaves it more vulnerable to other threats. Since 2025, measles has cost the country roughly $125 million in medical care, lost productivity and public health resources, according to one estimate. Public health experts are hopeful that the country will eventually reverse course, but some fear it will happen only after Americans see death and disability caused by measles in their own communities. “Short of that, I’m not sure how to change the direction of this ship,” Kimberlin said. “That would take a lot of small coffins in the ground.” Recent Posts See All The numbers behind a stunning upset in Mississippi New Yorkers are bracing. Newsletters♡Donate Now Menu Search Sign in Menu Programs & Podcasts Schedule Ways to Give Search Sign in Health Erica Zurek November 19, 2026 12:45 PM Minnesota measles cases hit 36-year high as U.S. loses elimination status With more cases expected in the coming weeks and months, health officials stress that vaccination remains the best way to protect individuals, families, and vulnerable community members. Ronaldo Schemidt | AFP via Getty Images Go Deeper. Create an account or log in to save stories. Log in Like this? Thanks for liking this story! We have added it to a list of your favorite stories. Show me! Save Share Quick Read Nearly all reported cases in the state involve individuals who have not received the recommended two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine. Children under the age of 18 accounted for the majority of these cases. Minnesota is experiencing its highest number of measles cases since 1990, with 203 cases reported so far in 2026. That is a 27 percent increase over the number reported last week. This surge has prompted health officials to urge residents to check their vaccination records to make sure they are up to date. According to the Minnesota Department of Health, the largest cluster of measles cases is in Todd County, where 177 cases have been identified. Nearly all reported cases in the state involve individuals who have not received the recommended two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine. Children under the age of 18 accounted for the majority of these cases. Earlier this week, measles was once again declared endemic in the U.S. after being declared eradicated in the country in 2000, marking a troubling backslide in the country’s public health status. The Pan American Health Organization reported that the virus has been circulating in the country for at least 12 months, leaving communities vulnerable to continued transmission. “It is a sad day for public health. Although this news did not come as a surprise, it is both devastating and alarming to those of us who work in public health. Eliminating measles, the most contagious disease on earth, from the U.S. was one of the most significant public health success stories in history,” said the Minnesota Department of Health in a statement regarding the loss of measles elimination status in the U.S. Turn Up Your Support MPR News helps you turn down the noise and build shared understanding. Turn up your support for this public resource and keep trusted journalism accessible to all. State health officials are concerned that the outbreak could worsen as measles continues to spread across the country, with more than 5,400 cases reported in the U.S. so far this year. The highly contagious disease can cause serious complications, including lifelong health problems, brain damage, pregnancy complications and death. Symptoms of a measles infection include high fever, cough, runny nose and watery eyes followed by a full-body rash. The disease can be especially dangerous for babies and young children. Health officials emphasize that vaccination is the most effective way to protect against measles and prevent the virus’s spread. “The measles, mumps and rubella vaccine is well-tested, highly effective and provides long-lasting protection,” said Dr. Brooke Cunningham, Minnesota’s health commissioner, encouraging residents to get vaccinated. The MMR vaccine is typically administered in two doses. The first dose of the vaccine is recommended at 12 to 15 months of age and may be given in combination with other vaccines. The second dose is recommended between 4 and 6 years of age. The vaccine has been in use for over five decades and is considered safe and effective by both the World Health Organization and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. It usually provides lifelong protection. Health officials say declining vaccination rates since the COVID-19 pandemic have left many children and communities vulnerable. Residents are advised to review their immunization records and contact a healthcare provider, local health department or pharmacy if they need the vaccine. With more cases expected in the coming weeks and months, health officials stress that vaccination remains the best way to protect individuals, families, and vulnerable community members. “The loss of measles elimination status is a historic and deeply troubling setback for American public health,” said Michael Osterholm, director of the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy, in response to the Pan American Health Organization’s formal withdrawal of the United States’ measles elimination status. “We know how to stop measles and better protect our communities; reversing this trend will require a renewed national commitment to vaccination and clear and consistent public health leadership.” With measles spreading, do you need a booster shot? news.title: US loses measles elimination status. Was Alabama affected?
news.excerpt: America is no longer considered measles-free after record case counts. Here's what happened and how Alabama has been affected.
news.rss_summary_html: America is no longer considered measles-free after record case counts. Here's what happened and how Alabama has been affected.

news.content_title: US loses measles elimination status. Was Alabama affected?
news.content: News Sports Restaurants Real Estate Opinion Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals NEWS US loses measles elimination status. Was Alabama affected? Jennifer Lindahl Montgomery Advertiser Nov. 18, 2026, 1:34 p.m. ET The United States has lost its measles elimination status for the first time since 2000, marking a major setback in the nation’s efforts to control a highly contagious disease that was once considered eliminated. The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) announced Nov. 17 that the United States no longer meets the requirements for measles elimination after the virus continued circulating for more than 12 consecutive months. The decision comes as measles infections have climbed nationwide, with more than 5,400 cases reported in 2026. Alabama has reported relatively few infections compared with states experiencing major outbreaks. However, state health officials confirmed a measles case involving an adult in the Huntsville area. Why did the United States lose its measles elimination status? PAHO determined that the same measles virus lineage had circulated for at least 12 consecutive months, meeting the threshold for losing elimination status. The United States achieved measles elimination status in 2000 after vaccination efforts successfully interrupted continuous domestic transmission of the virus. The designation did not mean measles could never enter the country again. Infections brought in by international travelers could still occur. However, public health officials were able to prevent the virus from spreading continuously within the United States. How many measles cases have been reported in Alabama? The Alabama Department of Public Health confirmed a measles infection involving an adult who lives in the Northern Public Health District. The individual had traveled internationally before testing positive for measles on Oct. 8. Health officials believe the person contracted the virus outside the United States. The CDC’s Nov. 12 national report lists two measles cases in Alabama for 2026, while ADPH’s current information identifies the October case. Which states have the most measles cases in 2026? Measles outbreaks have affected communities across the country, with Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Wisconsin and Utah among the hardest-hit states. According to CDC data updated Nov. 12, 2026, the states reporting the highest numbers of cases include: Pennsylvania: 1,529 cases South Carolina: 670 cases Utah: 536 cases Wisconsin: 505 cases Pennsylvania and Wisconsin have experienced significant increases in infections this year, while South Carolina and Utah have continued to deal with outbreaks that began in 2025. The CDC reported 43 measles outbreaks nationwide in 2026. By comparison, Alabama has reported two cases in the CDC’s national tracking data for 2026. U.S. measles cases reach highest level since 1991 The CDC reported 5,412 confirmed measles cases nationwide as of Nov. 12, 2026. That is more than double the 2,289 cases reported during all of 2025 and a significant increase from the 285 cases recorded in 2024. The 2026 total represents the highest annual number of measles infections in the U.S. since 1991. Health officials have identified declining vaccination rates as a major factor contributing to the resurgence. Declining vaccination rates raise concerns about outbreaks CDC data show that MMR vaccination coverage among kindergarten students declined from 95.2% during the 2019-2020 school year to 92.4% during the 2025-2026 school year. That leaves an estimated 280,000 kindergarten students without the protection provided by the recommended vaccination coverage. Health officials generally recommend that at least 95% of a community be vaccinated to help prevent widespread measles transmission. The measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is approximately 97% effective against measles after two doses. What is measles and what are the symptoms Measles is a highly contagious viral disease that spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. The virus can remain infectious in the air for up to two hours after an infected person leaves an area. People without immunity can become infected simply by entering a contaminated space. Symptoms typically develop seven to 14 days after exposure and include high fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes. A red rash usually begins on the face before spreading to the rest of the body. Small white spots may also appear inside the mouth. Although many people recover, measles can cause serious complications, including pneumonia, ear infections and inflammation of the brain. Young children, especially those younger than 5, face an increased risk of severe illness. Jennifer Lindahl is a Breaking and Trending Reporter in Alabama for USA TODAY’s Deep South Connect Team. news.content: हिंदी മലയാളം Print Edition Support Us Sign in Subscribe Health Agriculture Water Waste Climate Air Africa Data Centre Video Gallery Food Bookshop CSE Bulletins Subscribe Health Agriculture Water Waste Climate Air Africa Data Centre Video Gallery Food Bookshop CSE Bulletins Health US loses measles elimination status as global cases rise Declining childhood vaccination rates, pandemic-related immunity gaps and unequal access to healthcare are fuelling measles outbreaks, threatening decades of progress against a preventable disease A woman with a red, spotty rash on her upper back and shoulders caused by measles.Credit: efired / istockphoto Snigdha Das Published on: 18 Nov 2026, 3:16 am Copied Listen to this article Summary The US has lost its measles-elimination status after 12 months of sustained transmission. Mexico and Bolivia have also lost theirs, joining Canada. Measles is highly contagious and potentially fatal, causing complications such as pneumonia and encephalitis, particularly in young children. Two vaccine doses and 95 per cent population coverage are needed to preventsustainedtransmission. Falling vaccination rates are fuelling the global resurgence, driven by pandemic-related immunisationgaps, rising vaccine exemptions and unequal access to healthcare. The US has officially lost its measles-elimination status, reversing one of its most significant public-health achievements. On November 17, Dr Jarbas Barbosa, director of the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the regional arm of the World Health Organization (WHO), confirmed that the country had failed to contain sustained transmission of the highly contagious disease. Mexico and Bolivia have also lost their elimination status, joining Canada, which was stripped of the distinction last year. The development marks a setback for the Americas, which became the first WHO region to eliminate measles in 2016. The US had achieved elimination in 2000, becoming the first country in the world to do so. For the next 26 years, the disease remained largely under control, with occasional imported cases and local outbreaks failing to establish sustained transmission. Under PAHO's criteria, measles elimination status is lost when the same measles virus genotype and lineage circulate uninterrupted for 12 months or more within a country. "Losing measles elimination status is much more than losing a public-health designation. It means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period, putting families and communities at risk of preventable illness, hospitalisation and death," said Dr Barbosa in a media briefing. As of November 13, 2026, the Americas had reported 58,213 confirmed measles cases and 82 deaths, compared with 12,596 cases during the same period in 2025, Dr Barbosa said. Also Read Measles can ravage the immune system and brain, causing long-term damage — a virologist explains The resurgence is not confined to the Americas. In January 2026, the WHO announced that six countries in its European Region—Armenia, Austria, Azerbaijan, Spain, the UK and Uzbekistan—had lost their measles-elimination status. The decisions were made by the European Regional Verification Commission in September 2025, based on epidemiological data from 2024 showing that endemic measles transmission had been re-established in these countries. The developments underscore the reversal of one of the greatest public health achievements this century. What is measles and how does it spread? Measles is one of the world's most contagious infectious diseases. It spreads primarily through the air when an infected person coughs, sneezes or talks, releasing virus-containing respiratory particles. The virus can remain infectious in the air or on contaminated surfaces for up to two hours. An infected person can transmit the virus to as many as 18 susceptible individuals, making measles considerably more contagious than many other infectious diseases. Transmission can occur from four days before the rash appears to four days afterwards. The disease can affect people of any age, although children are particularly vulnerable, especially those who are unvaccinated or have weakened immune systems. According to the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, measles can cause complications including ear infections, diarrhoea and pneumonia. In more severe cases, it can lead to encephalitis, an inflammation of the brain that may result in permanent brain damage. Severe infections can require hospitalisation and can be fatal. Symptoms generally appear seven to 14 days after exposure to the virus. The disease typically begins with fever, a runny nose, cough and red, watery eyes. A characteristic red rash generally appears three to five days after the initial symptoms, beginning on the face and upper neck before spreading downwards to the trunk, arms, legs and feet. The rash typically spreads over about three days and lasts four to eight days before gradually fading. Although the rash is the most recognisable sign of measles, the disease can cause serious complications, particularly in young children, malnourished individuals and people with weakened immunity. Also Read We study pandemics, and the resurgence of measles is a grim sign of what’s coming Vaccination remains the most effective protection There is no specific antiviral treatment for measles. Vaccination is the most effective way to prevent measles and control outbreaks. According to the WHO, before the introduction of the measles vaccine in 1963 and the expansion of immunisation programmes, major epidemics occurred approximately every two to three years, causing an estimated 2.6 million deaths annually. Accelerated immunisation activities by countries, the WHO, the Measles and Rubella Partnership and other international partners prevented an estimated 59 million deaths between 2000 and 2024; annual measles deaths reduced from 780,000 in 2000 to 95,000 in 2024. Two doses are recommended to provide reliable immunity. Not all children develop sufficient protection after the first dose, making the second essential for closing immunity gaps and preventing outbreaks. In countries where measles is common, the first dose is generally administered at nine months of age. In other countries, it is usually given between 12 and 15 months. A second dose is administered later in childhood, with the timing varying across national programmes. Epidemiologists estimate that at least 95 per cent of the population needs to be fully vaccinated with two doses to prevent sustained transmission and maintain community-level protection. Such high community-wide vaccination coverage not only protects immunised individuals but also helps prevent transmission to those who cannot receive the vaccine, including young infants and some people undergoing cancer treatment. However, recent increases in transmission demonstrate how quickly progress can be undermined when immunisation coverage falls. Also Read 43% increase in measles deaths from 2021-2022: WHO Falling childhood vaccination rates weakening protection Despite the availability of a safe and cost-effective vaccine, WHO estimates that approximately 95,000 people died from measles in 2024, most of them unvaccinated or under-vaccinated children under five. The disease remains particularly prevalent in parts of Africa, Asia and the Eastern Mediterranean, where vaccination coverage is insufficient and access to health services can be limited. According to WHO, global vaccination coverage remains below the levels needed to prevent outbreaks. In 2025, approximately 84 per cent of children received their first dose of measles vaccine and 77 per cent received a complete vaccination course. PAHO also states that declining childhood immunisation rates are a major factor behind the return of sustained transmission in several countries. Also Read Measles could again become widespread as cases surge worldwide In the US, although nearly every state and Washington, DC, requires children to receive both doses before attending public school, exemptions are permitted. Medical exemptions are available for children with certain health conditions, while some states also allow exemptions on religious or personal-belief grounds. The number of children receiving non-medical vaccine exemptions has increased in recent years, while routine vaccination coverage has declined. During the 2024-25 school year, MMR vaccination (combination immunisation against meales, mumps and rubella) coverage among American kindergarten children fell to 92.5 per cent, according to CDC data. This was below the 95 per cent threshold considered necessary to prevent sustained measles transmission and represented the lowest coverage recorded since 2000. The shortfall leaves a growing proportion of children susceptible to infection. When vaccination coverage falls, measles can spread rapidly through schools and communities, particularly among unvaccinated children and those too young to receive the vaccine. The WHO identifies several overlapping factors behind the resurgence of measles, including declining vaccination coverage in countries that have failed to maintain the high two-dose coverage needed to prevent outbreaks, and growing immunity gaps caused by children missing routine vaccinations during the COVID-19 pandemic and in subsequent years. covid-19 The World Health Organization Vaccination Measles MMR Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) Related Stories School of change Bhagirath 14 Nov 2026 The choking games we play Ritu Rao 07 Nov 2026 Daily Court Digest: Major environment orders (October 22, 2026) Susan Chacko 22 Oct 2026 Climate crisis also a crisis of the mind Shruti Sharma 10 Oct 2026 Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information Opt out of the sale or sharing of personal information We won't sell or share your personal information to inform the ads you see.
