news.content: Opens in a new tab News Entertainment Culture Business Health IQ Beauty Videos Search NEWS All NewsPoliticsCrimeCommunity NewsObituariesJustice For All ENTERTAINMENT All EntertainmentTVMoviesPhotosMusicCoversSportsReality CheckCars CULTURE All CultureFashionTravelRelationshipsCocktail & BeerCreative Lens BUSINESS All BusinessBlack IntellectualsCEO to CEODiversity Equity & FocusSisters with SuperpowersHome Ownership & Real EstateEntrepreneurs & Business LeadersExecutive SuiteFinance & WealthMarketing & Branding HEALTH IQ Health IQBe the Match AtlantaFitnessFood & Nutrition BEAUTY All Beauty VIDEOS All Videos EXPERIENCES Browse Places & Events HŌTEL Visit Hōtel FEATURES HBCU CultureShop NewsletterPrivacy Policy Home » News U.S. Loses Measles Elimination Status After 26 Years as Outbreaks Surge Nationwide The decision means the US can no longer claim that measles transmission has been eliminated By Terry Shropshire Nov 18, 2026 6:58 pm (Image source: Youtube/ABC News) The United States has officially lost its measles elimination status for the first time in 26 years, marking a troubling reversal in one of the country’s most significant public health achievements. The announcement, made November 17, 2026, by the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), comes as measles outbreaks continue spreading across the country, with thousands of confirmed infections reported this year. The decision means the United States can no longer claim that measles transmission has been eliminated within its borders. Instead, the virus is considered endemic again, signaling that it has circulated continuously for at least 12 months. A Historic Public Health Achievement Reversed The United States first achieved measles elimination status in 2000 after years of successful vaccination campaigns and public health initiatives dramatically reduced the disease’s spread. However, that progress has been undermined by recurring outbreaks, declining vaccination coverage and pockets of communities where immunization rates remain below recommended levels. PAHO Director Dr. Jarbas Barbosa confirmed that an international monitoring commission recommended withdrawing the country’s elimination designation after determining that the same measles virus lineage had circulated uninterrupted for at least 12 months. “Losing measles elimination status is much more than losing a public health designation. It means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period, putting families and communities at risk of preventable illness, hospitalization and death,” Barbosa said, according to the Associated Press. The United States is not alone in losing its designation. Bolivia and Mexico also lost their measles elimination status following sustained transmission. Canada previously lost its designation in 2025. According to PAHO, the decision underscores the growing challenge of controlling measles throughout the Americas. Thousands of Measles Cases Raise Alarm The loss of elimination status comes during the country’s worst measles resurgence in more than three decades. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the United States recorded 5,412 confirmed measles cases in 2026 as of November 12, following nearly 2,300 cases in 2025. More than 7,000 cases have been reported since the outbreak that began in West Texas in 2025. The overwhelming majority of infections have involved people who were unvaccinated or whose vaccination status was unknown. Measles is among the most contagious infectious diseases in the world. One infected person can spread the virus to as many as 18 susceptible individuals, making outbreaks particularly difficult to contain in communities with low vaccination coverage. Symptoms typically include fever, cough, runny nose, red and watery eyes, and a distinctive rash that usually begins on the face before spreading across the body. Although some people recover without serious complications, measles can cause pneumonia, brain inflammation, blindness and, in severe cases, death. The infection can also weaken the immune system for months afterward. Declining Vaccination Rates Fuel Concern Health officials point to declining childhood vaccination rates as a significant factor behind the resurgence. The measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine remains the most effective protection against the disease. Public health experts generally recommend that at least 95% of a population receive two doses to maintain community protection and prevent sustained transmission. However, CDC data show that only 92.4% of U.S. kindergartners received their required MMR vaccinations during the 2025-2026 school year, compared with 95.2% during the 2019-2020 school year. That decline leaves communities increasingly vulnerable, particularly where vaccination rates are substantially lower than the national average. The CDC has invested $100 million in state and local health departments to help reach communities experiencing outbreaks and close vaccination gaps. The agency also pledged to work with healthcare providers, laboratories and community organizations to strengthen surveillance, improve vaccine access and respond more quickly to new infections. RFK Jr. Pledges to Restore Measles Elimination The announcement also places renewed attention on the federal government’s handling of vaccine policy under Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Kennedy, who has faced criticism over his history of vaccine skepticism, said the administration intends to stop measles outbreaks and restore the country’s elimination status. He has continued to recommend the MMR vaccine while pointing to disruptions in routine childhood immunization during the COVID-19 pandemic as one contributor to declining protection. The agency also reported that several states, including Texas, South Carolina, Virginia, Kansas, New Mexico and Wisconsin, have requested federal assistance to contain outbreaks. Public Health Experts Call for Urgent Action PAHO is urging governments throughout the Americas to strengthen vaccination programs, improve disease surveillance and respond more aggressively to outbreaks. As of November 13, 2026, the region had recorded 58,213 confirmed measles cases and 82 deaths, compared with 12,806 cases during the same period in 2025. Barbosa warned that the situation is serious but not irreversible. “This is a serious warning for our Region, but it is not an irreversible setback,” he said. “We know how to prevent measles, and we know how to stop its transmission.” Recommended Caleb Williams outsells Josh Allen to claim NFL’s top-selling jersey Why is Congress threatening SpaceX over Starshield? US loses measles elimination status, but Illinois has so far avoided major outbreaks Tuesday, Nov 17, 2026 - Posted by Isabel Miller * The New York Times... Measles has come roaring back in the United States, as vaccination rates have fallen and cases of the once-extinguished virus have soared. That backslide has now cost the nation its measles elimination status, after the virus spread uninterrupted for more than a year. “It’s a giant stain on our reputation,” said Jennifer Nuzzo, director of the Pandemic Center at the Brown University School of Public Health. “Everyone ought to be just utterly disgusted by the willing return back to an age of death and high cost.” The announcement, made Tuesday by the Pan American Health Organization, ushers in a new era in which major outbreaks could routinely disrupt communities around the nation, sickening thousands of children. It also marks a highly embarrassing reversal for a country that showed the rest of the world it was possible to rein in the wildly contagious virus when it won elimination status in 2000. State health officials have reported more than 7,700 cases of measles, including 10 deaths, since the resurgence first kicked off in a Mennonite community in Texas in January 2025. Hundreds have been hospitalized, many of them unvaccinated children. Infections have also risen among pregnant women and newborns, who are at increased risk of death and other dire health consequences. * The Sun-Times... While outbreaks have pummeled several states, Illinois continues to see a low count of measles cases. So far in 2026, 29 cases have been reported to the Illinois Department of Public Health. No one has died from the virus or been hospitalized this year. Cook County has only one reported case so far this year. Downstate Douglas County has reported the most with 11 cases. But in previous years, Illinois has reported single-digit case counts or no cases at all. [...] Illinois’ rate for the two-dose measles vaccine is holding steady among school-aged children, according to data from the Illinois State Board of Education. For the 2025-2026 school year, the state’s vaccination rate is 96.8%. Chicago Public Schools rate is 95.7%, an improvement after the district saw a dip in vaccinations coming out of the COVID-19 pandemic. [...] In the Chicago area, “we still do a great job of having most of our children get the two doses of the vaccine,” [Dr. Ravi Jhaveri, the division head of pediatric infectious diseases at Lurie Children’s Hospital,] said. “The risk for us locally is not that high. There will still be small clusters, small outbreaks.” * The county-by-county breakdown from the Illinois Department of Public Health... * Related... * WaPo | CDC declined to alert risk of measles in pregnancy. A journal released the data: The analysis said 112 pregnant women had measles during the 21 months from January 2025 through Sept. 28 of this year. The report found: Twenty-six of the pregnant women with measles were hospitalized for reasons other than labor, although the reason for hospitalization was not reported in every case. Eleven developed pneumonia, two experienced respiratory failure, and one was admitted to intensive care. [...] The analysis provides some of the first contemporary U.S. data on measles during pregnancy in decades and the first from the current outbreak. * NYT | What It Took for America to Wipe Out Measles: There is no known disease more contagious than measles. It can linger for hours in the air and people can spread it days before realizing they are sick. “The measles virus is relentless,” said Dr. Daniel Salas, who helps lead immunization efforts at the Pan American Health Organization, the organization responsible for reviewing the country’s elimination status. “It doesn’t forgive any kind of window of opportunity.” * Politico | In America’s measles epidemic, RFK Jr. is now on trial: Under Kennedy and CDC Director Erica Schwartz, the government “has mounted an aggressive response to measles outbreaks across the country,” HHS spokesperson Emily Hilliard said in a statement, noting the agency deployed experts to help states battle outbreaks and put $100 million in additional funding toward the effort.The two leaders recommend vaccination “as the most effective way to prevent measles,” Hilliard said. But this summer, as measles cases rose, President Donald Trump signed an executive order urging drugmakers to break up the combination shot that provides protection against measles, mumps and rubella, suggesting it was “quite lethal.” The order also directed the attorney general to go after states that don’t allow religious exemptions to vaccines. Public health advocates say the administration’s mixed messaging on vaccine safety and the insistence that shots are a “personal” choice are making the situation worse. 24 Comments » - Norseman - Tuesday, Nov 17, 26 @ 11:11 am: IL is a blue state where the leadership continues to support health expertise. I just can’t understand why so many, even if it’s a small percentage, refuse to acknowledge this and seemingly want to subject people to senseless death. - Political Malpractice - Tuesday, Nov 17, 26 @ 12:25 pm: So stupid. I distinctly remember my 1980s HS health class explaining the concept and urging us to do what is right for society, to be vaccinated for that rare case where someone truly could not be. - Dotnonymous x - Tuesday, Nov 17, 26 @ 2:19 pm: People with lower levels of education, health literacy, and cognitive ability statistically die at higher rates. In public health and epidemiology, researchers study “ignorance” across three distinct measurable categories, educational attainment, health literacy, and cognitive ability...all of which show a strong link to life expectancy. - JS Mill - Tuesday, Nov 17, 26 @ 3:32 pm: We have a plumber running DHS, a reality tv actor running the department of transportation, and an environmental lawyer and former addict running the department of health and human services. Was the expectation excellence? This is what happens when the “anybody can do it” people are in charge. - Demoralized - Tuesday, Nov 17, 26 @ 3:41 pm: This happened under RFK Jr.’s watch. There is no way he should remain the head of the nation’s public health system. - Loop Lady - Tuesday, Nov 17, 26 @ 4:12 pm: Public health initiatives protect the public at large for those who think their health decisions affect no one but themselves. Think again. - Huh? - Wednesday, Nov 18, 26 @ 1:18 am: Do you understand that the immune response to every single bacterial, viral infection and vaccination that you have every had will be erased if you get the measles? Ireland Politics Scotland Scotland Politics Wales Wales Politics Africa Asia China India Australia Europe Latin America Middle East In Pictures BBC InDepth BBC Verify Sport Business World of Business Technology of Business NYSE Opening Bell Technology Watch Documentaries Artificial Intelligence Intelligence Revolution AI v the Mind Tech Now Health Watch Documentaries Culture Watch Documentaries Film & TV Music Art & Design Style Books Entertainment News Arts Watch Documentaries Arts in Motion Travel Watch Documentaries Destinations Africa Antarctica Asia Australia and Pacific Caribbean & Bermuda Central America Europe Middle East North America South America World’s Table Culture & Experiences Adventures The SpeciaList To the Ends of the Earth Earth Watch Documentaries Science Natural Wonders Climate Solutions Sustainable Business Green Living Audio Podcast Categories Radio Audio FAQs Video Watch Documentaries BBC Maestro Discover the World Live Live News Live Sport Documentaries Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live US loses measles elimination status after 26 years amid record case numbers 3 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Madeline Halpert BBC's Madeline Halpert explains why the US lost its measles elimination status and what it could mean. After more than two decades, the US has lost its measles-free status, following two years of record case numbers and deaths. The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a specialised service of the United Nations, determined the US has had uninterrupted transmission of the same strain of measles for more than 12 months. Dr Jarbas Barbosa, director of PAHO, announced that Mexico and Bolivia have also lost their measles elimination status, attributing the resurgence in the region to persistent "gaps in vaccination". The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said it was committed to "regaining measles elimination status" by expanding access to vaccines. The US has seen 5,400 cases of measles this year alone, with 10 measles-related deaths, the most the country has seen since the 1990s. The measles virus - with its signature blotchy red rash - used to infect millions of children a year before a vaccine was invented. The extremely contagious virus can be fatal, and some patients can experience long-term complications including encephalitis and immune amnesia, which resets the immune system, leaving it with only limited ability to respond to new infections. The US recommends two measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) shots for children between ages one and six, which is 97% effective in protecting against the illness. PAHO, a group within the World Health Organization, revoked the US's measles-elimination after determining that the virus had circulated nonstop for more than a year. "These figures are a serious warning for our region," PAHO's director Barbosa said at a news conference on Tuesday. "Measles is resurging globally amid persistent gaps in vaccination." He added that Canada, which lost its status of having eliminated measles last year after seeing several large outbreaks, has made strides this year to interrupt transmission. Daniel Salas, the executive manager of immunisations at PAHO, said that the US and others who lost elimination status would be required to submit corrective action plans outlining how they would attempt to improve vaccination rates. US Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr Kennedy has attempted to make a series of sweeping changes to US vaccine recommendations and policies. The vaccine sceptic has also frequently cast doubt on the safety of MMR shot, as vaccination rates have declined across the US in recent years. Kennedy has argued that the rise in measles cases started before he took the helm at HHS and that neighbouring countries have also seen more infections. Responding to Tuesday's announcement, the CDC said the agency and its partners were "committed to stopping measles outbreaks, protecting Americans, and regaining measles elimination status". "Together, we will encourage MMR vaccination, expand access to vaccines, and help communities close gaps in protection," the agency said. CDC Director Erica Schwartz said the measles elimination designation was not what protected Americans. "Vaccination does," she said. "We know where transmission is occurring and we've invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities." In a post on social media, Kennedy said: "I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles." "We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust," he also said. "We will answer families' questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment." The UK, Spain and Austria were among European nations that lost their measles-free status earlier this year, along with countries including Russia, Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan. Nuwan Gunawardhana, an assistant professor of medicine with Columbia University Irving Medical Center, said the US losing its elimination status was "a huge leap backwards". The US was the first country to eliminate measles in the Americas thanks to vaccination campaigns, noted William Moss, a paediatric infectious disease specialist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. Dr Gunawardhana said it took massive efforts from public health officials and clinicians to build trust with patients to increase uptake of the MMR vaccine, leading to decades in the US with few infections and deaths. But that trust has been steadily eroding since the Covid-19 pandemic, when Dr Gunawardhana said patients were confronted with misinformation about the safety of vaccines and lost even more trust in public health systems. The vaccination rate for MMR across the US has fallen to 92.4%, below the 95% level that provides herd immunity, which limits the spread of measles and protects those who cannot get vaccinated, including newborns. Getty Images The vaccination rate for MMR across the US has fallen to 92.4%, below the 95% level that provides herd immunity - which limits the spread of measles An outbreak in Pennsylvania has infected over 1,400 people - likely a large underestimate - and killed seven people, according to state officials. Kennedy, the health secretary, has sparred with Pennsylvania officials over how it is counting the measles deaths, with CDC declining for now to record some of the deaths in its database. Last year, the health secretary fired all the members of a top vaccine advisory panel and replaced them with his own appointees, some of whom were vaccine critics. The panel recommended a number of vaccine changes - including no longer requiring the Hepatitis B vaccine for all newborns - but those recommendations were blocked by a federal judge. President Donald Trump this year also cast doubt on the safety of the MMR vaccine, issuing an executive order for the shot to be split into three separate immunisations for measles, mumps and rubella, a move public health experts say is costly and could sow confusion about an already safe vaccine. Doctors and public health officials say the misinformation from Kennedy and Trump has played a major role in falling vaccination rates. "It's confusing patients. It's confusing families," Dr Gunawardhana said. "We need a clear message from the top." The federal government's vaccine manoeuvres have left public health officials and states to fill in the gaps, offering their own separate recommendations upholding decades-long practices. Dr Gunawardhana said it took massive efforts from public health officials and clinicians to build trust with patients to increase uptake of the MMR vaccine, leading to decades in the US with few infections and deaths. But that trust has been steadily eroding since the Covid-19 pandemic, when Dr Gunawardhana said patients were confronted with misinformation about the safety of vaccines and lost even more trust in public health systems. The vaccination rate for MMR across the US has fallen to 92.4%, below the 95% level that provides herd immunity, which limits the spread of measles and protects those who cannot get vaccinated, including newborns. Getty Images The vaccination rate for MMR across the US has fallen to 92.4%, below the 95% level that provides herd immunity - which limits the spread of measles An outbreak in Pennsylvania has infected over 1,400 people - likely a large underestimate - and killed seven people, according to state officials. Kennedy, the health secretary, has sparred with Pennsylvania officials over how it is counting the measles deaths, with CDC declining for now to record some of the deaths in its database. Last year, the health secretary fired all the members of a top vaccine advisory panel and replaced them with his own appointees, some of whom were vaccine critics. The panel recommended a number of vaccine changes - including no longer requiring the Hepatitis B vaccine for all newborns - but those recommendations were blocked by a federal judge. President Donald Trump this year also cast doubt on the safety of the MMR vaccine, issuing an executive order for the shot to be split into three separate immunisations for measles, mumps and rubella, a move public health experts say is costly and could sow confusion about an already safe vaccine. Doctors and public health officials say the misinformation from Kennedy and Trump has played a major role in falling vaccination rates. "It's confusing patients. It's confusing families," Dr Gunawardhana said. "We need a clear message from the top." The federal government's vaccine manoeuvres have left public health officials and states to fill in the gaps, offering their own separate recommendations upholding decades-long practices. news.content: Latest U.S. Iran War Trump Remarks World Politics Entertainment HealthWatch MoneyWatch Crime Space Sports Brand Studio The Free Press Local News Atlanta Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas Live CBS News 24/7 Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas 48 Hours 60 Minutes Shows 48 Hours 60 Minutes CBS Evening News CBS Mornings CBS Morning News CBS Reports CBS Saturday Morning The Daily Report The Dish Face the Nation Sunday Morning The Takeout Things That Matter The Uplift CBS News Investigates CBS News Confirmed Podcasts Newsletters Download Our App CBS News Team Executive Team Brand Studio Paramount+ Join Our Talent Community RSS Feeds Atlanta | News Weather Meet Our Team News Tips 63° Contact Us Download with Damez Download Our App Advertise Memorials Watch CBS News Local News Georgia sees record spike in confirmed measles cases as U.S. grapples with outbreaks By Dan Raby Dan Raby Senior Digital Producer, CBS News Atlanta Dan Raby, the senior digital producer for CBS News Atlanta, has been covering everything happening around Georgia for more than a decade. Read Full Bio Dan Raby November 20, 2026 / 12:42 PM EST / CBS Atlanta Add CBS News on Google Georgia has seen more measles cases in 2026 than any other year since the state's Department of Public Health began tracking the annual number of cases. The spike in cases in the Peach State comes as the Pan American Health Organization announced the United States has officially lost its measles elimination status. International health officials consider measles eliminated when the virus is not locally spreading among residents. The designation hinges on whether a single measles chain has spread uninterrupted for at least 12 months. The United States has met that standard every year since 2000. As of Thursday, the Atlanta-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention have confirmed nearly 2,300 measles cases in the country with 43 new outbreaks (defined as three or more cases) this year. The biggest outbreak has been in Pennsylvania, where more than 1,500 cases have been confirmed. The measles virus, Paramyxoviridae from the Morbillivirus family, transmission microscopy view. BSIP/Universal Images Group via Getty Images The CDC data shows there have been at least six deaths connected with the virus, but the agency noted those numbers are likely to increase. CBS News reports that there have been eight deaths associated with measles in Pennsylvania alone, with other deaths reported in Wisconsin and New York. In Georgia, health officials have confirmed 28 cases of measles across the state, nearly triple the number reported in 2025 and 10 more than in 2019, which was the highest number of cases since the state started keeping records in 2002. The latest outbreak was in Macon County, where DPH confirmed three measles cases on Nov. 10. So far, there have been seven cases connected with the outbreak. While details about the original case remain limited, officials say he or she had contact with a confirmed measles case in Pennsylvania. Authorities believe the individual also visited a LongHorn Steakhouse on Hampton Court in Perry on the night of Oct. 7 while they were infectious. Other outbreaks in the state have been confirmed in Jasper County and Cobb County. Mexico also lost its measles-elimination status, following a resurgence of the virus there that included a massive outbreak in Chihuahua state. Bolivia, too, lost its status. Last year, Canada lost its measles-free designation for the first time since 1998. Georgia officials urge measles vaccinations The majority of cases across the country have been unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination status, the CDC reports. Only 4% of confirmed cases had at least one dose of the MMR vaccine. In a letter sent to physicians across the state in September, Georgia Department of Public Health Commissioner Dr. Kathleen E. Toomey asked doctors to encourage their patients to get vaccinated. "The MMR (measles, mumps, and rubella) vaccine is safe and highly effective. More than 95% of people who receive one dose develop immunity, and a second dose increases protection to approximately 98%. Vaccination also helps protect infants and others who cannot be vaccinated," Toomey wrote. A vial of the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine for children is displayed during an immunization event at the L.A. Care and Blue Shield of California Promise Health Plan Community Resource Center in the Panorama City neighborhood of Los Angeles on Oct. 24, 2025. PATRICK T. FALLON/AFP via Getty Images What are the symptoms of measles? Measles first infects the respiratory tract, then spreads throughout the body, causing a high fever, runny nose, cough, red, watery eyes, and a rash. The rash generally appears three to five days after the first symptoms, beginning as flat red spots on the face and then spreading downward to the neck, trunk, arms, legs, and feet. When the rash appears, the fever may spike over 104 degrees Fahrenheit, according to the CDC. The virus is highly contagious, spreads through the air, and can stay on surfaces for up to two hours after an infected person has been in a room. The Associated Press contributed to this report. news.content_original: Latest U.S. Iran War Trump Remarks World Politics Entertainment HealthWatch MoneyWatch Crime Space Sports Brand Studio The Free Press Local News Atlanta Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas Live CBS News 24/7 Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas 48 Hours 60 Minutes Shows 48 Hours 60 Minutes CBS Evening News CBS Mornings CBS Morning News CBS Reports CBS Saturday Morning The Daily Report The Dish Face the Nation Sunday Morning The Takeout Things That Matter The Uplift CBS News Investigates CBS News Confirmed Podcasts Newsletters Download Our App CBS News Team Executive Team Brand Studio Paramount+ Join Our Talent Community RSS Feeds Atlanta | News Weather Meet Our Team News Tips 63° Contact Us Download with Damez Download Our App Advertise Memorials Watch CBS News Local News Georgia sees record spike in confirmed measles cases as U.S. grapples with outbreaks By Dan Raby Dan Raby Senior Digital Producer, CBS News Atlanta Dan Raby, the senior digital producer for CBS News Atlanta, has been covering everything happening around Georgia for more than a decade. Read Full Bio Dan Raby November 20, 2026 / 12:42 PM EST / CBS Atlanta Add CBS News on Google Georgia has seen more measles cases in 2026 than any other year since the state's Department of Public Health began tracking the annual number of cases. The spike in cases in the Peach State comes as the Pan American Health Organization announced the United States has officially lost its measles elimination status. International health officials consider measles eliminated when the virus is not locally spreading among residents. The designation hinges on whether a single measles chain has spread uninterrupted for at least 12 months. The United States has met that standard every year since 2000. As of Thursday, the Atlanta-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention have confirmed nearly 2,300 measles cases in the country with 43 new outbreaks (defined as three or more cases) this year. The biggest outbreak has been in Pennsylvania, where more than 1,500 cases have been confirmed. The measles virus, Paramyxoviridae from the Morbillivirus family, transmission microscopy view. BSIP/Universal Images Group via Getty Images The CDC data shows there have been at least six deaths connected with the virus, but the agency noted those numbers are likely to increase. CBS News reports that there have been eight deaths associated with measles in Pennsylvania alone, with other deaths reported in Wisconsin and New York. In Georgia, health officials have confirmed 28 cases of measles across the state, nearly triple the number reported in 2025 and 10 more than in 2019, which was the highest number of cases since the state started keeping records in 2002. The latest outbreak was in Macon County, where DPH confirmed three measles cases on Nov. 10. So far, there have been seven cases connected with the outbreak. While details about the original case remain limited, officials say he or she had contact with a confirmed measles case in Pennsylvania. Authorities believe the individual also visited a LongHorn Steakhouse on Hampton Court in Perry on the night of Oct. 7 while they were infectious. Other outbreaks in the state have been confirmed in Jasper County and Cobb County. Mexico also lost its measles-elimination status, following a resurgence of the virus there that included a massive outbreak in Chihuahua state. Bolivia, too, lost its status. Last year, Canada lost its measles-free designation for the first time since 1998. Georgia officials urge measles vaccinations The majority of cases across the country have been unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination status, the CDC reports. Only 4% of confirmed cases had at least one dose of the MMR vaccine. In a letter sent to physicians across the state in September, Georgia Department of Public Health Commissioner Dr. Kathleen E. Toomey asked doctors to encourage their patients to get vaccinated. "The MMR (measles, mumps, and rubella) vaccine is safe and highly effective. More than 95% of people who receive one dose develop immunity, and a second dose increases protection to approximately 98%. Vaccination also helps protect infants and others who cannot be vaccinated," Toomey wrote. A vial of the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine for children is displayed during an immunization event at the L.A. Care and Blue Shield of California Promise Health Plan Community Resource Center in the Panorama City neighborhood of Los Angeles on Oct. 24, 2025. PATRICK T. FALLON/AFP via Getty Images What are the symptoms of measles? Measles first infects the respiratory tract, then spreads throughout the body, causing a high fever, runny nose, cough, red, watery eyes, and a rash. The rash generally appears three to five days after the first symptoms, beginning as flat red spots on the face and then spreading downward to the neck, trunk, arms, legs, and feet. When the rash appears, the fever may spike over 104 degrees Fahrenheit, according to the CDC. The virus is highly contagious, spreads through the air, and can stay on surfaces for up to two hours after an infected person has been in a room. The Associated Press contributed to this report. MEDINDIA MEDINDIA Consult Online Doctor Courses Explore Healthy Living News Health A-Z Calculators Articles Drugs Directories Education More Search Medindia Medindia » News » Research News » USA Loses Measles Elimination Status After 26 Years: Cases and Deaths Surge USA Loses Measles Elimination Status After 26 Years: Cases and Deaths Surge Written by Colleen Fleiss Reviewed by The Medindia News Review Team on Nov 15 2026 11:45 PM Add MedIndia on Google Set MedIndia as a preferred source on Google to consistently get trusted, expert-backed health and wellness content in your search results. Why has the USA lost its measles elimination status after 26 years? Discover what is driving the outbreak, rising measles cases and the warning signs. The United States has lost a major public health achievement after measles regained a foothold in the country, ending its 26-year record of measles elimination. The development marks a significant setback for American public health authorities, who had maintained measles elimination status since 2000 through vaccination programmes, disease surveillance and outbreak-control measures. According to reports published on November 13 and 14, 2026, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) determined that the United States no longer met the criteria for measles elimination after prolonged transmission of the virus. (1✔) The decision comes amid a major resurgence of measles across the country, with thousands of confirmed infections and additional deaths reported in 2026. The development also raises questions about declining childhood vaccination coverage and the ability of public health systems to prevent the return of diseases once considered eliminated. Measles Measles is a viral infection with symptoms of fever,and rashes. Measles is prevented by vaccination and staying away from the infected individuals. Why Did the United States Lose Its Measles Elimination Status? The United States first achieved measles elimination in 2000. However, elimination does not mean that the virus has disappeared worldwide or that imported cases cannot occur. It means that continuous local transmission of measles has been interrupted. According to PAHO, the assessment considers whether the same measles virus strain has continued circulating within a country for at least 12 months. The current US outbreak began in January 2025. Despite public health interventions, transmission continued through multiple outbreaks, allowing the virus to establish sustained circulation. In January 2026, PAHO announced that the United States and Mexico would undergo a review of their measles elimination status following outbreaks that began in 2025. The subsequent review found that the United States had lost its elimination status. This is particularly significant because the country had maintained that achievement for more than two decades. Test Your Knowledge on Measles Measles, also known as morbilli or rubeola or red measles, is a highly contagious, rash-causing infection belonging to paramyxovirus family. It also causes upper respiratory symptoms and fever. Efforts are being made to eradicate measles from the ... What Do US Government Health Figures Reveal About the Outbreak? The latest figures from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) show how extensively measles has spread. According to the CDC's November 13, 2026 update: (2✔) 5,412 Confirmed measles cases in 2026 47 US jurisdictions reporting cases 43 Reported measles outbreaks in 2026 96% Cases associated with outbreaks Source: CDC surveillance data as of November 12, 2026. The figures represent a substantial increase compared with previous years. The country reported 2,289 confirmed measles cases in 2025, compared with just 285 in 2024. Measles Outbreak in Texas: 597 Cases, 62 Hospitalizations, 2 Deaths How long is measles contagious? From 4 days before to 4 days after the rash. Stay informed and protected during this Texas outbreak. Measles Symptoms and Treatment: Early Signs, Rash and Available Care Measles usually begins with a high fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes. Small white spots called Koplik spots may appear inside the mouth before the characteristic red rash develops. The rash starts on the face and hairline before spreading downwards to the neck, trunk, arms and legs. Symptoms generally appear 7–14 days after exposure. (3✔) There is no specific antiviral treatment for routine measles infection. Management focuses on supportive care, including adequate fluids, rest and fever management. Vitamin A supplementation may be recommended for children with measles under medical supervision, particularly in severe cases. Antibiotics are not effective against the measles virus but may be prescribed if secondary bacterial infections develop. Severe complications, such as pneumonia or encephalitis, may require hospitalization and specialized medical care. Anyone suspected of having measles should contact a healthcare provider before visiting a medical facility to prevent further transmission. Measles Resurgence: Tackling Viral Outbreak As compared to previous years, India's capital has seen a sharp increase in measles cases, with 543 cases reported in 2022. Falling MMR Vaccination Coverage Adds to the Concern One of the most important factors behind the American measles resurgence is declining childhood vaccination coverage. The CDC reports that MMR vaccination coverage among US kindergarteners dropped from 95.2% during the 2019–2020 school year to 92.4% in 2025–2026. The decline means approximately 280,000 kindergarteners were potentially at risk during the 2025–2026 school year. (4✔) The CDC explains that measles outbreaks can spread rapidly when the virus enters communities with lower vaccination coverage. Although 95% coverage is an important community-immunity target, local vaccination gaps can still allow outbreaks even when national coverage appears relatively high. The agency also points to increased measles activity globally, which creates more opportunities for infected travelers to bring the virus into the United States. What Happens Next? Why has the USA lost its measles elimination status after 26 years? Discover what is driving the outbreak, rising measles cases and the warning signs. The United States has lost a major public health achievement after measles regained a foothold in the country, ending its 26-year record of measles elimination. The development marks a significant setback for American public health authorities, who had maintained measles elimination status since 2000 through vaccination programmes, disease surveillance and outbreak-control measures. According to reports published on November 13 and 14, 2026, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) determined that the United States no longer met the criteria for measles elimination after prolonged transmission of the virus. (1✔) The decision comes amid a major resurgence of measles across the country, with thousands of confirmed infections and additional deaths reported in 2026. The development also raises questions about declining childhood vaccination coverage and the ability of public health systems to prevent the return of diseases once considered eliminated. Measles Measles is a viral infection with symptoms of fever,and rashes. Measles is prevented by vaccination and staying away from the infected individuals. Why Did the United States Lose Its Measles Elimination Status? The United States first achieved measles elimination in 2000. However, elimination does not mean that the virus has disappeared worldwide or that imported cases cannot occur. It means that continuous local transmission of measles has been interrupted. According to PAHO, the assessment considers whether the same measles virus strain has continued circulating within a country for at least 12 months. The current US outbreak began in January 2025. Despite public health interventions, transmission continued through multiple outbreaks, allowing the virus to establish sustained circulation. In January 2026, PAHO announced that the United States and Mexico would undergo a review of their measles elimination status following outbreaks that began in 2025. The subsequent review found that the United States had lost its elimination status. This is particularly significant because the country had maintained that achievement for more than two decades. Test Your Knowledge on Measles Measles, also known as morbilli or rubeola or red measles, is a highly contagious, rash-causing infection belonging to paramyxovirus family. It also causes upper respiratory symptoms and fever. Efforts are being made to eradicate measles from the ... What Do US Government Health Figures Reveal About the Outbreak? The latest figures from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) show how extensively measles has spread. According to the CDC's November 13, 2026 update: (2✔) 5,412 Confirmed measles cases in 2026 47 US jurisdictions reporting cases 43 Reported measles outbreaks in 2026 96% Cases associated with outbreaks Source: CDC surveillance data as of November 12, 2026. The figures represent a substantial increase compared with previous years. The country reported 2,289 confirmed measles cases in 2025, compared with just 285 in 2024. Measles Outbreak in Texas: 597 Cases, 62 Hospitalizations, 2 Deaths How long is measles contagious? From 4 days before to 4 days after the rash. Stay informed and protected during this Texas outbreak. Measles Symptoms and Treatment: Early Signs, Rash and Available Care Measles usually begins with a high fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes. Small white spots called Koplik spots may appear inside the mouth before the characteristic red rash develops. The rash starts on the face and hairline before spreading downwards to the neck, trunk, arms and legs. Symptoms generally appear 7–14 days after exposure. (3✔) There is no specific antiviral treatment for routine measles infection. Management focuses on supportive care, including adequate fluids, rest and fever management. Vitamin A supplementation may be recommended for children with measles under medical supervision, particularly in severe cases. Antibiotics are not effective against the measles virus but may be prescribed if secondary bacterial infections develop. Severe complications, such as pneumonia or encephalitis, may require hospitalization and specialized medical care. Anyone suspected of having measles should contact a healthcare provider before visiting a medical facility to prevent further transmission. Measles Resurgence: Tackling Viral Outbreak As compared to previous years, India's capital has seen a sharp increase in measles cases, with 543 cases reported in 2022. Falling MMR Vaccination Coverage Adds to the Concern One of the most important factors behind the American measles resurgence is declining childhood vaccination coverage. The CDC reports that MMR vaccination coverage among US kindergarteners dropped from 95.2% during the 2019–2020 school year to 92.4% in 2025–2026. The decline means approximately 280,000 kindergarteners were potentially at risk during the 2025–2026 school year. (4✔) The CDC explains that measles outbreaks can spread rapidly when the virus enters communities with lower vaccination coverage. news.content_title: Virginia Health Department confirms measles case in Central Virginia
news.content: The Virginia Department of Health confirmed another measles case Tuesday, the same day that an international health organization announced that the virus is no longer considered to be eliminated in the United States. The latest case involves a child who’s 4 years old or younger. The child may have exposed others at the Centra Southside Community Hospital emergency department in Farmville between 10 p.m. Saturday and 12:15 a.m. Sunday, according to a news release from the Health Department. The child also may have exposed others at the University of Virginia Medical Center in Charlottesville between 5:15 a.m. and 10:15 a.m. Monday. So far this year, Virginia has reported 186 confirmed measles cases. Unvaccinated people made up 95% of those infections, while vaccinated people made up 1%. Health officials did not know the vaccination status of the remaining 4% of people infected. In Virginia, measles cases have resulted from both international travel and household exposure, according to the Virginia Department of Health. The department’s news release did not specify whether the latest case resulted from travel or community transmission. The Health Department advises people who think they have come in contact with a positive case to report the exposure through a short survey . The survey notifies local health officials. For those who are not vaccinated, symptoms should be monitored, and contacting a healthcare provider before going to the office or emergency department is advised. Earlier this year, a measles outbreak began in Buckingham County and eventually spread to Cumberland County. The outbreak resulted in 154 confirmed cases before state health officials declared it over. The outbreak lasted 97 days. The United States first declared measles eliminated in 2000, meaning the country had gone more than 12 months without continuous transmission of the virus. International travelers could still bring measles into the country, but high vaccination rates helped prevent those cases from triggering sustained outbreaks. Between 2001 and 2019, the United States recorded 3,873 confirmed measles cases, according to a study published in the medical journal Clinical Infectious Diseases . In early 2025, a series of outbreaks began across the country and have continued throughout 2026. From the start of 2025 through Nov. 13, 2026, states reported 7,701 measles cases, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. On Tuesday, the Pan American Health Organization, an international public health agency that works to protect and improve health across the Americas, announced that the United States had lost its measles elimination status. Several factors have contributed to the rise in cases, including inconsistent messaging from federal health officials, declining public trust in vaccines, and cuts to public health funding and staffing. Those cuts have affected measles prevention and response efforts at the federal, state and local levels. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s public comments about vaccines have also contributed to uncertainty surrounding vaccination. Far Southwest Virginia has some of the lowest measles vaccination rates in the state. In Scott County, 33.9% of 7-year-olds have completed the recommended measles vaccination series — the lowest rate in Virginia. The statewide average for the same population is 88.1%. Other counties across the region also fall well below the 95% vaccination threshold generally needed to prevent sustained community transmission of measles. Virginia generally requires children to provide proof of immunization , including two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, to attend public school. The state allows certain medical and religious exemptions. Vaccination rates among 7-year-olds who have completed the measles vaccine series include: Lee County: 65.7% Wise County: 69.3% Dickenson County: 67.7% Buchanan County: 66.9% Tazewell County: 63.1% Russell County: 64% Washington County: 66.8% Grayson County: 70.3% Patrick County: 55.7% Henry County: 79.6% Related stories

news.content: Find us on Google 📌 America's birthday 🎂 Start the day smarter ☀️ Get the USA TODAY app U.S. Politics Sports Entertainment Life Money Travel Opinion Crossword ONLY AT USA TODAY: Newsletters For Subscribers Real Estate From the Archives USA TODAY PLAY Crossword Marvel Comics eNewspaper Magazines Investigations Video Podcasts Humankind Advertise Your Business WITNESS (True Crime) Just Curious Best-selling Booklist Top Workplaces Nomination Legals Press Releases Cars Boats Grocery Shopping Holidays OUR PORTFOLIO: Real Estate 10BEST USA TODAY Store Shopping Money Essentials WITNESS (True Crime) Southern Kitchen Home Internet Services HEALTHCARE Virginia Commonwealth University Add Topic Young child dies in Virginia's first measles death of 2026 Bill Atkinson Petersburg Progress-Index Nov. 20, 2026, 5:25 p.m. ET Hear this story Virginia has recorded the first death of the year related to measles. The Virginia Department of Health said in a statement late in the afternoon Nov. 20 a child younger than 4 years old died. The department did not say where the child lived or whether or not the child was vaccinated. "To protect the family’s privacy, VDH will not provide any further information regarding this death," the statement read. Just hours before the death was announced, VDH noted an increase in measles activity in some areas of Virginia and urged people to "be proactive in protecting themselves and their communities from measles and avoiding future tragedies." The news came three days after a young child in the same age range tested positive for measles at UVA Health University Medical Center in Charlottesville, but VDH would not say if the cases were linked. On the same day the child was reported sick in Charlottesville, the United States lost its measles-free status by the World Health Organization. Measles can cause serious complications, including pneumonia, brain inflammation, complications during pregnancy and death. Virginia cases rise above 200 this year Virginia has reported 220 measles cases in 2026, including 40 among children aged 0 to 4 and 75 among those aged 5 to 12, state health department data showed as of Nov. 19. Of those cases, 179 were in unvaccinated individuals, 39 were in people whose vaccination status was unknown and two were in vaccinated individuals. Virginia health officials have reported increased measles activity driven largely by outbreaks in central region. Buckingham County has reported 127 cases, the highest in the state, while neighboring Charlotte County has recorded 34 cases. Measles cases growing around the nation Pennsylvania, the hardest-hit US state, reported an eighth measles-related death and confirmed 1,631 measles cases, as of Nov. 20. Wisconsin has also reported two deaths, while New York state recorded its first measles-associated death, involving a child. The CDC has confirmed six measles-associated deaths so far in 2026, though it does not specify the states where the deaths were recorded. A discrepancy between state and federal death tallies arose earlier this year after the CDC, under US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., began using National Center for Health Statistics mortality data instead of state figures. The sharp increase in US measles cases has coincided with declining immunization rates and rising vaccine hesitancy under Kennedy, who has for years spread doubts, without scientific evidence, about the safety of measles vaccines. Reporting from Reuters was used in this story. Bill Atkinson (he/him/his) has won numerous awards during his 40-year journalism career. A Petersburg native, Bill is a 1984 graduate of Virginia Commonwealth University in Richmond with a degree in mass communications. He specializes in coverage of breaking news, crime, government, and local/state/national politics. He is an avid history buff and a lifelong Washington Commanders fan. Reach him at batkinson@progress-index.com with news tips and story suggestions. Featured Weekly Ad

news.content: 34° Bellingham Sections Latest News Elections Lifestyle Sports Events Newsletter Listen to News Talk KGMI 96.5 FM and 790 AM | Listen Live Enter to win tickets for the Pickford Film Center! × Home News Local Crime Business Weather Education Elections Obituaries Closings Trending Sports Northwest Sports KPUG Radio Lifestyle Local Experts Events Health and Wellness We Are Whatcom Lifestyle Lookout Outdoors Seasonal Guide Deals Listen to Local Radio Stations KGMI Radio Daily News Poll Program Schedule Morning News Afternoon News KGMI Konnects with Joe Teehan Farming Show Saturday Morning Live In the Shop My Bellingham Now Radio Real Estate Wealth Wake Up Community Connection The Aging Hour Whatcom Report Jobs HireMeWA Join Our Team Contests Contest Rules About Submit News Advertise With Us Meet Our Team Newsletter Signup Our Ethics Policy Local health agencies speak out about measles prevention This comes as the U.S. lost its measles elimination status this week. By Dianna Hawryluk November 17, 2026 12:06 pm Facebook X More LinkedIn Email SMS ContributedPhotographed early in 2014 in the Philippines capital city of Manila, this baby was in a hospital with measles (rubeola). Image courtesy of James Goodson/CDC WHATCOM COUNTY, WA (MyBellinghamNow.com) – Local and regional health authorities are speaking out following the U.S. losing its measles elimination status. Losing elimination status means that a country or region has experienced uninterrupted transmission of the disease with the same genetic strain for at least 12 months according to the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO). PAHO rescinded the elimination status as the CDC reported 5,412 confirmed measles cases nationwide in 2026. Last year saw nearly half the same number of cases confirmed in the U.S. Washington had a total of 58 cases in 2026, mostly in the first half of the year. That’s up from 12 cases confirmed in 2025. Whatcom County Health and Community Services says that outbreaks of any infectious disease, such as measles, can be prevented if at least 95% of the population is vaccinated. Their most recent data shows that 87% of kindergarteners have received both doses of the MMR vaccine, which has a 97% efficacy rate. My Bellingham Now previously reported on two measles cases in Lynden last year, but no additional cases have since been reported in Whatcom County. Both Whatcom County Health and Community Services and the West Coast Health Alliance are urging people to stay up to date with MMR vaccines, especially for children. The American Academy of Pediatrics has long recommended children receive the first dose of the MMR at 12 months old before getting the second dose around age 4. Facebook X More LinkedIn Email SMS Seahawks beat Raiders to enter bye, Huskies bowl-eligible, prep volleyball state results, state football schedule and more | Northwest Sports Update JSN had another masterclass and Drew Locke improved to 4-0 with the Seahawks this season. By Jason Upton November 16, 2026 4:48 pm Facebook X More LinkedIn Email SMS Associated PressSeattle Seahawks quarterback Drew Lock (2) celebrates after an NFL football game against the Las Vegas Raiders in Las Vegas, Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026. (AP Photo/John Locher) Seahawks News The Seahawks are heading into their bye week on a high note. The ‘Hawks beat the Raiders 21-13 in Las Vegas yesterday to improve to 6-4 on the season. No. 1 pick Fernando Mendoza scored his first career touchdown after a Drew Lock fumble to give the Raiders an early lead. But it was all Seattle from there, as Jaxon Smith-Njigba led the way with 171 yards and a touchdown and the Seahawks’ defense racked up six sacks and 12 quarterback hits. They have the week off before traveling to face their rival 49ers in a crucial divisional matchup next week. Week 10 of the NFL season wraps up tonight when the Baltimore Ravens host the Los Angeles Chargers on Monday Night Football. Jacoby Brissett will look to help Baltimore stay in the playoff hunt in his Ravens debut at quarterback, while the Chargers are still searching for their first win of the season. Coverage begins at 4:00 and kickoff is at 5:15 on KPUG. Huskies/Cougs News The Huskies earned a crucial win over the weekend. They beat Michigan State 21-14 in East Lansing on Saturday to earn their sixth win of the season and become eligible for a bowl game. Both teams traded a pair of touchdowns before Jayden Limar ran in the winning score for UW with just two minutes left to cap off an 8-play, 78-yard drive. It came after the Huskies arrived in East Lansing at 3 a.m. that morning, just 15 hours before kickoff, due to delays from the FAA’s decision to ground all flights for several hours on Friday. Next up, they’re back at home to host 6th nationally-ranked Indiana on Saturday. Meanwhile, the Cougs thumped Colorado State 73-7 to snap their six-game skid and earn their second win of the season. Junior running back Kirby Vorhees ran for 197 yards and four touchdowns. Prep Football News The state quarterfinals are set in prep football. Four Whatcom County teams are still standing after the opening round of the state tournament over the weekend. In Class 1A, Meridian edged Seton Catholic 42-41 on the road to earn their first state football tournament win since 2018. The 9th-seeded Trojans will now travel to face top-seeded Royal at 3 p.m. on Saturday, as they look to dethrone the 6x defending state champs. Mount Baker dominated Tenino 41-0 to earn their second shutout win of the postseason. The 5th-seeded Mountaineers will now travel to face 4th-seeded Rochester at 7 p.m. on Saturday. Lynden Christian had the week off with a first-round bye, as the 3rd-seeded Lyncs now gear up to host 6th-seeded Zillah at Blaine High School on Saturday at 4:00. In Class 2A, Lynden beat Fife 42-25, as the 2nd-seeded Lions moved on to face 10th-seeded Franklin Pierce. Lynden will again host the game from Ferndale High School at 1 p.m. on Saturday. And in Class 3A, Ferndale fell to Eastside Catholic 51-14, as the Golden Eagles ended their season with a 8-3 record. Prep Volleyball News It was a successful weekend for Whatcom County’s prep volleyball teams at the state tournament. Lynden Christian shocked 6x defending state champion Chelan on Friday and went on to advance to their first state championship appearance since 2018 before falling to Cashmere. Meridian also made an impressive run and took home a 4th-place finish. In Class 2A, defending state champion Lynden got upset by Ridgefield on Saturday. The Lions ended up defeating Sehome in the 3rd place game, as the Mariners earned 4th. Meanwhile, Ferndale earned a big win as the 3A district tournament came to a close. The Golden Eagles swept Edmonds-Woodway on Saturday to book a ticket to the state tournament, which takes place this coming weekend in Yakima. Prep Girls Soccer News All three of Whatcom County’s girls soccer teams were bounced from the state tournament over the weekend. On Friday, Ferndale lost to Mercer Island in the Round of 16. On Saturday, Sehome lost to Ridgefield in the 2A quarterfinals and Lynden Christian fell to University Prep in the 1A quarterfinals. WWU Vikings News Playoff soccer is still alive at the college level in Bellingham. Western’s women’s soccer team beat Cal Poly Pomona 1-0 yesterday in their first match of the national tournament. Junior midfielder Layne Davis scored her first goal of the season to propel the win. It came against an impressive opponent, as Cal Poly Pomona won the 2024 national championship and made the final four a year ago. The 4th nationally-ranked Vikings now advance to face Concordia Irvine in the West Regional Final, which takes place in Bellingham at 3 p.m. this Friday. By Dianna Hawryluk November 17, 2026 12:06 pm Facebook X More LinkedIn Email SMS ContributedPhotographed early in 2014 in the Philippines capital city of Manila, this baby was in a hospital with measles (rubeola). Image courtesy of James Goodson/CDC WHATCOM COUNTY, WA (MyBellinghamNow.com) – Local and regional health authorities are speaking out following the U.S. losing its measles elimination status. Losing elimination status means that a country or region has experienced uninterrupted transmission of the disease with the same genetic strain for at least 12 months according to the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO). PAHO rescinded the elimination status as the CDC reported 5,412 confirmed measles cases nationwide in 2026. Last year saw nearly half the same number of cases confirmed in the U.S. Washington had a total of 58 cases in 2026, mostly in the first half of the year. That’s up from 12 cases confirmed in 2025. Whatcom County Health and Community Services says that outbreaks of any infectious disease, such as measles, can be prevented if at least 95% of the population is vaccinated. Their most recent data shows that 87% of kindergarteners have received both doses of the MMR vaccine, which has a 97% efficacy rate. My Bellingham Now previously reported on two measles cases in Lynden last year, but no additional cases have since been reported in Whatcom County. Both Whatcom County Health and Community Services and the West Coast Health Alliance are urging people to stay up to date with MMR vaccines, especially for children. The American Academy of Pediatrics has long recommended children receive the first dose of the MMR at 12 months old before getting the second dose around age 4. (AP Photo/John Locher) Seahawks News The Seahawks are heading into their bye week on a high note. The ‘Hawks beat the Raiders 21-13 in Las Vegas yesterday to improve to 6-4 on the season. No. 1 pick Fernando Mendoza scored his first career touchdown after a Drew Lock fumble to give the Raiders an early lead. But it was all Seattle from there, as Jaxon Smith-Njigba led the way with 171 yards and a touchdown and the Seahawks’ defense racked up six sacks and 12 quarterback hits. They have the week off before traveling to face their rival 49ers in a crucial divisional matchup next week. Week 10 of the NFL season wraps up tonight when the Baltimore Ravens host the Los Angeles Chargers on Monday Night Football. Jacoby Brissett will look to help Baltimore stay in the playoff hunt in his Ravens debut at quarterback, while the Chargers are still searching for their first win of the season. Coverage begins at 4:00 and kickoff is at 5:15 on KPUG. Huskies/Cougs News The Huskies earned a crucial win over the weekend. They beat Michigan State 21-14 in East Lansing on Saturday to earn their sixth win of the season and become eligible for a bowl game. Both teams traded a pair of touchdowns before Jayden Limar ran in the winning score for UW with just two minutes left to cap off an 8-play, 78-yard drive. It came after the Huskies arrived in East Lansing at 3 a.m. that morning, just 15 hours before kickoff, due to delays from the FAA’s decision to ground all flights for several hours on Friday. Next up, they’re back at home to host 6th nationally-ranked Indiana on Saturday. Meanwhile, the Cougs thumped Colorado State 73-7 to snap their six-game skid and earn their second win of the season. Junior running back Kirby Vorhees ran for 197 yards and four touchdowns. Prep Football News The state quarterfinals are set in prep football. Four Whatcom County teams are still standing after the opening round of the state tournament over the weekend. In Class 1A, Meridian edged Seton Catholic 42-41 on the road to earn their first state football tournament win since 2018. The 9th-seeded Trojans will now travel to face top-seeded Royal at 3 p.m. on Saturday, as they look to dethrone the 6x defending state champs. Mount Baker dominated Tenino 41-0 to earn their second shutout win of the postseason. The 5th-seeded Mountaineers will now travel to face 4th-seeded Rochester at 7 p.m. on Saturday. In Class 2A, Lynden beat Fife 42-25, as the 2nd-seeded Lions moved on to face 10th-seeded Franklin Pierce. Lynden will again host the game from Ferndale High School at 1 p.m. on Saturday. And in Class 3A, Ferndale fell to Eastside Catholic 51-14, as the Golden Eagles ended their season with a 8-3 record. The Lions ended up defeating Sehome in the 3rd place game, as the Mariners earned 4th. Meanwhile, Ferndale earned a big win as the 3A district tournament came to a close. The Golden Eagles swept Edmonds-Woodway on Saturday to book a ticket to the state tournament, which takes place this coming weekend in Yakima. Prep Girls Soccer News All three of Whatcom County’s girls soccer teams were bounced from the state tournament over the weekend. On Friday, Ferndale lost to Mercer Island in the Round of 16. On Saturday, Sehome lost to Ridgefield in the 2A quarterfinals and Lynden Christian fell to University Prep in the 1A quarterfinals. Report Public Documents & Policies Station History Station Updates & Press News Briefs Illinois health chief slams Trump administration after U.S. loses measles elimination status St. Louis Public Radio | By Rob Edwards Published Nov. 17, 2026 at 12:44 p.m. CST Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Measles is a highly contagious virus. According to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, if one person is infected, up to 9 out of 10 people nearby will also be infected unless they are protected. Illinois’ top health official is criticizing the Trump administration following an international health organization’s decision to strip the United States of its measles elimination status. The Pan American Health Organization, a regional branch of the World Health Organization, announced Tuesday that measles is no longer eliminated in the U.S. because the virus has circulated in the country nonstop for more than a year. The designation had been held by the United States since 2000, when health officials determined the country had interrupted the continuous domestic transmission of measles. In a statement responding to the announcement, Dr. Sameer Vohra, Illinois Department of Public Health director, blamed declining national vaccination rates for the reversal and sharply criticized the Trump administration. “The loss of measles elimination status in the U.S. is the direct result of declining national vaccination rates,” Vohra said. “When measles/mumps/rubella (MMR) vaccination rates are high, communities experience far fewer outbreaks and, as a result, a lower likelihood of serious illness or death. This is a serious failure of the Trump administration.” Vohra said the country maintained its elimination status for decades because of evidence-based vaccination efforts and argued that renewed efforts to improve immunization rates could help the U.S. regain that standing. “The U.S. maintained measles elimination status for decades because evidence-based science shows immunization works, and a commitment to improving vaccination rates can get us back to a place where measles cases are nearly non-existent,” he said. The United States has experienced a resurgence of measles outbreaks over the past two years, with more than 5,400 cases reported in 2026 as of mid-November. Illinois health officials have confirmed 29 cases of the virus this year. Missouri health officials have confirmed 24 cases of measles so far in 2026. Have a question or comment about this story? news.content_zh: 伊利诺伊州卫生官员在 2026 年确认了 29 例 麻疹 病例,而密苏里州报告了 24 例。由于泛美卫生组织宣布该病毒已不间断传播一年多,美国已失去 麻疹 消除状态。这标志着与 2000 年美国中断国内 麻疹 传播 指定的逆转。伊利诺伊州公共卫生部主任 Sameer Vohra 博士将 疫苗接种 比率下降归咎于这一失败,并批评特朗普政府。CDC 指出,麻疹 具有高度传染性,附近每 10 名未接种疫苗的人中多达 9 人可能会感染该病毒。截至 11 月中旬,2026 年报告了 5,400 多例病例,凸显了 暴发 的死灰复燃。Vohra 强调,基于证据的 疫苗接种 努力几十年来一直保持消除状态,提高免疫率可以帮助美国重新获得这一地位。目前情况仍在调查中,重点是应对病毒传播的公共卫生措施。

news.content: News Sports Business Opinion Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals HEALTHCARE Ohio measles cases up 700% from 2025 as US loses elimination status Chad Murphy James Powel Mary Walrath-Holdridge USA TODAY NETWORK Nov. 20, 2026, 12:50 p.m. ET Ohio is experiencing its third measles outbreak of 2026, with cases increasing by 82% in the past week. The state has reported 358 cases in 28 counties this year, a nearly 700% increase from all of 2025. Nationally, measles cases have reached a 35-year high, and the United States has lost its measles elimination status. Health officials state the vast majority of cases are among unvaccinated individuals and urge vaccination as the best protection. As another person may have spread measles across five locations in Western Ohio, two more counties joined the list of confirmed cases as the state's third measles outbreak of 2026 continues. Ohio added 31 new cases in the past week, a 82% increase from the 17 new cases reported the week before, the Ohio Department of Health reports. ODH is reporting 358 cases in 28 of 88 Ohio counties so far this year, according to its summary of infectious diseases dashboard, updated Nov. 12. That number is nearly seven times (696.5%) more than the 45 cases reported in all of 2025. Paulding and Jackson counties joined the list this week with one case each. Geauga and Wayne counties had the most new cases, with nine and eight each, respectively. Nationally, the United States has officially lost its measles-free status. The disease had been declared eradicated from the US in 2000 in what the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention called a "historic" accomplishment. Measles cases nationwide have hit a 35-year high. As of Nov. 13, Johns Hopkins University counted 5,739 measles cases in the U.S. in 2026, and as of Nov. 5, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported 5,182 confirmed measles cases in 45 states plus Washington, D.C. – more than double last year's total of 2,289, USA TODAY reports. That's the highest annual total since 1991. The vast majority of cases in Ohio are among unvaccinated individuals, per ODH. “It’s unfortunate that these outbreaks have become more common in Ohio over the past few years, because this disease is preventable,” Dr. Bruce Vanderhoff, ODH director, said a July 30 statement. “This serves to emphasize the importance of being fully vaccinated. I strongly encourage you to protect yourselves and your children by getting vaccinated.” Measles growing in Ohio. These counties report cases in 2026 Ohio counties reporting measles cases since Jan. 1, 2026, include: Ashland: 8 Ashtabula: 58 (five new cases) Cuyahoga: 3 Franklin: 8 Gallia: 3 Geauga: 65 (nine new cases) Hancock: 1 Harrison: 18 Holmes: 14 (four new cases) Jackson: 1 (one new case; first time on the list) Knox: 5 Mahoning: 2 (one new case) Medina: 28 Meigs: 4 Mercer: 4 Morgan: 3 Morrow: 13 Ottawa: 1 Paulding: 1 (one new case; first time on the list) Pike: 26 (two new cases) Portage: 1 Stark: 1 Trumbull: 16 (one new case) Tuscarawas: 15 Van Wert: 3 Vinton: 1 Wayne: 54 (eight new cases) Wood: 1 The total number of new cases in the by-county list this week totals 32. That differs from overall total of new cases because one new measles case last week was credited to an unknown county. The case count for the year reflects previous outbreaks in Cuyahoga County in January and Franklin County in February. The ages of those with confirmed cases range from 15 months to 20 years old, according to various health departments. Measles cases have been growing in Ohio over the past several years, with one case in 2023, seven in 2024 and 45 cases in 2025. Weekly Ohio measles cases by the numbers Total cases in Ohio this year have continued climbing, as reported by ODH: 327 cases in 26 counties on Nov. 12 310 cases in 25 counties on Nov. 5 296 cases in 24 counties on Oct. 29 260 cases in 24 counties on Oct. 22 252 cases in 23 counties on Oct. 15 228 cases in 21 counties on Oct. 8 206 cases in 20 counties on Oct. 1 196 cases in 16 counties on Sept. 24 180 cases in 15 counties on Sept. 17 133 cases in 15 counties on Sept. 10 122 cases in 14 counties on Sept. 3 107 cases in 12 counties on Aug. 27 99 cases in 12 counties Aug. 20 69 cases in 11 counties on Aug. 13 45 cases in 10 counties on Aug. 6 Measles kills six in Pennsylvania; infant dies of measles in Wisconsin Pennsylvania confirmed its sixth measles-related death of the year on Nov. 4, while New York announced its first measles death in 30 years on Nov. 2, according to USA TODAY. Wisconsin also reported a grim milestone on Nov. 5, with health officials saying that its first measles death since 1990 was that of an infant. Measles cases on the rise as Ohio vaccination rates fluctuate in state, U.S. Vaccination rates for measles have declined in recent years, resulting in a growing number of states no longer reporting rates consistent with herd immunity. Herd immunity occurs when more than 95% of people in a community are vaccinated. Most people are then protected, even if they cannot get the vaccine themselves, because those around them are immune and cannot spread the disease. Vaccination coverage among U.S. kindergartners decreased from 95.2% during the 2019–20 school year to 92.5% in the 2024–25 school year, well under the threshold necessary for effective herd immunity, according to the CDC. Ohio's vaccination rate for the 2025-26 school year slipped well below the herd immunity threshold, making it susceptible to outbreaks. In Ohio, MMR vaccine — which protects against measles, mumps and rubella — coverage rate for children and adolescents was 91.5% for 2023. Previous years ranged from an 80% to 90% immunization rate: 2019: 81.8% 2020: 88.0% 2021: 91.7% 2022: 89.0% Declining protections have also been attributed to the growing anti-vaccine movement, which was bolstered by the confirmation of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary. In addition to making anti-vaccine comments, Kennedy also downplayed pediatric deaths related to measles and touted false cures and preventive measures, such as the use of vitamin A. During the height of a 2025 Texas outbreak, Kennedy encouraged inoculation against measles, pulling back from his previous anti-vaccine messaging. Kennedy is now encouraging the measles vaccine. Trump signs executive order to separate MMR vaccine President Donald Trump in August 2026 signed an executive order to split the childhood measles, mumps and rubella vaccine into three shots and delivering them at separate medical visits as well as "calling for more vaccine flexibility and research" and fewer childhood vaccinations, according to USA TODAY. "You have the MMR, we want it in three separate vaccinations, given at separate times. Together there could be a possibility they're quite lethal and separately, it looks like they are not at all lethal, but just very effective," said Trump from the Oval Office as he signed the order. But the MMR vaccine is not lethal, and medical research shows no health benefit or reduced risk from splitting it. In contrast, separating the shots increases injection pain, leaves children unprotected longer, and lowers overall vaccination rates, according to experts. The MMR vaccine has been in existence since 1971, according to the World Health Organization. Measles cases hit 35-year high in United States, country loses 'eliminated' status The United States declared measles eliminated in 2000 after recording just 86 cases that year, according to USA TODAY, citing the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. But a series of outbreaks that began in early 2025, centered initially in Gaines County, Texas, has helped drive the virus' resurgence. The United States has officially lost its measles-free status three decades after the "historic public health achievement" that eliminated the highly infectious disease from the country, the Pan American Health Organization, the part of the World Health Organization that tracks infectious disease in the Americas, announced Nov. 17. Defined by the WHO as freedom from the continuous spread of a disease for at least 12 months, the United States achieved measles elimination status in 2000 in what the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention called a "historic" accomplishment. Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, director of PAHO, pointed to gaps in vaccination coverage as a significant culprit. Can you get measles if vaccinated? Two doses of MMR are 97% effective against measles, ODH reports. If you are up to date on the measles vaccine, the risk of getting sick is very low. Are measles deadly? Measles can be deadly. ODH states that complications from measles are more common among children younger than 5 years of age, adults older than 20 years of age, pregnant women, and people with compromised immune systems. As many as one out of every 20 children with measles gets pneumonia, the most common cause of death from measles in young children. What does measles look like? Signs, symptoms Symptoms usually appear seven to 14 days after exposure, but they can take up to 21 days. Symptoms include a rash, high fever, runny nose, cough, loss of appetite and red, watery eyes. The rash usually lasts five to six days and begins at the hairline, moves to the face and upper neck, and proceeds down the body. Diarrhea and ear infections are common complications of measles. More severe complications such as pneumonia and encephalitis, a swelling of the brain, may also occur. The measles virus can live for up to two hours in air where an infected person coughed or sneezed. If other people breathe the contaminated air or touch an infected surface and then touch their eyes, noses, or mouths, they can become infected. People infected with measles can spread it to others from four days before through four days after a rash appears. Are measles itchy? Not usually, according to the Cleveland Clinic. How to protect yourself against measles Both ODH and the CDC say the best way to protect yourself against measles is to be vaccinated. USA TODAY reporters James Powel and Mary Walrath-Holdridge contributed to this report. Spinal Stenosis Is Not From Tight Muscles.
