(Mary Conlon / Associated Press) By Laura Ungar Nov. 20, 2026 8 AM PT 5 min Click here to listen to this article Share via Close extra sharing options Email Facebook X LinkedIn Threads Reddit WhatsApp Copy Link URL Copied! Print 0:00 0:00 1x This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here. Now that measles is officially back in the U.S., some Americans are asking: Do adults need a booster shot? Generally, experts say, the answer is no. “Most people are protected without getting a booster shot” because they’ve either been vaccinated or had measles as kids, said Dr. Richard Martinello at Yale School of Medicine. The U.S., Mexico and Bolivia lost their measles-free status this week after stubborn outbreaks erased decades of progress. Last year, Canada lost its measles elimination designation. Advertisement Doctors say getting two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine is the best way to protect against one of the most contagious viruses in the world. The vaccine usually protects people for life, as does having had the disease. Americans born before 1957 are considered to have “presumptive evidence” of immunity because almost everyone back then got measles during childhood. For some people, boosters may be a good idea But doctors say certain people should consider getting boosters. One group is healthcare workers born before 1957 without proof of immunity. They’re more likely than the general public to come in contact with people who have measles, so they may get it or even spread it to vulnerable patients. Adults vaccinated between 1963 and 1967 also might want to think about boosters. During those years, some children received an inactivated vaccine that uses a killed version of the virus, which was less effective than the current vaccine containing live, weakened virus. Doctors said people who know they got the inactivated vaccine or aren’t sure should get at least one dose of the live MMR vaccine. One dose is 93% effective at preventing measles, while two doses is 97% protective. Until 1989, only a single dose was standard. Now the recommendation is for adults to have at least one documented dose of MMR. Two doses is recommended for certain people in high-risk groups who don’t have other evidence of immunity. Advertisement “People who have had no shots should go get vaccinated, if they weren’t born before 1957,” said Dr. Joshua Sharfstein at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. “If they have had only one shot, they may want to consider whether they’re in a risk group for a second shot.” That risk group, he said, includes people in school, healthcare workers, international travelers or people living with family members who have compromised immune systems. In places with active measles outbreaks, health officials sometimes recommend that everyone have two shots, Sharfstein said. For people who have had only one shot, especially in an area where measles is circulating, “it’s always a good idea to talk with your physician about whether another shot is needed,” Martinello said. Tracking down your vaccination status But what if you don’t know how many shots you received or even if you’ve been vaccinated? The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention suggests asking your parents or doctor, checking with your high school or college health services or reaching out to previous employers that required immunizations. You can also try contacting your state’s health department; some states have registries that include adult vaccines. If you’re still unsure about your vaccination status, you can talk with your doctor about an MMR immunity blood test that can show whether you have antibodies against measles. But Martinello said this isn’t an ideal measure of how safe you are from the virus. Though the test is accurate, he said, scientists don’t know how to link the result perfectly with the level of protection someone might have. Regardless, doctors said getting a booster just to be safe won’t harm you unless you’re in a group that is not supposed to get the vaccine at all, such as pregnant women. Advertisement Now that measles is circulating in the U.S., doctors said it’s crucial to take measures to protect yourself. “This is a moment to not just check for yourself, but also encourage others to make sure that they are adequately vaccinated,” Sharfstein said. “Too many people took measles for granted ... or just didn’t think about measles. But now it’s something to think about.” Ungar writes for the Associated Press. news.content: Play Now Log InSign Up National News Measles Cases Among Pregnant Women Rise Sharply, Alarming Doctors By iHeartRadio Nov 16, 2026 Photo: chameleonseye / iStock Editorial / Getty Images Doctors across the United States are raising concerns as more than 100 pregnant women have been confirmed to have measles in 2026, leading to a rise in babies born with congenital measles and putting both mothers and their newborns at serious risk. According to preliminary figures published in a medical journal, 13 cases of congenital measles were reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) from the start of 2025 through the end of September, a phenomenon not seen in decades. Congenital measles occurs when a pregnant woman passes the virus to her fetus, which can cause severe complications or even be fatal for newborns. The recent spike is closely linked to declining vaccination rates, prompting experts to warn that the U.S. could soon lose the measles-free status it has held since 2000. The CDC's alert, released in partnership with NEJM Evidence, highlighted 112 confirmed cases of measles during pregnancy, most of which were among women who had not been vaccinated or whose vaccination status was unknown. Pennsylvania experienced a record 97 confirmed measles cases among pregnant women in 2026, the highest in decades. Pennsylvania’s Department of Health has issued advisories to healthcare providers and the public, underlining the risks of both maternal complications—such as pneumonia, pregnancy loss, and premature delivery—and the potential for congenital measles in newborns. Dr. Sharee Livingston, an OBGYN in Central Pennsylvania, told ABC News, "You have to watch the mother fetus dyad so closely because of the risk of fetal death." She described the situation as "a very challenging position to be in" for all involved. Congenital measles may result in symptoms like fever, rash, jaundice, and severe complications such as pneumonia, encephalitis, and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), a rare brain disorder that can be fatal, sometimes developing more quickly in these infants. The CDC and health experts stress that the best prevention is for women to ensure they are vaccinated with the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine before becoming pregnant. The MMR vaccine cannot be given during pregnancy, but unvaccinated pregnant women exposed to measles can receive immunoglobulin antibodies to help reduce the risk of infection and complications. National MMR vaccination coverage for kindergarteners was 92.4% in the 2025–26 school year, but experts warn outbreaks are more likely when community rates fall below 95%. Many communities remain under this threshold. As outbreaks continue, experts and officials urge increased preconception counseling and vaccination for those planning pregnancy, as well as for family members and others who may be in close contact with pregnant women or newborns. supplementary_news.content_title: The United States’ measles elimination status is officially gone. Who should get a booster?
supplementary_news.content: Although measles boosters aren’t typically recommended, certain people could use another shot, especially with so many outbreaks ongoing in the US. Matt Rourke/AP The United States has officially lost its measles elimination status, the Pan American Health Organization announced Tuesday. Measles is once again considered endemic in the country, due to more than a year of continuous local transmission. Measles is also re-established in Bolivia and Mexico, Dr. Jarbas Barbosa da Silva Jr., director of PAHO, said Tuesday, adding that the current situation requires “urgent action.” “Losing a measles elimination status has broader implications than losing a public health designation. It means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period of time, putting families and communities at risk of preventable illness, hospitalization, and death,” Barbosa said. Ad Feedback Dr. Peter Hotez, co-director of the Center for Vaccine Development at Texas Children’s Hospital in Houston, put it simply: “Basically, measles is back.” Countries that lose elimination status are required to submit a corrective action plan to PAHO that outlines how they’ll regain elimination status. The US is expected to submit its plan in the coming weeks, Barbosa said. “We will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status. I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles,” US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said in a social media post Tuesday. “We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust. We will answer families’ questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment. We will support Americans who become ill, regardless of vaccination status, and for the first time equip health care providers with guidance to diagnose and treat measles and its complications.” Dr. Erica Schwartz, director of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, said Tuesday that the agency knows where transmission is occurring and that it has invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities. “The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does,” Schwartz said in a statement. “Losing a designation doesn’t mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks.” The United States held its measles elimination status for 26 years, and the vast majority of people in the US are protected from the highly contagious virus. But doctors say that if you haven’t been vaccinated, now is the time. Although measles boosters aren’t typically recommended, certain people could use another shot, especially with so many outbreaks ongoing in the US. The country has tallied more than 5,000 cases this year, and the chance of being exposed to the virus is much higher than it has been in decades. What the numbers say At least 5,412 confirmed measles cases have been reported in the United States this year, mostly among unvaccinated people, according to the CDC . Experts say that figure is most likely an undercount. This is the highest number of infections in the US in more than three decades, and unless many more people get vaccinated, it will probably continue to grow. Compared with the millions of people who get the flu each year, 5,000-plus cases may not sound like a lot. But measles is one of the most contagious viruses in the world. If a person with measles walks into a room with 10 unvaccinated people, about nine would catch the virus, research suggests. By comparison, the flu would probably spread to only one person. And measles sticks around: Even after an infected person leaves the room, the virus can linger in the air for at least two hours. A few years ago, when the US had only a handful of cases, most of them happened when someone traveled to countries where the disease was endemic and returned with the virus. Now, most cases in the US result from exposure to someone in the neighborhood, research shows , so it may be at your door sooner than you think. Most people in the US have been vaccinated against the measles, but cases are rising because the vaccination rate has fallen. Experts say that about 95% of a population must be vaccinated to reach what’s called herd or community immunity: when there are enough people vaccinated that the virus can’t get a foothold and will fade away. Before the vaccine was introduced in the US in 1963, the country had 3 million to 4 million measles cases every year, and 400 to 500 people died from the disease annually. Once communities reached the 95% threshold, case numbers fell to almost nothing. What to know about the vaccine The measles vaccine was combined with mumps and rubella vaccines in 1971 to help streamline childhood immunization schedules, improve vaccination rates and reduce the number of shots children would need . The vaccine can be given to older children and adults, as well. And if an unvaccinated person is exposed to the virus, getting a shot within 72 hours could offer some protection or at least result in less serious illness, the CDC says. The MMR vaccine is considered extremely safe. There may be mild side effects, such as soreness, redness and a mild rash at the injection site. Some children may briefly develop a fever or joint pain. Rare risks include febrile seizures, which happen in about 1 in 3,000 to 4,000 children, resolve on their own and cause no long-term harm. Serious allergic reactions are extremely rare. Although a later-retracted study in the 1990s suggested a link between the MMR vaccine and autism, large-scale research involving millions of children has established that there is no link. Who gets the MMR shot Typically, the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that children get the first dose of the combined MMR vaccine between 12 and 15 months old and a second dose between ages 4 and 6. But anyone older than that can also get vaccinated. With a flu or Covid-19 vaccine, doses are recommended every year because those viruses mutate more quickly. But the measles virus stays pretty much the same from year to year, and two doses of the MMR vaccine should provide good protection for life. For people who live in a region where there’s an outbreak, some doctors suggest giving a dose of the MMR vaccine between 6 and 11 months of age in what’s called a zero dose. It’s then recommended that the child receive the first and second doses on the usual schedule. Immunologist Dr. Elisabeth Adkins Marnik says you can also ask your pediatrician to give your child the second dose of the vaccine before age 4. “I personally made the decision to get my daughter a second dose early when measles started circulating so much in the community and I knew we were also going to be doing a lot of traveling,” said Marnik, a science communicator who works to translate evidence into clear and empathetic public communication. “I just didn’t want to take any risks, and getting it a little bit early is fine. It just gave us extra peace of mind.” Who might need more protection There are others groups whose protection might be lacking and who can be vulnerable to infection, or who might be uncertain about whether they’re protected. Here’s what you need to know: If you were born before 1957 The CDC considers adults born before 1957 to be immune to measles, essentially because, before the vaccine, nearly every child caught the virus at some point. If you’ve gotten one dose A single dose of the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine is considered 93% effective at preventing measles. In fact, only one dose was recommended until 1989, when the US government changed the recommendation to two doses after a measles outbreak among vaccinated school-age children. Two doses of MMR boost measles protection to 97%. If you were vaccinated before 1989 and did not receive a second shot, you may want to consider getting one now. If you’ve gotten two doses Doctors don’t typically suggest boosters for people who received two doses of MMR. If you aren’t sure If you don’t know whether you were vaccinated as a child or whether you have been fully vaccinated, talk to your healthcare provider, who may want to give you another shot. Other people who might want an additional shot are those who received the first version of the measles vaccine between 1963 and 1968, which used a killed virus and may not offer as much protection. Testing for measles immunity You can get tested at a doctor’s office or pharmacy. When you have an infection or get vaccinated, your immune cells produce antibodies against the virus that can stay in your body for years and help you fight infection. A simple blood test looks for these antibodies to determine whether you have immunity. Doctors also sometimes order these tests for people with weakened immune systems to see how much immunity they have. The CDC does not recommend this kind of testing, and doctors say it is not necessary if you have had two doses of the vaccine. But this titer test may give you some peace of mind. “Titer tests are not perfect, but certainly if they’re positive, a person likely has a good bit of protection,” said Dr. Jesse Goodman, a professor of medicine and infectious disease at Georgetown University and director of its Center on Medical Product Access, Safety and Stewardship. “But if you’re pretty sure you didn’t get vaccinated or you didn’t get a second dose, you might as well just go ahead. There’s no harm in being vaccinated again.” Measles can cause serious problems The disease can cause serious symptoms. About 11% of Americans who have had measles this year were so sick that they had to go to the hospital, according to the CDC . There have also been at least 10 deaths in people who had measles, according to state data — the most the country has seen in decades. Measles can cause a rash, fever, red eyes, sensitivity to light and cough. It may also lead to severe complications such as pneumonia or encephalitis, a swelling of the brain that can cause convulsions, deafness or brain damage. For pregnant people, measles may cause premature birth or miscarriage , and they can pass the virus to their baby. Measles can also trigger immune amnesia , a condition in which the immune system forgets how to fight other diseases. Some groups are more vulnerable to measles complications, including older adults, infants and young children, as well as people who have suppressed immune systems because they take certain medications or are undergoing cancer treatment. But anyone can develop severe complications. “Most children who get measles as young children are fine and recover, but it can make them pretty sick. Anywhere from 1 in 5 to 1 in 10 even healthy children will end up in the hospital,” Goodman said. Spreading the word Even if you have been vaccinated — and chances are, you have — herd immunity grows as more people get the shot. Although trust in the vaccine has slipped recently, most people still say they believe in it. Studies show that peers and trusted community members can be persuasive, particularly because it can take time to convince people who are reluctant to get the shot. Marnik advises not to get discouraged if people you know don’t change their minds right away. Misinformation about vaccines is increasingly sophisticated, and it can be spread through close friends, anonymous voices online or even leaders . “So it’s no wonder parents are confused and have questions.” Talk to people who are hesitant about vaccines with empathy, she says. Most people just want what is best for their children. “Oftentimes, it takes time and multiple conversations with somebody who is hesitant for them to entertain potentially making the decision to get vaccinated,” Marnik said. “Losing elimination status is a sad thing, but it really makes it so much more urgent to get vaccinated, because now we know that the likelihood people are going to be exposed to measles is so much higher. “I think we can course-correct. We can rebuild trust. It’s just going to take time,” she said. “This didn’t happen overnight, and we’re not going to be able to change it overnight.” CNN’s Deidre McPhillips and Brenda Goodman contributed to this report. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, November 21, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Animal Morbilliviruses Mirror Genetic Mutations Driving Fatal Human Measles Brain Complications by November 17, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 7 mins read 0 Animal Morbilliviruses Mirror Genetic Mutations Driving Fatal Human Measles Brain Complications Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Persistent central nervous system infections caused by animal morbilliviruses share fundamental genetic and phenotypic characteristics with human measles virus variants that cause subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, according to a comparative analysis published in One Health Outlook by Rik L. de Swart and Rory D. de Vries examining recent findings from Daniel Roji and colleagues. Morbilliviruses persisting in wild animal hosts evolve analogous molecular mechanisms that favor long-term viral maintenance in brain tissue, characterized primarily by the inactivation of the matrix protein and the acquisition of hyperfusogenic fusion proteins. Measles virus is an enveloped pathogen possessing a negative-strand RNA genome and represents one of the most infectious viral agents affecting humans. Transmitted via the respiratory route, measles virus initiates infection by targeting myeloid and lymphoid cells through the high-affinity cellular receptor CD150, also known as SLAMF1. This initial phase generates a cell-associated viremia that disseminates the virus throughout host lymphoid tissues, accompanied by infected immune cell infiltration into peripheral organs. In later stages of pathogenesis, the virus utilizes a second receptor, nectin-4, located at epithelial adherens junctions to infect epithelial cells and keratinocytes. The widespread depletion of memory immune cells induces lymphopenia and prolonged immune amnesia, leaving patients susceptible to opportunistic secondary infections such as pneumonia, diarrhoea, and otitis media. While the adaptive immune response typically clears acute measles and provides lifelong immunity, measles virus can in rare instances establish a persistent central nervous system infection. This persistent state can resurface after a clinically silent incubation period lasting several years as subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, a neurological disease that is invariably fatal. Therapeutic interventions currently available provide at best transient clinical improvement, and the infection relentlessly progresses despite high concentrations of measles-specific antibodies in both serum and cerebrospinal fluid. Genomic characterization of measles virus recovered from the brains of deceased subacute sclerosing panencephalitis patients reveals extensive biased hypermutation, often displaying profiles characteristic of adenosine deaminase acting on RNA (ADAR1) activity. Although specific mutational patterns diverge across individual clinical cases, they exhibit marked functional convergence. Specifically, genomes isolated from persistent central nervous system cases consistently encode nonfunctional matrix (M) proteins alongside hyperfusogenic fusion (F) glycoproteins. Inactivation of the matrix gene occurs through premature stop codons, corruption of the translation initiation codon, or hypermutation yielding inactive proteins. Because virion budding requires structural interaction between the matrix protein and the cytoplasmic tail of the fusion glycoprotein, loss of matrix function abolishes the assembly and release of infectious viral particles. Concurrently, mutations in the fusion gene destabilize the fusion trimer, driving a hyperfusogenic phenotype that permits cell-to-cell spread even in host cells lacking CD150 or nectin-4 receptors. In neural tissues where standard morbillivirus receptors are absent, the synaptic cell adhesion molecules CADM1 and CADM2 can trigger viral membrane fusion in cis. This receptor-independent fusion mechanism facilitates the gradual, progressive transfer of viral ribonucleoprotein complexes across synaptic junctions, resulting in widespread brain infection in the absence of budding virions. Related animal morbilliviruses demonstrate comparable pathogenic trajectories across their natural host species. Canine distemper virus in carnivores, phocine distemper virus in seals, and cetacean morbillivirus in whales and dolphins frequently trigger severe disease outbreaks. While canine distemper virus often produces acute neurological complications reminiscent of measles inclusion body encephalitis due to severe immune suppression, it can also produce delayed encephalitis. For instance, old dog encephalitis develops years after initial canine distemper infection, marked by chronic demyelination and persistent viral antigen despite the inability to isolate infectious virus. Similar delayed, chronic central nervous system infections have been observed in stranded harbor seals and dolphins. In the primary study evaluated by de Swart and de Vries, Daniel Roji and colleagues characterized the genomes of morbilliviruses that persisted for multiple years in wild animal brains: canine distemper virus in a lynx, cetacean morbillivirus in a striped dolphin, and phocine distemper virus in two harbor seals. Notably, the harbor seals stranded in 2001 and 2014, approximately 13 and 12 years after major phocine distemper epizootics in 1988 and 2001, mirroring the prolonged latency period observed in human subacute sclerosing panencephalitis. Genomic analysis showed that the viral sequences from the lynx, the dolphin, and one of the seals harbored premature stop codons or hypermutation disrupting the matrix protein, together with mutations conferring thermal instability and hyperfusogenicity in the fusion protein. To evaluate the biological effects of these mutations, the researchers conducted in vitro fusion assays in Vero cells with and without expression of species-specific CD150 receptors from seals, dolphins, dogs, and humans. In three of the four evaluated viruses, cell-to-cell fusion in receptor-negative cells was markedly increased. Furthermore, entry assays using vesicular stomatitis virus particles pseudotyped with morbillivirus glycoproteins bearing truncated cytoplasmic tails confirmed reduced entry capacity in CD150-expressing cells, corroborating the functional shift away from canonical receptor-dependent entry. Detailed experimental investigation of the lynx canine distemper virus isolate revealed that a single amino acid substitution in the fusion protein, designated P479A, was sufficient to explain the hyperfusogenic phenotype. Recombinant canine distemper virus harboring this P479A substitution displayed severe attenuation in CD150-expressing Vero cells and required passaging exclusively through infected canine B cells. However, despite impaired propagation in lymphoid cells, the mutant virus exhibited enhanced infectivity and dissemination in organotypic brain slice cultures derived from ferrets. This shift closely parallels previous experimental findings by Schmitz and colleagues, where chimeric measles virus bearing a fusion gene from a human subacute sclerosing panencephalitis case lost lymphotropism while efficiently propagating through human neural networks. The study highlights how naturally occurring animal morbillivirus infections provide critical insights into human neuropathology, particularly given the absence of tractable animal models that reproduce the multi-year latency of subacute sclerosing panencephalitis. Emerging organoid cultures allow researchers to evaluate the functional consequences of specific viral mutations, yet they cannot determine whether such mutations act as initial seeding requirements for neuroinvasion or emerge during subsequent intra-host persistence. A comparative One Health framework tracking natural morbillivirus infections in diverse hosts could identify predictive molecular biomarkers, potentially enabling the early detection of persistent central nervous system infection before fatal neurological damage occurs. Expanding the current understanding of viral persistence, Roji et al. argue that naturally occurring animal infections offer a distinct advantage for studying subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE). Because clinical reports of SSPE typically focus on the terminal stage of disease, baseline knowledge of the progression during years of silent incubation is limited. By studying animal cases across various species, the researchers suggest that these instances function as natural experiments. This One Health perspective identifies molecular signatures that might not be observable in controlled, short-term laboratory studies. The similarity in latency—such as the 12 to 13-year gaps observed in harbor seals—provides a baseline for comparing these animal morbilliviruses to the human measles virus. Such comparisons offer a platform to investigate the host-specific drivers that allow for prolonged persistence within the central nervous system. To establish these functional parallels, the study team utilized a tiered experimental approach to link specific genomic mutations to viral behavior. Initial fusion assays conducted in Vero cells provided a controlled environment to observe how the presence or absence of host-specific CD150 receptors influenced viral activity. The researchers tested the interaction of CD150 from multiple species, including seal, dolphin, dog, and human origins. A critical finding was the observation that most of these persistent virus variants exhibited enhanced membrane fusion in cells that lacked the high-affinity receptors typically required by morbilliviruses. To further test this, the authors used vesicular stomatitis virus particles pseudotyped with morbillivirus glycoproteins. These experiments specifically focused on particles with truncated cytoplasmic tails. By demonstrating reduced entry in cells expressing CD150, the team confirmed a shift in functional requirements, moving the viruses away from canonical receptor-dependent entry and favoring receptor-independent cell-to-cell spread. The study provided an in-depth analysis of the CDV isolate derived from a lynx, identifying a specific mutation in the fusion gene, P479A, as the primary determinant for the hyperfusogenic phenotype. While the team was unable to isolate the live virus directly from the lynx brain tissue, the generation of recombinant CDV strains allowed for detailed testing. These engineered viruses confirmed that the presence of the P479A amino acid change resulted in clear attenuation within standard Vero-CD150 cultures. When forced to propagate, these mutant viruses could only thrive in canine B-cells. However, when these recombinant strains were introduced to organotypic brain slice cultures derived from ferrets, the virus showed efficient spread. This specific observation strongly mirrors experimental results from previous studies on SSPE-associated measles virus, where researchers demonstrated that chimeric viruses containing the fusion gene from an SSPE patient lost their ability to infect lymphoid cells but gained the capacity for efficient dissemination throughout neural networks. Despite these advancements, the authors highlight significant limitations. It remains unclear whether these mutational profiles represent seeding mutations—essential for the virus to initially cross the blood-brain barrier—or if they are the consequence of long-term evolution and adaptation occurring after the virus has already established a foothold in the central nervous system. Without longitudinal models that capture the entire span of the infection, this distinction remains a critical gap. The researchers note that while newer organoid-based models provide higher resolution for examining functional changes, they currently offer only a snapshot rather than a predictive timeline. Looking forward, the study aims to refine the use of comparative pathogenesis as a diagnostic tool. The ultimate goal for this One Health approach is to identify molecular signatures that hold predictive value for disease progression. If researchers can establish a link between genomic traits and the likelihood of chronic persistence, it could lead to the development of early biomarkers. Detecting these patterns during the clinically silent phase could eventually enable clinicians to initiate targeted antiviral interventions before the virus causes irreparable damage. By mapping the evolutionary pathways that consistently lead to CNS persistence across diverse hosts, the researchers believe it is possible to transition to a more proactive strategy, improving the management of this condition. Nvidia ago EXCLUSIVE Nvidia's accounting is a focus of US SEC investigation, sources say The US Securities and Exchange Commission is probing Nvidia's NVDA.O accounting practices, said two people briefed on the matter, adding to the legal woes facing the scandal-hit chip giant. While much attention has focused on the US leader’s recent setbacks, his host also came to the talks with a weakening economic hand. Jamie McGeever United States ago US Vice President Vance declines to say he would have ordered Iran strikes US Vice President JD Vance on Friday declined to say whether he would have authorized strikes on Iran to prevent the country from developing a nuclear weapon, sidestepping President Donald Trump's calls for him to say the attacks were necessary and that he would carry them out again. Entertainment ago GTA VI shatters records with $3.8 billion in first-day sales "Grand Theft Auto VI" raked in $3.79 billion in sales within the first 24 hours of its launch, becoming the world's biggest entertainment release ever, as fans around the world celebrated the blockbuster title that is now a global cultural phenomenon. Now it's got a stake in it Grand Theft Auto, banned in Saudi Arabia until last year, is now being embraced not only by its gamers - a category that includes Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman - but also by its sovereign wealth fund, which the prince chairs. Iran War ago Iraqi security forces deploy in Iran-backed militia stronghold Iraqi security forces deployed in Jurf al-Sakhar, a stronghold of the Kataib Hezbollah armed group, under a deal that seeks to limit the reach of Iran's most powerful Shi'ite militia ally in the country without provoking a confrontation. REUTERS/Alaa Al-Marjani ago Araqchi says Iran wants diplomacy to end war, Trump says terms unacceptable Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said Tehran still hoped diplomacy could end its war with the United States, while US President Donald Trump said Iran wanted a deal but one that was not acceptable to him. ago Saudi Arabia says it intercepts three Houthi missiles targeting Riyadh The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Saturday it had intercepted and destroyed three ballistic missiles fired towards Riyadh, marking the second Houthi attack on the Saudi capital in a few days, after its tallest skyscraper was struck on Thursday. Updated: November 20, 2026 @ 8:38 pm Full Forecast Watch Live Watch Live Link Home About Us Contact Us News Local Nation & World Videos Elections Obituaries KHQA.com Weather Radar Maps Almanac Weather Call Road Conditions Closings KTVO Skycam Network Features Next Gen Ag Countdown to Christmas Send Us Your Photos Lottery Sports High School PrimeTime More Sports Student Athlete of the Month Newsletter Sign Up KTVO Spotlight Schedule Contact People Copyright Careers EEO Privacy Terms Community Events News Team Legal EEO Public File Report FCC Info FCC Applications Public File Assistance Contact Watch Live Share This Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Local News Featured Adair County Health Department confirms case of measles virus Stephanie Nau-KTVO Nov 19, 2026 Nov 19, 2026 Updated 23 hrs ago Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save KIRKSVILLE, Mo. — Amid rising reports across the country, the Adair County Health Department has now confirmed one case of the highly contagious measles virus in their area. Less than a week before the department’s announcement, the United States officially lost its 26-year elimination status against the virus. One Adair County resident reportedly presented signs and symptoms of the measles virus before testing later came back positive. The health department says it’s in the process of contacting those who may have been exposed, asking that they be monitored for symptoms. This year, there have been 10 reported deaths in the United States due to the virus, a stark increase from only 3 in 2025. Measles is a highly contagious viral illness with symptoms that can include rash, high fever, pneumonia, and other severe conditions. If you think you may have been exposed to the virus, watch for symptoms for 3 weeks and contact local health officials if you start showing the signs. To avoid further contamination, do not show up at your doctor's office without calling ahead to get clear instructions on how to proceed. Colorado Salamanca Salina Cruz Tehuacán Tepic Toluca Tuxpan Tuxtla Gutiérrez Veracruz Xalapa Zacatecas Zamora/La Piedad Nosotros RSS Redes Sociales Mapa de sitio Políticas de Privacidad Guaymas entre rubeola y varicela, médicos se mantienen alertas Por: Mariela Martínez Guaymas Fecha: 18-11-2026 Compartir en facebook Compartir en X Compartir en Whatsapp La Organización Panamericana de la Salud recomienda reforzar la vigilancia epidemiológica y de laboratorio El médico Sergio Ruiz Bustamante indicó que en su consultorio particular no se han registrado casos de sarampión al norte de Guaymas, pero sí se han detectado en esta última semana 1 caso de rubeola y otro de varicela. La rubeola es una infección viral que se contagia o disemina con facilidad a otras personas, se distingue por el sarpullido que produce, y es llamada sarampión de tres días. "La aparición de la varicela ha sido cada vez más intensa hace aproximadamente siete días a mediados de noviembre tuve un caso clínico de rubeola, es una cosa muy rara, pero existe aún" comentó el médico Sergio Ruiz Bustamante. NO ES LO MISMO LA RUBEOLA QUE EL SARAMPIÓN Cabe destacar que la rubéola no es lo mismo que el sarampión, pero ambas enfermedades comparten síntomas como el sarpullido. Los virus que causan la rubeola y el sarampión son diferentes. El virus de rubéola no es tan contagioso ni causa una enfermedad tan grave como el sarampión. Cabe destacar que la vacuna contra sarampión cubre a la enfermedad, además de paperas y rubeola de por vida. Sin embargo, médicos esperan una crisis de sarampión ante el panorama de falta de vacunación y con el aviso de la Organización Panamericana de la Salud que sacó de la lista a México de un país libre de la enfermedad. "Lo que estamos esperando es que no se desate ninguna epidemia de sarampión, porque también lo que tiene mucha posibilidad de que inicie es la hepatitis debido a los derrames de aguas negras, este si es un problema muy fuerte en el Puerto de Guaymas" indicó. La Organización Panamericana de la Salud recomienda reforzar la vigilancia epidemiológica y de laboratorio, asegurar el diagnóstico oportuno y el manejo clínico adecuado de los casos, priorizar la vacunación y fortalecer la preparación y organización de los servicios de salud en cuanto al movimiento activo del sarampión. Esto incluye la aplicación de medidas de prevención y control de infecciones, la disponibilidad de equipos de protección personal, y la adecuada comunicación de riesgos a la población y a los profesionales de la salud Compartir en facebook Compartir en X Compartir en Whatsapp Noticias Relacionadas Destacada EN VIDEO Viernes 20 de noviembre 2026 20-11-2026 ¿Quién escucha al campo? 20-11-2026 A FONDO 19-11-2026 19 DE NOVIEMBRE 2026 19-11-2026 VER MÁS Más de Meganoticias Ver Más+
